Sports.title: Boulter blown away by Muchova at US Open
Sports.content:
Katie Boulter suffered a nightmare US Open exit in a punishing straight sets defeat to Karolina Muchova in under an hour at Flushing Meadows.

The British No 1 was broken in all seven of her service games in a chastening 6-1 6-0 defeat inside 58 minutes on Louis Armstrong Stadium.

Boulter traded breaks with Muchova at the start of the first set only for the 2026 Wimbledon finalist to pull clear and put on a clinic for her beleaguered opponent.

Boulter double faulted eight times and produced 22 unforced errors in a nightmare, error-strewn performance that left her hopes of progressing in tatters.

"Ultimately, it was a bad day at the office - times two," said Boulter. "I struggled with the conditions. I struggled with the roof, the noise, I let things distract me.

"I let it get to me. I'm not usually aware of everything going on. It made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. I have to deal with it better."

'All-round Muchova can do anything'

Sky Sports Tennis' Tim Henman:

"It was a tough day at the office for Boulter, and that is where Muchova deserves so much credit. She is such an all-round player. The focus was definitely on Muchova rather than what Boulter didn't do.

"The highlight reel from the match was outstanding. There were so many incredible shots and great rallies. She's got the variation, using the little short chip cross-court, following the ball in and knocking off volleys at the net. She can do anything.

"She has reached the French Open and Wimbledon finals and is great on hard courts. If she can stay healthy, she has the experience, mentality, confidence and belief to win one of these tournaments one day."

Image: Katie Boulter failed to hold serve once in a chastening US Open exit to Karolina Muchova

'Bad day at office for Boulter'

Sky Sports Tennis' Laura Robson:

"You've got to focus on the positives, and that was how well Muchova played.

"She showed us every trick in the book. She has so much in her repertoire. She's playing with a lot of confidence for something who hasn't played a lot since Wimbledon.

"Not a good day at the office for Boulter."

Muchova in mix for maiden Grand Slam?

Sky Sports Tennis' Jonathan Overend:

"Karolina Muchova has yet to win a Grand Slam in her career but played some exceptional tennis. On that evidence, she has brilliant potential in this tournament.

"A day to forget for Katie Boulter. She just wasn't there and lost her serve seven times out of seven. That does not give you a chance."

Jones overcomes rain delays to reach round two

Fran Jones got a win on the board for the Brits in her rain interrupted first-round match against Magda Linette despite a terrible start when play resumed.

Jones had won the first set when rain forced a halt on Tuesday night, with the 25-year-old qualifier fuming at having to sit shivering under a towel for 20 minutes while officials decided whether to take the players off court.

They returned to Court Five 17 hours later, only for the heavens to open again without a ball being hit, and when play did eventually resume Linette won the second set in 23 minutes.

But Jones hit back impressively in the third to win 6-4 1-6 6-3 and reach round two for the first time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Jacob Fearnley against Martin Etcheverry from the US Open.

Fearnley beaten by Etcheverry in four

Jacob Fearnley finally ran out of lives against Argentinian Tomas Martin Etcheverry.

The 25-year-old from Edinburgh had been beaten in qualifying, got a reprieve as a lucky loser, and was then 5-2 down in the fourth set against Martin Landaluce in round one before wriggling out of danger.

However, there will be no third chance for Fearnley after a 6-3 6-3 3-6 6-3 defeat.

Choinski's four-day first-round run brought to end

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Botic Van de Zandschulp vs Jan Choinski from the US Open

Britain's Jan Choinski made it to day four at the US Open, but was still a first-round casualty.

The towering German-born 30-year-old was beaten in straight sets by fellow beanpole, Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp.

Getting to the first Wednesday at Flushing Meadows is usually a notable achievement for a British player.

But Choinski's stay at the tournament was only extended after his first-round match was pushed back by the rain in New York.

A handful of players were already through to round three by the time Choinski took to the court, but he was soundly beaten in the big-serving battle 6-3 6-1 7-6 (5) in just under two hours.

Sports.title: Burnley battle back to hold Middlesbrough
Sports.content:
Ugo Raghouber's first goal for Burnley earned only their second point from their opening four Championship matches as they came from behind to draw 1-1 with Middlesbrough.

The French midfielder, signed from Lille in July, steered in a 54th-minute equaliser after taking on Zeki Amdouni's pass and being allowed to run unchallenged.

Aidan Morris had swept Middlesbrough into a 23rd-minute lead, scoring his first goal after more than two years at the club, with a stylish finish from 20 yards after being set up by fellow American Sebastian Berhalter.

For Burnley, the point was a lift after a testing week.

Head coach Nicky Hayen, whose side were beaten 4-1 at Norwich last Saturday, had to rethink his attack after last season's top scorer Zian Flemming was sold to Ipswich for £20million late on transfer deadline day, and decided to bring in Andreas Hountondji - out on loan for the past season and a half - in for his first Clarets start since November 2024.

Middlesbrough might have gone ahead as early as the third minute when leading scorer Will Lankshear sprinted on to a long pass from goalkeeper Radek Vitek that caught Burnley defender Hjalmar Ekdal ball watching, but could only bundle the ball wide as home stopper Max Weiss closed in on him.

Vitek had to be alert on the quarter-hour mark to push away a 20-yard shot from Dastan Satpayev, the Chelsea loanee making his home debut, who had created the opening after exchanging passes with Amdouni.

But it was Middlesbrough who struck first through Morris, one of four Americans now at the club. The delighted travelling support greeted the goal with the chants of 'USA, USA' that have become familiar at their games this season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Middlesbrough's Aidan Morris makes it 1-0 in their Championship clash with Burnley.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ugo Raghouber levels the score for Burnley in their clash with Middlesbrough.

The match had a physical edge to it, with Vitek angry after being caught by Satpayev as he chased a back pass, and Lankshear booked for treading on Hannibal Mejbri's foot.

Morris almost added a second Middlesbrough goal two minutes before half-time following a loose Connor Roberts clearance, striding forward and smashing a shot against Weiss' left-hand post from 25 yards.

Then Lankshear slipped past Anel Ahmedhodzic after Kyle Joseph flicked Adilson Malanda's pass into his path, and crossed low for Riley McGree to steer wide on the stretch from six yards.

But Burnley improved after half-time and drew level when Raghouber guided a shot into the corner from just outside the penalty area.

Then the impressive Satpayev ran at Alfie Jones and twisted inside the Middlesbrough centre-back, his sliding shot being stopped by the trailing leg of the wrongfooted Vitek.

Substitute Aaron Ramsey fired just wide with 12 minutes left as Burnley chased a winner, but they had to settle for a point.

The managers

Burnley's Nicky Hayen:

"We started with good intentions in the first 10 minutes. But then they scored the goal and then there was a certain fear in the team.

"We were dropping back. We were not putting pressure in the right way. That's something we changed in the second half.

"Then you see that we play with a lot more courage and then we felt after that goal with the support of the fans that you can change that game.

"But I have to be fair also, physically we're not there yet at the moment because we have also new signings who didn't have a proper pre-season, who didn't play a lot of friendly games."

Middlesbrough's Kim Hellberg:

"We were the better team from my point of view and controlled things, playing good football. We created a lot of chances, especially in the first half, and kept them to very few.

"They had a spell in the second half, maybe 15 minutes, where they were quite strong but didn't create so many chances.

"But sometimes we were not good enough with the ball, and Burnley got the crowd with them.

"Otherwise, I think it was a very good performance. We would have wanted three points, but we had to settle for one.

"We're still getting there with a lot of players coming back and we're building them up, which means we will just get better. But I think this was a big step forward in terms of how we want to look as a football side.

"I think this, in general, was one of our best performances this season in terms of how we looked against very strong opponents."

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: Charlton hit back to hold West Brom
Sports.content:
Charlton's 100 per cent record was brought to and end but they remain unbeaten as Tyreece Campbell's second-half strike earned a 1-1 draw against West Brom.

Nathan Jones' side were looking to continue their blistering start to the campaign - but spent the majority of the game on the back foot against the Baggies.

They frustrated the home side who finally broke the deadlock with a thunderous Callum Styles strike just before the hour mark.

But having soaked up waves of pressure - Campbell fired home from close range after 69 minutes to earn a point for his side.

It was Albion who had the upper hand over the high flying Addicks in the opening 20 minutes at The Hawthorns.

Felix Horn Myhre headed over after just two minutes before Callum Styles tried his luck from range.

Ousmane Diakite saw a shot deflected wide after good work from lively full debutant Kareem Tunde, who was causing problems for the visitors on the right flank.

He pulled a shot wide from distance on the 20-minute mark, while Isaac Price tested Charlton shot stopper Arthur Okonkwo, with Albion dominating possession.

But despite having more of the ball and a handful of half chances - the Baggies were struggling to turn their territory into clear-cut opportunities against a resilient Charlton back line.

The second period began in much the same fashion as Price saw an effort flash wide just seconds after the restart - with Albion flying back out of the blocks.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Callum Styles has broken the deadlock for West Brom against Charlton delightful half-volley.

Albion had Charlton camped in their own quarter, but again they were holding firm. It felt like the Baggies were going to need something special to break the Addicks' rearguard, and so it proved after 59 minutes.

After half-time substitute Rabby Nzingoula had drawn a top save out of Okonkwo, Styles ended a 16-month wait for a goal as he rifled home from 18 yards out, after Charlton failed to clear a Price corner.

It was exactly what Albion deserved but having dominated possession and restricted Charlton to nothing by way of chances - Jones' side levelled 10 minutes later with their first shot on target.

They countered down the left and Miles Leaburn headed substitute Ivan Mesik's cross into the path of Campbell - who fired home through a crowd of bodies to land Albion with a sucker punch.

Up to that point Charlton had hardly troubled the home side - but they somehow found themselves on level terms.

After the goal sparked a spell of pressure from the visitors, it was Albion who were again back on the front foot heading into the final throes of the game.

But they could not find an equaliser and were left to settle for a frustrating point.

The managers

West Brom's James Morrison:

"I'm frustrated we didn't win the game to be honest. We were really good in the first half and lacked that last little bit.

"At half time it was a case of we have got them where we want them, we're tiring them out and we just need to kick it up a level.

"We did that and they have one opportunity where they get into the box and it ends up in our goal.

"When we are dominant and they are not getting a kick, we need to not let them get in and around the box, or stop the cross.

"They are good at what they do, and proved that by picking up the results they have, but we have to be better around the box.

"But in a short period of time we have come a long way, especially having brought in a lot of new signings who are finding their feet, so that is positive."

Charlton's Nathan Jones:

"We are on that trajectory with what we did at Luton during my two spells there.

"We built a team to go through the leagues, I went and then came back and built a team that was on the brink of promotion and got promoted.

"We are on that trajectory, after four games we are in a good place, and let's not mess about, we are favourites to go down.

"Not one of the favourites, we are the favourites and people are saying they can't sustain it, but that is fine.

"We gave the ball away too much at times in the first half and were not brave enough.

"After they scored and we made subs, we were much better and got back into it. It's optimistic to say we should have gone on to win it, but we did finish strongly and it is a great point."

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: Walsh winner helps send Chelsea through in Women’s Champions League
Sports.content:
Chelsea booked their spot in the Women's Champions League league phase after a 1-0 win over Real Sociedad in the second leg of their third qualifying round tie.

The Blues sealed a 6-2 aggregate victory during a lacklustre match in Spain, which saw Keira Walsh score the only goal of the game in the 54th minute.

The England midfielder's strike subsequently secured Chelsea's place in Friday's draw for the league phase of the competition.

Blues boss Sonia Bompastor made four changes to the side that won 5-2 in London last week, with Lucy Bronze, Kadiesha Buchanan, Lexi Potter and Wieke Kaptein all starting.

Ellie Carpenter caused problems in the early stages of the first half by sending a series of teasing crosses into the box.

Lauren James blasted the ball past the post and Walsh latched onto another brilliant cross from Carpenter, but Julia Arrula easily saved before being called into action to deny Carpenter.

With the score goalless at half-time, Giulia Dragoni was introduced after the break to make her Chelsea debut.

Aggie Beever-Jones had the best chance of the game 53 minutes in after being played through by Carpenter and her strike was palmed away by Arrula.

However, from the resulting corner Chelsea suddenly opened the scoring from a short routine which reached Walsh outside the box and the midfielder curled the ball home.

Hannah Hampton pushed Ainhoa Marin's strike behind for a corner as Sociedad enjoyed a brief threatening spell.

Nelly Las dragged a shot wide for Chelsea, who comfortably navigated the closing stages of the match to reach the league phase.

Bompastor 'excited' to advance

Chelsea boss Sonia Bompastor speaking to the club's official website:

"I'm pleased with the result. We kept a clean sheet, which is always important, and when you do that, you always have a bigger chance to win games.

"I'm glad we could rotate the team with the starting 11, but also the players who came in.

"I think today we gave some really good opportunities to the young players to come and experience a Champions League game, so when you have the opportunity to do that, I think it's always something really positive.

"I'm happy and really excited now to be in the Champions League this season. The goal was for us to qualify, which is what we have done.

"People will probably think when you are Chelsea, it's easy to do, but we played against a really strong team in Real Sociedad.

"Over the two legs, they showed some really good quality, and I think these two games are a really good preparation for us to come into the season in the league."

Sports.title: Wrexham earn first win of the season at Millwall
Sports.content:
Wrexham got their first win of the Championship season in style as Millwall were swept aside 3-0 at the New Den.

Alex Neil's home side were coming off the back of a chastening 5-1 thrashing by Southampton on Saturday and their formerly steadfast defence suffered another horror show as their hopes of repeating last season's promotion push were dealt a blow.

After starting with two clean sheets in victories over Bristol City and Norwich, it is now eight goals conceded in two games after Wrexham put them to the sword with some clinical finishing.

Defender Zak Sturge was unfortunate in turning Issa Kabore's effort past his own goalkeeper in the first half, but there was nothing lucky about the goals scored by Phil Parkinson's side after the break as Kieffer Moore and Jacques Ekomie provided excellent finishes to hoist the visitors into the top half of the table.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kieffer Moore doubles Wrexham's lead against Millwall.

It means the Welsh side finally got their campaign going after drawing with Cardiff and Watford before losing at home to Birmingham.

They were better team throughout. Mark Sykes drilled an effort narrowly wide of the post for Millwall after 11 minutes, the only time they truly threatened.

At the other end, Max Cleworth's header from a deep Matty James free-kick sailed harmlessly wide, as neither side offered much in the opening 25 minutes.

There was an element of fortune about the opening goal in the 28th minute. Moore played a through ball to send Kabore clear inside the area. His strike hit Sturge and spun out of the reach of goalkeeper Max Crocombe to hand the visitors the lead.

Lyndon Dykes fired wide on the half-volley in stoppage time at the end of a first half in which the home side carried little threat and rarely troubled Anthony Patterson.

Lewis O'Brien was guilty of a dreadful miss at the start of the second half, leaning back and scooping the ball over the crossbar after being played in eight yards out by Moore.

But Wrexham would not have long to wait for their second goal and it arrived a minute later. Moore picked up the ball in space 20 yards out and was given time to move it on to his right foot, take aim and send a perfectly placed drive into the bottom corner.

The game was over as a contest with just over 20 minutes to go. Substitute Danny Imray got free down the right and pulled the back to near the penalty spot where Ekomie was waiting, evading the attentions of Jake Cooper to sweep a finish into the corner and wrap up the win, as home supporters began to stream out of the stadium.

The managers

Millwall's Alex Neil:

"A disappointing night at the office. We had to change our shape because of a lack of wide players.

"I didn't think it was a great game of football. In the first half I thought the game was in the balance. I thought we gave as good as we got.

"The start of the second half it was relatively in the balance again. I thought it changed when we lost Casper. He was very influential in the game."

Wrexham's Phil Parkinson:

"I am pleased to get the first win of the season. I felt it was deserved. I am pleased with the response after getting beaten by Birmingham.

"In reality we probably should have had more points than we've got, but you've got to respond and I felt like we did.

"Coming to Millwall is one of the hardest grounds to come to. It's about quietening the crowd and trying to get an element of control in the game.

"But also dealing with the physicality. It was a huge team Neil picked. We had to deal with that. I felt we were very comfortable in that.

"As the game went on we got better and better in terms of dictating the game with the ball."

Sports.title: Premier League money has lost all meaning amid chaotic spectacle of excess | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
There was a research study a few years back into a key period in the life of the TV show Location, Location, Location. You know the one. Half an hour of mid-morning drift. Hosted by two people whose common quality is they both look as if the minced essence of Wellington boots, the Volvo XC40 and the phrase “picky bits” has been reconstituted into human shapes, then sent out to judge people for buying houses.

The big reveal was always the bit where they came back a year later and saw how much the value had shifted. Because all conversations about houses are, in the end, an excuse to talk about money. Oh wow, it’s gone up by £20,000. You are good. Oh no, you’re now bankrupt and your flat looks like a hostage cell with fairy lights. Unlucky. You are bad.

What the study found was that prices basically always increased. Ripping out the stairs, living in a tent in the garden, arguing about what to do with the two-and-a-halfth bedroom – all of this was irrelevant. These were the boom times of the early 2000s, UK housing recast as a global money trap, an endlessly whirling laundromat, a bricks and mortar central bank bond.

These people could have bought their run-down three-bed, left it empty and done absolutely nothing for two years. The price would have still gone up. That drama about exactly which shade of Anaconda Breath Morgue And Cakebread Mega-Gloss to use in the underfloor wine cave? Just doesn’t matter. Buy the soil. Shut the door. Let money do its thing.

And yes, this is a way of talking about the 2026 summer transfer window, and the way in which everyone has basically now been Chelsea-ed. Think back four years to the start of the age of Clearlake, the first post-Roman spree. At that time it seemed impossible there could be a profitable outcome. Chelsea were out there buying the vintage copper-plate statement bidet. Chelsea were digging out a third sub-basement. Who will redeem this expense? Who will provide a similarly deranged response to such overinvestment?

Well, it turns out the market will do this for you. If you’d predicted then that Chelsea would miss out on the Champions League and go through five permanent managers, but still make a profit from selling Enzo Fernández, would anyone have believed it?

View image in fullscreen Todd Boehly has overseen big changes on and off the pitch during his time at Chelsea. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Or that Mykhailo Mudryk could run around briefly like a deranged hamster, get banned for failing a drugs test and still become a potential growth asset? This is pre-subprime crash energy. Yes, you can install a solar-powered mega-wetroom that fires sourdough breadsticks directly into your eyes. Whatever. Ownership is all. Money will take care of you.

There are still levels to this. The one Chelsea thing to shift in the window is that the curtain has now been drawn on those initial eight months, the period where Todd Boehly became the world’s worst director of football, a director of football who basically didn’t know what football was.

That period has now been safely capped off. Only two players remain. Rough out the numbers and Chelsea spent something like £200m in fees, wages, leaks and cuts, with only Malo Gusto and Wesley Fofana to show for it. No real damage. Money comes, money goes. We roll on.

This is the lesson of the latest summer transfer window. Right now it doesn’t really matter what you do in the Premier League. Just being in it is the thing. With one caveat, which is that nobody actually knows what’s happening here. We can marvel at a record window. We can see the biggest spenders are Manchester City on £457.5m, the lowest Crystal Palace on about £50m, the highest net Liverpool on £216.8m. We can pore over Aston Villa buying the bones of a new squad for £56.7m net gain.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool’s £123m signing Bradley Barcola checks out Anfield. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

But we can’t know what it means, at least not financially. This is part of the design of money on this scale. As the then Federal Reserve chair Alan Greenspan put it in a famous speech on the mysteries of big money: “How do we know when irrational exuberance has unduly escalated asset values, which then become subject to unexpected and prolonged contractions?”

Nobody knew what this meant then. Nobody knows what it means now. “Irrational exuberance” is a good phrase, one Greenspan later said came to him in the bath. It was designed to convey the essential point: opacity, vagueness, invisible flows. If not for those actually riding the tide, because someone is always making money. Someone out there actively wants the Premier League’s financial chaos, and is benefiting from it gloriously.

Otherwise, reading the runes is just a matter of guesswork. Money moves between networked entities. Everyone inside wins. Everyone outside pays for it. But still, this feels new, if only in its extremity.

This was captured by the weirdness of Sky Sports’ transfer deadline programme on Tuesday. At one point a man appeared strumming a guitar, smiling as if he had just filleted a litter of kittens in his basement, and sang a Bradley Barcola Liverpool song to the tune of Don’t Dream It’s Over, like this is all just normal and fine.

Later there was a golden period at about 5.30pm where every deal just seemed wrong and impossible, a fever dream after an over-ripe seafood risotto. Aston Villa have paid £47m for an 18-year-old winger. Gabriel Jesus is going to Barcelona. Jack Grealish is having a medical at Everton, an event that seems to prove the non-linear nature of time, a medical that is always happening, never not happening, a constant time-space event.

View image in fullscreen Gabriel Jesus at his Barcelona unveiling. Photograph: Javier Borrego/AFP7/Shutterstock

Meanwhile two private jets are on the tarmac in Lyon as three clubs try to sign Malick Fofana. “We STILL don’t know what Malick Fofana is thinking,” the man with the microphone concluded, mournfully, and this seemed profoundly true and on point. We don’t. Does Malick Fofana even know this? If so, how can he? Nobody else has a clue what’s going on.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is worth trying to list the best deals. Harry Wilson on a free can only be good. Djed Spence to Inter is great. Forza, Djed. Barcola to Liverpool for £123m is lots of money, but he’s really young and knows how to score once he’s settled.

Newcastle seem to have had a good window, racking up a list of signings that scream inside knowledge and good data, and chime with Matthias Jaissle’s mercurial vibe. Manchester City’s signings have to be good. There’s so many of them, and they’re all excellent players. That midfield is surely just too big to fail.

Arsenal will also be fine, despite not signing a 1950s-style hotshot goal ace with dynamite in his boots and the brain of a hungry magpie. Yes, they’ve lost two, maybe three attackers. But these are Jesus and probably Gabriel Martinelli, meat in the room, plus Leandro Trossard, replaced by basically the same guy. Arsenal won the league with Kai Havertz, Martin Ødegaard, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze short of their ceiling. If you can’t score enough to win with that lot then it’s really not the players.

Manchester United’s window looks quite good, but also scattergun. Carlos Baleba may be great, or may wander around like a lost child in Lidl before being loaned to Monaco. Tottenham have mined the club’s DNA, gone back to their spiritual roots, and signed players who will be really good for four games, then disappear and get tattoos.

Meanwhile Everton have swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. What does it mean? Can you even visualise this as an event? Beto and Iliman Ndiaye have gone, taking away a third of last season’s league goals. Welcome, Everton fans, to the fully immersive Thierno Barry multiverse.

Otherwise the main takeaway is the meaninglessness of big football money. Most notably the size of the most basic fees. Little wonder there is a sense of alienation from familiar notions of team building, blocks in place, footballers as recognisable avatars of graft and cultural chemistry. These are stocks, talent units, a flow of resources.

View image in fullscreen Caleb Yirenkyi challenges Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly on his Coventry debut, having joined for £23m this summer. Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

Remember the Peter Odemwingie deadline day fiasco, where Odemwingie sat fuming in his car while the world was sucked into this human drama? That whole thing was about the unbridgeable leap from £2m to £3m. Coventry have just signed Caleb Yirenkyi from Nordsjælland for £23m. Does “Caleb Yirenkyi” really exist? Are you sure?

Who pays in the end for this circulation of funds? You, for starters. There is no such thing as football money. It’s all TV rights, state propaganda funds and hard private investment from the kind of people who really don’t give without taking back in the end.

On one level books are being balanced, accounting rules satisfied, clubs swapping assets at fees driven in part by regulatory requirements. More obscurely Boehly once talked about a rush of cash being diverted football’s way as a sub-avalanche from quantitative easing in the US, because money just has to go somewhere. No, me neither.

All that seems certain is money is being pushed around the board. And that it feels wildly abstract. The window was thrilling, its possibilities endless, a shot of blood for the new season. Beyond this, big football and big finance are playing their own game, in a way that goes beyond the human scale and into a world of pure money. The message below the headlines is clear. This thing belongs to them. Your job, human consumer unit, is simply to look at it and have feelings.

Sports.title: Deadline-day shambles leaves Everton and David Moyes fighting the odds again
Sports.content:
To be placed in the same bracket as owners whose lack of ambition, lack of resources and/or incompetence has contributed to the longest trophy drought in Everton’s history, particularly 20 months into a reign that has accompanied the move to a glittering new stadium and the clearing of onerous debt, should be cause for considerable discomfort and embarrassment at The Friedkin Group (TFG) on Wednesday. The slight on Everton’s owner is neither unkind nor unfair. At least Farhad Moshiri had a go before the taps were turned off.

TFG may have restored financial stability to Everton after the near-ruinous chaos of Moshiri’s final years and his attempts to sell to 777 Partners but its reputation as “winners” – as the club’s chief executive, Angus Kinnear, labelled his American employers – has been shredded in the space of four days. The description always appeared generous given its approach to the summer transfer window, part two of Everton’s strategic rebuild according to Kinnear. But from accepting Nottingham Forest’s £35m bid for Harrison Armstrong on Saturday morning to Folarin Balogun walking away from a £40m move from Monaco on Tuesday night, and more in between, TFG has positioned itself as just another Everton owner unable or unwilling to realise the club’s potential and to give an expectant fanbase grounds for optimism.

Evertonians hoped for an overdue departure when TFG acquired the club in December 2024 and proceeded to refinance damaging loans and the long-term repayment costs of Hill Dickinson Stadium. The shambles of deadline day, however, was all too familiar and has caused serious damage to its standing among supporters.

David Moyes kept his counsel throughout pre-season as Everton spent £16.5m on Hayden Hackney, rising to £25m for last season’s Championship player of the year, £18m on each of Merlin Röhl and Tyrique George, who he had on loan last season, £7m on Christian Nørgaard and swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. The most Everton paid up front for a player all summer would prove to be £18m.

When Moyes did eventually speak in public it was to stress, repeatedly, the need for Everton to sign more players, more quality and to keep their best talents. At the end of last season he had 22 outfield players at his disposal. At the start of deadline day he had 20 outfield players. By the end of transfer deadline day he had 18.

That total includes one striker, Thierno Barry, no back-up for either full-back and, strictly speaking given that Ainsley Maitland-Niles did not start out in the position, no natural right-back. Everton sold their most creative asset, Iliman Ndiaye, to Manchester City in a below-market price £65m deal despite the Senegal international having three years on his contract. They sold Beto, their only striking alternative to Barry, before securing a replacement and were left desperately scrambling around for one when Balogun’s medical went awry.

View image in fullscreen Everton have sold Iliman Ndiaye (left) and brought in Merlin Röhl (right) for £18m in the summer transfer window. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

Manchester United said no to a loan offer for Joshua Zirkzee that arrived a few hours before the deadline. Tammy Abraham said no to leaving Aston Villa. Finally Balogun, having arrived later than scheduled for his medical and seen Everton renegotiate the terms of his fee with Monaco, compounded the chaos by also saying no despite signing a deal sheet shortly before 11pm. Barry looked out of his depth for much of his debut season in the Premier League. Now he is the precious commodity that Everton cannot afford to lose.

Kinnear, perhaps in response to Moyes raising concerns over Everton’s business for the first time, gave several local interviews two weeks ago that painted a rosy picture of the club’s finances, transfer strategy and ambition. Subsequent events have cost him credibility on every count. The chief executive also got his manager’s back up by claiming TFG regarded not qualifying for Europe last season as “a failure” and that the squad is better placed to sustain a European challenge while striving to end Everton’s 31-year wait for a trophy.

Moyes’s team face-planted during last season’s run-in, failing to win any of their last seven games when Europe was in reach. He has been challenged to go further with fewer resources. An added annoyance for Moyes and supporters is that Everton have started this season brightly, only to be surrounded by problems entirely of the hierarchy’s making.

It was Kinnear who implemented a new “senior leadership team” at Everton and the move away from a director of football model. The team consists of the technical director, Nick Cox, director of scouting and recruitment, James Smith, director of football strategy and analytics, Chris Howarth and head of player trading, Nick Hammond. Moyes is also part of the leadership team, although he has appeared to be on a different page this summer. There has been sensible, cost-effective recruitment for Hackney, Röhl and Johnson but the end to the window invites criticism of the leadership team’s effectiveness and expertise. It resembles a case of too many chiefs and no clear direction, especially given some of the targets Everton went for in the final days.

View image in fullscreen Harrison Armstrong is Everton’s first academy prospect to establish himself in the first team since Anthony Gordon. Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty Images

The collapse of the Balogun deal has caused turmoil at Everton but a player getting cold feet over a move or a medical jeopardising a deal can happen. It is events under Everton’s control, and decisions they have taken, that are of greater concern. TFG’s decision to accept Forest’s offer for Armstrong, the first academy prospect to graduate through the ranks and establish himself since Anthony Gordon six years ago, was the first indication that Everton were struggling to meet the new squad cost ratios. So much for a new financial era at Hill Dickinson.

TFG merits some credit for listening to supporters over the proposed sale of Armstrong and pulling the plug. To then consider selling Ndiaye to Tottenham for £60m and spending £35m on Richarlison, however, was another alarming sign.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Everton have been looking for a right-back since Moyes returned to the club in January 2025, and needed one before then. Moyes wanted Guéla Doué from Strasbourg but the 23-year-old was deemed too expensive. Doué joined Bayer Leverkusen on deadline day for £25.7m. At least five alternatives were explored before Everton, their £9m deal for Fulham’s Kenny Tete having fallen through, signed Maitland-Niles as the £4.3m answer to one glaring problem.

A bigger weakness lay up front. No Premier League club of serious intent would enter a second season with their striking options limited to Beto and Barry. An upgrade was essential. Instead, Everton downgraded. So much for the leadership team’s vision and the owner’s ambition.

Everton are the lowest net spenders in the Premier League over the past five years and, more by accident than design, ended this summer making a net profit of £25m on transfers. TFG committed £78m on signings in a summer where, by the calculations of the football finance expert Kieran Maguire, the average spend per Premier League club was £181m. Everton’s outlay does not include the significant cost of re-signing Jack Grealish on loan.

TFG’s frugal spending and efficiency drive – redundancies were made behind the scenes at Everton this summer – has fuelled talk of Dan Friedkin and co looking to sell the club. However, the owners have allocated £40m to cover the compensation payable to Burnley should Everton fail in their appeal against the outcome of a profitability and sustainability breach case, and are investing almost £14m in infrastructure projects at Hill Dickinson, Goodison Park and Finch Farm training ground.

What is certain is the anger TFG would face if they attended Sunday’s home game against Manchester United. Dan Friedkin has yet to attend a match at Hill Dickinson, where some season ticket prices were increased by up to 10% this season.

The Everton fans’ forum and Everton fan advisory board issued statements on Wednesday criticising the club’s amateurish, unambitious approach to the transfer window. The 1878s, the group of volunteers responsible for the impressive tifos and banners at the stadium, has withdrawn its support for the foreseeable future. “We do not feel that our fanbase’s ambitions and the club’s ambitions align right now – what happened yesterday has proved that even more,” the group said.

It looks a long road back to acceptance for TFG, Kinnear and Everton’s senior leadership team.

Sports.title: Walsh caps Champions League progress for Chelsea despite Real Sociedad grind
Sports.content:
Chelsea ensured there will be three Women’s Super League teams in the league phase of the Champions League as Keira Walsh’s second-half strike against Real Sociedad extended their three-goal margin from the first leg of the third-round qualifier.

The 5-2 win against the Spanish side in Chelsea’s first game at Wimbledon’s Cherry Red Records stadium gave Sonia Bompastor’s side a commanding lead in the tie, after a rusty start had forced them to come from a goal down. It wasn’t a particularly pretty performance, though, and that continued into the second leg against La Real, who will now drop into the Europa League.

Bompastor, who returned to the dugout after serving a one-match ban in the reverse game, made four changes for the trip to San Sebastián, probably with one eye on the WSL opener on Saturday against Aston Villa. The scorer of Chelsea’s second last week, Veerle Buurman, was named on the bench, alongside Katie McCabe, Sjoeke Nüsken and Alyssa Thompson. Among those to come in was the 20-year-old midfielder Lexi Potter, who scored in her first league start for Chelsea, a 2-1 win against Brighton, in March.

There were only two changes for the home team. The change that mattered most, though, was the one that had taken place in the ­dugout. In between these two critical ­Champions League qualifying games, Arturo Ruiz, the Real Sociedad ­manager, exited and was unveiled as the new Brighton manager following the shock departure of Dario Vidosic. If Vidosic’s exit had been a surprise, Brighton poaching Ruiz was a bigger one. Gorka Álvarez, who left Real Sociedad in 2025 following three seasons managing the reserves and a year as an assistant to SD Eibar’s women’s team, was hurriedly brought in to lead them in their Liga F opener against Logroño on Saturday, a 2-0 loss, and the second leg against Chelsea.

It was a mountain of a task ­facing the 40-year-old and, in many respects, a bit of a free hit, with few expecting Real Sociedad to come close to overturning a three-goal ­deficit against European heavyweights.

However, setting the tone for his tenure and building confidence was important. La Real did well against the visitors, holding Bompastor’s side at bay until Walsh swept in from a corner in the 54th minute to kill any outlandish hopes there may have been of a comeback.

Until then, the London side ­struggled to create clear chances with La Real mirroring their well-organised display in the first half of the first leg.

Ellie Carpenter, playing further forward, ahead of Lucy Bronze on the right, was Chelsea’s best outlet but they couldn’t capitalise on her balls into the middle. Walsh’s side-footed effort in the first half was weak and easy for the goalkeeper Julia Arrula. Aggie Beever-Jones had a good chance to break the deadlock moments before Walsh’s goal but the forward’s strike was too central and Arrula made an easy save.

The perfectionist that Bompastor is, she will be unhappy with the nature of the two games, but the reality is that reaching the league phase, for a team desperately wanting European glory, was what mattered most. In the end the result was comfortable, even if the performance wasn’t, and Chelsea had the chance to give debuts off the bench to their new signings Nelly Las and Giulia Dragoni, and minutes to the talented 17-year-old Chloe Sarwie.

They will have also benefited from valuable competitive minutes before they kickstart their WSL campaign by hosting Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Bompastor said: “Today we gave some really good opportunities to the young players to come and experience a Champions League game, so when you have the opportunity to do that, I think it’s always something really positive. I’m happy and really excited now to be in the Champions League this season. The goal was for us to qualify, which is what we have done.”

Sports.title: Championship roundup: Wrexham rout Millwall to seal first league victory
Sports.content:
Wrexham powered to their first Championship win this season with a ruthless 3-0 rout of injury-plagued Millwall on Wednesday.

The Welsh side had drawn with Cardiff and Watford before losing at home to Birmingham prior to this match. But they bounced back in emphatic fashion in south London to kickstart their bid for promotion to the Premier League after narrowly missing out on the playoffs last term.

The Millwall defender Zak Sturge deflected Issa Kaboré’s cross into his own net for a first-half own goal. Wrexham’s striker Kieffer Moore lashed in the second from 20 yards soon after half-time and Jacques Ekomié wrapped up the victory with a close-range finish.

After starting with two clean sheets in victories over Bristol City and Norwich, it is now eight goals conceded in two games for Millwall, who were thrashed 5-1 by Southampton on Saturday. Millwall lost their striker Josh Coburn and midfielder Casper De Norre to injuries during the game as their fitness woes mounted 24 hours after Nigeria winger Femi Azeez joined Brighton for £15m.

Rumarn Burrell scored both goals as QPR beat Cardiff 2-1 at Loftus Road to extend their impressive start to the season.

Perry Ng pulled a goal back for Cardiff but it was not enough to stop Julien Stéphan’s second-placed side from moving to 10 points from their opening four matches.

Ugo Raghouber’s first goal for Burnley earned them only their second point from four matches as they came from behind to draw 1-1 with Middlesbrough at Turf Moor.

The French midfielder, signed from Lille in July, steered in a 54th-minute equaliser from Zeki Amdouni’s pass. Aidan Morris had swept Middlesbrough into a 23rd-minute lead, scoring his first goal after more than two years at the club, with a stylish finish from 20 yards.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Relegated from the Premier League last season, Burnley are in a testing period that included a 4-1 loss at Norwich last Saturday and the sale of the Dutch forward Zian Flemming to Ipswich on transfer deadline day.

Charlton lost their 100% record but remain unbeaten after Tyreece Campbell’s second-half strike secured a 1-1 draw at West Brom. Nathan Jones’s side trailed to a thunderous Callum Styles strike just before the hour mark, before Campbell fired home from close-range on 69 minutes.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 13: Tottenham Hotspur
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 5th (NB: this is not necessarily Suzanne Wracks’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 5th

Prospects

Last season Tottenham matched their best Women’s Super League season with a fifth-place finish. However, they ended with four points more than in 2021-22 and closed the gap on fourth from 10 points to four. That is all the more impressive given their 11th place the preceding season.

It’s fair to say then that Martin Ho has rejuvenated the side. That has come with increased support from the wider club. This summer their recruitment strategy has turned heads with top young talents such as the club-record signing Alice Sombath and the goalkeeper Selma Panengstuen added alongside experienced WSL performers such as Shekiera Martinez and Kirsty Hanson. The club secured their top five targets early in the window too, to give the team as full a pre-season together as possible.

They secured three friendly wins, against Granada and Birmingham, which sandwiched a 2-1 defeat against Real Madrid, and Bristol City. Their 5-0 defeat of Bristol City was particularly pleasing for Ho, who said: “As I’ve said to the players, we have a good enough squad with depth in it that we can really compete.” The manager is working his players hard, with many speaking about the intensity of training. Martinez said: “The intensity is really high, the training has been really tough, so I can’t wait until the league starts.” Players are enjoying the burn, though, because they have bought into Ho’s vision for the way the team should play and his and the club’s ambitions for the short, medium and long term. How well Tottenham will do when other teams are also investing heavily is hard to predict, but many regard Spurs as the dark horses who could frustrate the top teams and big-spending London City Lionesses.

Off-field picture

Backing for the women’s team has ramped up a gear from top to bottom after the departure of the former chair Daniel Levy. The arrival of Vinai Venkatesham as chief executive in April 2025 has probably played a part, given his vocal and active backing of the Arsenal women’s team while he was at Tottenham’s rivals. There has been some change this summer, with Andy Rogers departing as managing director of the women’s team after 24 years at the club in various roles. Financially, the club have increased their investment in the women’s team, with turnover up from £3.39m in 2023-24 to £4.41m in the year ending June 2025. Their next accounts will probably show further investment. In July the club were dealt a blow after a high-court decision to block plans for a new women’s and girls’ football academy in Whitewebbs Park.

The manager

Ho was patient in his approach to the squad he inherited last summer, keen to not write anyone off despite their flirtation with relegation. Toko Koga and Cathinka Tandberg were the only additions and Ho gave everyone a chance to show what they could do when playing the way he wanted. That earned him a lot of loyalty and respect and his careful and thoughtful approach to squad development alongside his tactical outlook have made him a key factor when players choose to join. That is reflected in the number of his former players who have signed up to work with him again, including Signe Gaupset in January and Hanson and Panengstuen this summer. Repeating or building on his debut season will be tricky with other teams also investing ambitiously, but Ho seems very capable of doing either.

Star signing

Sombath’s big fee will have made a lot of people very excited but the recruitment of Hanson is perhaps the shrewdest of the signings. The understated 28-year-old joined from Aston Villa having finished as the third-highest goalscorer in the WSL last season. Hanson, one goal behind Alessia Russo and nine behind the Golden Boot winner, Khadija Shaw, was the highest-scoring midfielder in the league. She is an exciting addition to Spurs’ spine, is hugely consistent and is in her prime.

View image in fullscreen The Scotland international Kirsty Hanson has joined Tottenham and signed a long-term contract. Photograph: Ali Painter/WSL/Getty Images

Stat attack

Tottenham had a very weird 2025-26 in front of goal. Excluding penalties, they scored 1.55 times more than expected. They were close to hitting par. Yet they were up by 8.12 goals against xG in open play but down by 6.57 on set pieces. Their per-game average for the latter (0.30) was worse than any men’s side in Europe’s big five leagues. Making more of their set plays could have a huge impact.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Set for a breakthrough

There are big expectations around Sombath. The 22-year-old centre-back has joined from the eight-time European champions Lyonnes, having been ushered into the senior set-up there by the now Chelsea manager, Sonia Bompastor. Sombath won a Champions League title and five league titles with the French club and has learned her trade under the tutelage of the influential centre-backs Wendie Renard and Griedge Mbock. She is able to play at right-back or centre-back and featured in each of France’s four games at the 2025 European Championship after getting her first cap in November 2024.

What they say

“I’m training now with her and I think she’s so underrated. It’s better when people call you underrated and all your teammates know how good you are. I think Drew is really good. So, she really surprised me. ‘Surprised me’ sounds bad, but it’s more just that now I’m training with her every day, I’m like: ‘Wow’” – Victoria Pelova on the new captain, Drew Spence

Where are they playing their home games?

Spurs will continue at Leyton Orient’s Brisbane Road, with select showpiece fixtures at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The first of those will be on 25 October when they host Arsenal, and Manchester United will be welcomed to the main stadium in February. In the year ending June 2025, matchday revenue was down from £513,00 to £433,000. There will be a desire to get more people watching to help offset some of the increased investment. The football is delivering for fans who go or tune in so the club need to find a way to capitalise on that.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Durán inspires Celtic to convincing victory after Dalglish ovation
Sports.content:
The Celtic striker Camilo Durán inspired the Scottish champions’ 3-0 win over Aberdeen, while Rangers snatched a 2-1 victory against Falkirk on Wednesday.

Durán has scored six goals in five matches for Martin O’Neill’s side after his latest eye-catching contribution at Parkhead. The Colombian netted in the 14th minute with the latest in his series of spectacular strikes since joining from Qarabag in the close-season. Durán collected Benjamin Nygren’s pass and unleashed a long-range drive that cannoned in off the crossbar.

O’Neill may find it difficult to put the winger back on the flanks when the striker Kasper Høgh recovers from a thigh injury. Nygren and Yang Hyun-jun were also on target as Celtic killed off the game before the break.

Although they suffered a humiliating Champions League exit against Lask, Celtic have made a perfect start to their title defence with four successive wins. It was an emotional night in Glasgow as Kenny Dalglish was given a warm ovation on the pitch before the match. Dalglish launched his iconic career with Celtic before joining Liverpool in 1977. The 75-year-old revealed earlier this year that he was receiving treatment for cancer.

Celtic are two points clear of second-place St Mirren, whose 1-0 win at Kilmarnock – their first at Rugby Park for 13 years – was secured by Fraser Taylor’s maiden goal for the club in the third minute.

Lawrence Shankland’s double gave Rangers a dramatic win over Falkirk to ease the pressure on their manager, Derek McInnes. With McInnes serving the first of a two-match touchline ban (reduced from four matches) for comments made as Hearts manager last season, he watched from the stands as Shankland saved him from another chastening result.

View image in fullscreen Rangers’ captain, Lawrence Shankland, celebrates his second goal against Falkirk. Photograph: Kirk O’Rourke/Rangers FC/Shutterstock

Shankland, who scored from the spot in the 1-0 win at Aberdeen on Sunday, fired Rangers ahead with a fine strike in the seventh minute. Kosta Nedeljkovic, making his first Rangers start since signing on loan from Aston Villa, turned an Ethan Ross cross into his own net to give Falkirk an unexpected equaliser just before the break. But Scotland star Shankland, who signed from Hearts in the close-season, reduced Rangers’ anxiety when he curled in the winner after 79 minutes.
