Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.

"Obviously the nation was hurt massively, but in terms of the current group of players I don't think they're dwelling too much on that hurt.

"To be honest, we're just riding the wave of the confidence we've got as a group - which I think this young group deserves - from the last two games and we're looking forward to Thursday night and then see what comes after that.

"But to see how the nation is feeling now is incredible and we've got a duty to try and make them even happier."

Image: Troy Parrott's goals inspired Ireland to stunning wins over Portugal and Hungary that secured a play-off spot

Ireland are only in Prague because they backed up a scratchy Group F victory over Armenia with an unexpected 2-0 win against Portugal in Dublin before going to Hungary and coming out on top in a five-goal thriller in which Troy Parrott scored the decisive goal with the last kick of the game.

Coleman is one of only two players - 34-year-old Robbie Brady is the other - in the current squad to have been to a major tournament, and the experience they had in earning their trip to Euro 2016 in France could prove invaluable this time around.

Image: Coleman and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson are bidding to lead Ireland to World Cup qualification for the first time since 2002

Martin O'Neill's team reached the finals by beating Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1 on aggregate in a play-off after a hard-fought 1-1 draw in Zenica in the first leg.

Coleman said: "Maybe two years ago it would have been a lot for the young lads to take.

"But everyone now has stepped up and are prepared for what's to come and we absolutely, no doubt about it, understand it's going to be a tough game for us, but it's also going to be a tough game for them as well."

Head coach Hallgrimsson, who is without suspended defender Liam Scales and injured midfielder Josh Cullen, as ever exuded calm as he fulfilled his media duties on Wednesday morning, simply asking for more of the same from his players.

He said: "We all know by now why we got good results and good performances, and that's the key, not be over-ambitious tomorrow, stay on point, focus on why we are here and trying to improve that, not only this game, continuously."

Czech boss says Soucek still key player despite not being captain

Image: West Ham's Tomas Soucek is no longer captain of his country

Czech Republic boss Miroslav Koubek said "full-fat" Tomas Soucek remains a key player for his country despite being stripped of the captaincy.

The 31-year-old West Ham midfielder has been replaced as skipper by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci after being removed from his position amid the fall-out from the 2-1 defeat by the Faroe Islands in October.

However Koubek, who himself took over from Ivan Hasek as head coach in December, still counts Soucek among his most important players ahead of Thursday night's World Cup play-off semi-final against the Republic of Ireland in Prague.

He said: "Tomas Soucek is an outstanding player with a great career. He doesn't have the captain's armband at this moment for reasons you all know, but nothing changes.

"It does not mean he will lose his value. He is still a 'full-fat' player, if I can use these words."

Image: Miroslav Koubek's first game in charge of the Czech Republic is against Ireland

Soucek's removal as captain has prompted speculation in the Czech media that he could even lose his place in the team, although Koubek remained coy over his team selection.

The 74-year-old said: "I don't read the newspapers, so I don't know. You will see tomorrow."

Koubek's side will welcome Ireland to the Fortuna Arena, the home of domestic champions Slavia Prague, knowing they will have to find a way to stop in-from striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in his country's last two qualifiers against Portugal and Hungary to get them to the play-offs.

Asked about his analysis of Heimir Hallgrimsson's team, he said: "One thing I noticed: they put a lot heart into their game. Ireland will definitely be a very tough opponent.

"But we will have a similar mindset, it will be a hard match, definitely.

"As for Parrott, he is outstanding, he is doing great. He is very fit, we know how he works. We do have some information, so now it will all be about eliminating him in a smart way. We will just have to stop him."

Krejci, however, has little doubt that it will be he and his team-mates who ultimately fight it out with either Denmark of North Macedonia for a trip to the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

He said: "We will make it. We will reach our goal. We will qualify for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Jimmy Batten dead at 70: Tributes flood in for British champion boxer who was forced to retire with brain damage
Sports.content:
Jimmy Batten dead at 70: Tributes flood in for British champion boxer who was forced to retire with brain damage

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former British boxer Jimmy Batten has passed away at the age of 70.

The ex-British light-middleweight champion had been battling brain damage from his boxing career, as well as Parkinson's disease.

He made a name for himself in the 1970s and 1980s, and had his most famous fight in 1982 when he lost against Roberto Duran via unanimous decision. Many had expected him to lose early, having been stopped by Mario Maldonado in the first round just six months earlier, but a gutsy performance saw him take it all the way.

Batten was part of Terry Lawless's famous London gym having started boxing at the age of six, with the likes of John H Stracey, Maurice Hope and Charlie Magri hailing from the same place.

Stracey paid tribute to his friend on social media, posting: 'So sad to hear about my dear friend Jimmy Batten passing away.

'My great stablemate and sparring partner of many, many years… God bless you, my friend.'

Former British boxer Jimmy Batten (pictured) has passed away at the age of 70

Batten was famed for going the distance against Roberto Duran in his 1982 defeat

One fan, meanwhile, wrote on social media: 'More sad news. RIP Jimmy Batten. I knew he hadn't been well for a while but such terrible news, aged just 70. A GENUINE British boxing legend.'

Another shared: 'Rest well Jimmy', alongside praying emojis.

Batten's final fight was in 1983, when he was beaten by Prince Rodney to finish competing with a record of 40 wins and nine defeats.

Upon his retirement, Batten took up acting, but started to battle brain damage soon after his retirement and had to attend speech therapy to cope with the effects.

He also worked as a comedian and a doorman, and briefly as a boxing trainer, and spent time in prison after an altercation with three customers while a doorman.

He said of his career, via BoxingScene: 'Why would I change anything? I loved every minute of it. I'm just sad that I can't do it anymore.

'There's not many people who can say they were British champion and went the distance with Duran, is there?'

Sports.title: Time is running out for Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury: AJ is still yet to sign Battle of Britain deal, reveals Frank Warren
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has still not signed the contract, so the Battle of Britain against Tyson Fury remains in jeopardy.

Time is running out.

Promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by this weekend, says: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place. '

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Anthony Joshua (pictured) is still yet to sign the deal to fight Anthony Joshua, Frank Warren has revealed

Warren (right) said Tyson Fury (left) has signed and is already in training for a potential bout

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given 10 days to agree a deal on August 26 - seven days ago - with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Sports.title: Ex-British boxing champion Darren Barker shares heartfelt Ricky Hatton message as he sets off on epic 1,800-mile fundraising challenge
Sports.content:
Ex-British boxing champion Darren Barker shares heartfelt Ricky Hatton message as he sets off on epic 1,800-mile fundraising challenge

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Darren Barker has issued an emotional message about Ricky Hatton as he continues his inspiring 'The Longest Round' fundraising challenge, in memory of the boxing great.

Barker, former IBF world middleweight champion, set off from Edinburgh on Wednesday morning on a mega 1,800-mile endurance challenge to Morocco across land and sea.

The challenge sees him cycle from Edinburgh to Dover, swim the English channel (21 miles), cycle from Calais to Gibraltar before he ends off the adventure with an open-water swim across the Strait of Gibraltar into Morocco (nine miles).

The challenge will push Barker to the absolute limits, testing him both physically and mentally but he's determined to complete it for Ricky and 'for all the people out there suffering'.

Barker is raising funds for suicide prevention charity Campaign Against Living Miserably (CALM), in which Hatton had been an ambassador of.

Darren Barker is currently on a 1,800-mile endurance challenge in honour of Ricky Hatton

And speaking ahead of the challenge, the 44-year-old said: 'Last September, I had the honour and the privilege to speak to Ricky Hatton on a podcast. And days later he wasn't with us, so it really struck home and hit hard. And made me really understand what a terrible illness mental health is. I want to do something for Ricky, I want to do something to spread awareness.

'I feel like I owe this to Ricky. He gave up his time to speak to me, so this is something I need to do for him, and I want to do - and I need to do for the bigger picture. I need to do this for all the people out there suffering, to know that it's OK to not be OK. I want to encourage these people to have these uncomfortable conversations, and hopefully save lives in the future.'

He added: 'He will always be a hero of mine. He was the man that brought the big nights to British boxing. The man that brought the big crowds.

'But away from boxing, he was so likeable - he was the man next door - everyone could relate to Ricky. So funny, charming, just a real good guy with a big heart and someone that people could look up to. He is massively missed.'

Barker spoke from the heart as he explained what 'The Longest Round' and CALM mean to him.

Barker spoke to Hatton on a podcast a few days before his friend was found dead at his home

He continued: 'It means an awful lot. It means that I, along with the team, and everybody else following this - that we have an opportunity to make a real difference here. This is about changing lives, helping people. This is bigger than swimming and cycling, this is a huge opportunity to try and make a difference, and that's what I want to do.

'You, I guess, go through your early stages of life, being selfish, and you're on your own journey, trying to fulfil dreams and aspirations to do this and that, and then you kind of - in my situation anyway - achieve that - and it's about what next. And for me, it feels right to help and just try and raise money and awareness for something now that has really resonated with me.

'Even myself as a retired fighter, grieving the loss of boxing, grieving the loss of my brother, my grandad - understanding that grief is a part of mental health. So along with everyone else, this isn't just me - I may be getting on the bike and in the sea - but this is all of us pulling together and being there for one another. Let's be nice to one another, let's be there, let's support. So much hardship in the world as it is, so if we all pull together - we're halfway there you know.'

Barker is being sponsored by Just Eat, alongside the likes of the Royal Navy, INEOS Grenadier, kp-pharma and Pretty Sailing, and they have been providing the former world champion with food daily to keep him going during this gruelling challenge.

'We've been fuelling heavily. Lots of protein, the carbs have been so important for the energy. Been eating lots and lots throughout the day. It has been quite difficult during the challenge but we've been snacking.

'Lots of gels, lots of electrolytes, just fuelling correctly and it has been pivotal because I could not do it without it. We've also had some brilliant Italians, lots of pasta, lots of chicken. It has been great, it has been thoroughly enjoyable.'

Any donations can be made to: https://www.justgiving.com/page/thelongestround

Sports.title: Where next for Moses Itauma? Filip Hrgovic's savage verdict has shattered the Mike Tyson hype as Britain's fallen prodigy begins his long road back, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
The most alarming contribution to the inquest into the slaying of Moses came from the national hero of Croatia who was the real story of a Saturday night at the O2 which was dark for British boxing but dazzling to behold.

Filip Hrgovic said of our young Itauma: ‘No, I didn’t feel his power.’

That will be as devastating to the lad previously hailed as the next Mike Tyson as James Bond being told he is no longer attractive to women.

It will hurt even more than the punches which sent him reeling from domination to defeat and hospital on the evening he was supposed to become the second youngest world heavyweight champion of all time.

Power has been Moses Itauma’s middle name since he began felling giants like saplings. Suddenly, at 21, he is being likened to Samson who lost his mythological strength when he had a haircut.

Were there clues in how Hrgovic survived the first eight rounds of this IBF world title fight and countless punches, every one of which looked as if it would have knocked out a horse?

Moses Itauma saw his hope of becoming the second youngest heavyweight world champion ended by Filip Hrgovic

Hrgovic, right, declared afterwards that he 'didn't feel his power' in another blow to Itauma

To suggest as much would be to downplay the superhuman heart and phenomenal resilience of chin with which Hrgovic realised his own lifelong ambition of global glory. Just in time at 34.

Nevertheless, Itauma could not finish him off. Which brings other factors into issue. It is concerning, also, that Britain’s young lion should gas out on the first time in his career he was required to go beyond six rounds. Trainer Ben Davison finds himself under inquisition as to whether presumption of another early KO left Moses short on stamina build-up. Or did he simply punch himself out?

Whatever the reason, it was worrying to see one so young that exhausted as he staggered to extinction as early as the ninth round. Certainly Hrgovic put into words what many of us felt. That he was beaten in a large part by experience. The new champion who had vowed to ‘smash the kid’s face and send him back to high school’ had this to say after he had done just that: ‘He is a tremendous talent but he boxed like an amateur and must learn to fight like a professional.

‘With more experience he would have known he was winning every round and what he should have done was box out the fight to a points decision behind his jab. Not keep trying to knock me out. Although I did know he would tire the longer the fight went.’

But no power in his punches? Of being dropped once, a flash knock-down in the second round, Hrgovic said: ‘I didn’t feel it. He is very fast and caught me off balance with a punch I didn’t see.’

And so it would come to pass that in the battle of their ages it was from the kid’s corner that the white towel came fluttering in. By then not to great surprise. As early as the fifth round Itauma was beginning to grimace at the physical demands being made of him and the heavy hits he, too, was taking. In the eighth he launched a desperate assault which Hrgovic not only rode out but also inflicted damage of his own.

To his credit Itauma prodded out some punches at the start of the ninth but looked more like a fish floundering out of water. Hrgovic speared him with what he called ‘strength which came from Jesus Christ’.

So what next for he who was hailed as the next Mike Tyson? Hrgovic’s advice: ‘Several easier fights to gain more experience and rebuild his confidence. And I do think that with his speed of hand he will become a world champion one day.’

Hrgovic highlighted how he had used his experience to see off the challenge of Itauma

Hrgovic showed phenomenal resilience to achieve his lifelong dream at the age of 34

Hrgovic advised Itauma to take some easier fights to rebuild his confidence after the defeat

Promoter Frank Warren sympathised: ‘A first defeat does take away that aura of invincibility and we will give Moses the time it takes to recover from that. He is still a very special talent.’

Meanwhile, heavyweight life goes on. Warren has announced October 17 at the O2 for a lip-smacking WBO world-title rematch of the thunderous Battle of Britain between champion Daniel Dubois and white-collar graduate Fabio Wardley. Hrgovic will make his first championship defence against Cuba’s mandatory challenger Frank Sanchez and makes a prediction when he says: ‘I want to go on to a title unification fight against Daniel.’

And may it please the lords of the ring that Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury get their act together in November, whether it be in London or New York.

It will be some while before Itauma rejoins the fray, from the back of the queue. He went home from hospital the morning after his downfall to begin recuperation from the battering and also a leg injured as he reeled against the ropes.

The psychological wounds will take much longer to heal. Though it is not impossible. Muhammad Ali, Joe Louis, Joe Frazier, George Foreman and Lennox Lewis – to name but a few – all lost more than one fight and came back as champions.

But Moses Itauma the next Mike Tyson? Even as Filip Hrgovic goes home to a much-deserved hero’s welcome in Zagreb, one thing we do know for sure is that if the original Iron Mike had landed just one of the punches he took on Saturday night, he would have been knocked out.

Sports.title: Boxing legend Tony Mundine dies aged 75 - as his ex-NRL star son Anthony Mundine flies back to Australia from the Middle East
Sports.content:
Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died.

The 75-year-old is understood to have suffered a heart attack on Sunday.

His son Anthony Mundine – a former NRL star who followed in his father's footsteps and forged a successful boxing career after leaving the game – is reportedly flying back from the Middle East, Code Sports reported.

Mundine senior made history as the only Australian boxer to fight professionally across four weight divisions, in which he held the Australian titles for middleweight, light heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight classes.

He also fought for the World Boxing Association (WBA) middleweight title in 1974.

His impressive record from 96 fights is 80 wins, 64 of those being KO victories.

When Anthony took to the ring in 2000 following a successful rugby league career, his father served as his primary trainer.

Under his guidance, Anthony rose to the top of the sport, twice winning the WBA super-middleweight title in 2003 and 2008, the IBO middleweight title in 2009, and the WBA interim super-welterweight title in 2011.

Tony Mundine (left) has died, with his son Anthony (right) on his way back to Australia

Tony was inducted into the Australian boxing hall of fame in 2005 (pictured in his boxing days)

He became his son's trainer during his highly successful boxing career

Tony was born in the town of Baryulgil in north-eastern NSW, on the lands of the Bundjalung people.

He played for Grafton Rugby league club before being offered a place at the Redfern All Blacks in the South Sydney Junior Rugby League.

Between seasons, he trained at a gym run by Ern McQuillan, who took him on in a fighter-trainer contract.

In later life, he resided in Redfern where he ran the Redfern Gym.

He was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia in 1986 for service to sport and to Aboriginal youth.

In 2005, he was inducted into the Australian Boxing Hall of Fame.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma LOSES IBF world heavyweight title clash in huge upset: British star leaves arena on a stretcher after being stopped by Filip Hrgovic in ninth round
Sports.content:
Moses rose to the mountain summit and was left there as a brother Christian climbed over him and walked on to the promised land.

There was a hugely significant difference from his biblical namesake.

Itauma was flattened in a fight against Filip Hrgovic the Croatian Iron Man of such astonishing violence that it was frightening.

A fight so brutal that the most trumpeted UK boxing prodigy for decades had to be carried out of the ring on a stretcher - make that his shield - and on to hospital.

The other promise - that of becoming the second youngest world heavyweight champion of all time behind Mike Tyson - went unfulfilled.

Hopefully not for good.

Moses Itauma has suffered his first pro defeat at the hands of Croatian star Filip Hrgovic

Itauma, 21, was taken away from the ring on a stretcher after a brutal contest

But not the prediction of a fight across their ages to remember for years to come.

Twenty-one played 34 and the kid lost - after flooring and pounding Hrgovic for eight rounds.

By his own admission Hrgovic did ‘not know where I found the strength and energy to beat him to the ground in the ninth.

But he did venture to add: ‘ I knew he would tire at some point.'

As Itauma was submerged by a torrent of punches the towel fluttered in from his corner.

He lived to fight. Maybe only just.

Prior to the showdown, questions had hung over London’s 02.

Was Moses too young to fulfil all the prophesies?

Was Fil the Croat too late in life to seize the Holy Grail?

Hrgovic claimed the vacant IBF world heavyweight title after surviving plenty of heavy punches - and dealing his own

Had Itauma lost his cool at the very last with that schoolboy shove at the weigh-in. Or had he been asked to help sell the last few tickets somewhat surprisingly still for sale on Friday evening?

Had Hrgovic — who was fighting a British boxer for the fifth consecutive time — eventually succeeded in getting under the skin of the lad whose face he threatened to smash?

Would we be treated to the promised slugfest and brutal knockout? Which of them might be launched to stardom?

As they say, anything can happen in heavyweight boxing — and Itauma was to find that out to his cost later.

Among those who were looking most keenly for answers were potential future opponents for Itauma. Daniel Dubois, another big-hitting English heavyweight prodigy who already wears the WBO world championship belt, and white collar puncher Fabio Wardley.

Those two meet this October in a rematch of their midsummer slugfest in which Dubois prevailed by brute force and willpower in the 11th round — and the pair squared up to each other in the ring before the main event, which was scheduled for 12 rounds.

That will all have to wait for now. Itauma, who was born in Kezmarok, Slovakia, but raised in Kent after moving at eight years old, stormed out of the blocks.

Both had pledged to go for a quick kill in the fervent 02. Itauma was as good as his word. His first five big shots won the first but Hrgovic’s chin proved resilient.

Itauma is the most trumpeted British heavyweight prodigy for decades, but this is a setback

Moses tested it to better effect at the onset of the second and scored a flash knockdown. But the Croat rallied and slowly came into the fight, shaking Itauma three times in the third.

In the fourth, there were worrying signs for the man from Zagreb as a cut appeared above his right eye. Itauma kept examining the Hrgovic chin but he could not land the early finish.

To his credit, Hrgovic was giving as good as he got as he traded blows with Itauma in the fifth during some brutal exchanges.

It was pretty much the same story in an astonishing sixth that tested the resilience of both to the limit as they tried to land a killer blow. By now, both fighters appeared to be struggling as the gas tank appeared to empty.

It was new ground for Itauma in the seventh as he had never gone beyond six rounds.

In his impatience, some of his swings became wild. But not all. By the end of the round, Hrgovic was being treated for a swelling above his left eye.

It looked all over in the eighth as Itauma unleashed a flurry of big shots. But Hrgovic refused to down tools and found a second wind in the ninth as he put paid to Itauma’s hopes of a historic victory.

Other men were brave beyond the call. But the most rousing salute of all must go Croatia's first world heavyweight champion.

Filip Hrgovic. What a man.

Sports.title: Filip Hrgovic insists he knew Moses Itauma would 'gas out' in world heavyweight title fight - but backs the beaten British star as 'the future'
Sports.content:
Filip Hrgovic declared he knew that Moses Itauma would 'gas out' after handing the Briton a shock defeat in their heavyweight world title fight.

Itauma had been the heavy favourite heading into the showdown at the O2 Arena and was bidding to become the second youngest heavyweight world champion in history after Mike Tyson.

The 21-year-old, who had won all 14 of his previous fights, looked on course for victory after knocking down Hrgovic in the second round and continued to control the fight.

Hrgovic, however, remained resilient and held off Itauma with the British star looking exhausted by the end of the eighth round.

The Croatian seized his chance in the ninth and pinned a struggling Itauma back, with the towel eventually thrown in to end the contest.

Hrgovic, who became Croatia's first heavyweight world champion, insisted he knew early on in the fight that Itauma would tire and despite 'losing every round' would be able to take advantage of his rivals' conditioning late on.

Filip Hrgovic has insisted he knew Moses Itauma would 'gas out' in their world title fight

Itauma controlled much of the fight but the contest was stopped in the ninth round after the visibly exhausted British fighter struggled against Hrgovic

'You're going to be sending Moses back to high school. Let me ask my young friend something. Is chin important? Is chin important?' Hrgovic said.

'He didn't seem to think so, but I think he may have answered that question. Look, chin is important.

'He's an amazing fighter. I want to thank him for accepting this fight, to give me a chance to become a new superstar in the heavyweight division.

'I'm the present, and he's definitely the future. He's an amazing fighter. He's one of a kind. He's the best I've been in the ring with, but he needs more experience.

'From the first round, I saw him gassing out. He started fast. I knew he was going to gas out.

'I knew when my chance came, I needed to push. That is what I did.'

Itauma, who left the ring on a stretcher and went to hospital for checks, has been backed to bounce back from the defeat.

'Filip done amazing to ride through the storm! I’ll say this now! Moses Itauma will be world champion! He will learn so much from tonight,' Bellew wrote on X.

Hrgovic insisted Itauma is still 'the future' with several stars backing Itauma to learn and bounce back from the first defeat of his career

'The biggest thing I’ll take from tonight is just how brave and tough Moses was.

'We knew Filip was super tough. Tonight we learned Moses is also tough, Once he learns to pace a 12 round bout he’s gonna rule for a while!

'Filip Hrgovic’s chin needs to studied…'

Eubank Jr added: 'Not sure what happened tonight. Moses was fighting well & then gassed out it seems… at his young age this should simply not be happening.

'Time to rethink his training camp moving forward I think. Congratulations to Filip Hrgović becoming the new heavyweight champ.'

Sports.title: Quiet, Bible-reading Moses Itauma boasts near-decapitating punching power and is on the cusp of greatness as he looks to emulate Mike Tyson - but here's why Filip Hrgovic will NOT be a walkover, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
I’m going to punch your nose bone into your brain.

So Mike Tyson spoke from the dark depths of his New York upbringing in the crack cocaine quarter of Brownsville by way of petrifying his opponents.

No weapon against you shall prosper. Every tongue which rises against you in judgement you shall condemn.

So Moses Itauma quotes biblically from Isaiah 54:17 before entering the ring.

As Itauma stands on the brink of becoming the second youngest world heavyweight champion in boxing history, so comparisons with the legend who still holds that distinction multiply.

Teddy Atlas, one-time trainer of Iron Mike whose motivational tools included a loaded gun pointed at Tyson in a changing room, is taken by a likeness in their near-decapitating power.

Moses Itauma will look to bring his huge punching power to bear against Croatia's Filip Hrgovic in their IBF world title fight on Saturday

Itauma tries to bring his huge punching to bear against Croatian hard-man Filip Hrgovic in this Saturday night’s fight at London’s O2 for the vacant IBF world title. He does so grateful for the compliment, while stressing the variance in their personalities.

‘I’m flattered to hear that from such a respected figure in boxing,’ he says. ‘Of course I like being compared with the great Mike Tyson as a fighter. But we are different people. I’m not braggadocious. I don’t threaten or bad-mouth people. I respect all my opponents.’ Of whom all 14 have been beaten out of sight, 12 of them by knock-out, none lasting longer than six rounds.

By Itauma standards that is a lengthy statement. Mostly when asked questions about his growing reputation, his own potential for greatness, his thrilling impact on this business, the skills as well as the punching, his stock reply is: ’Honestly I don’t see myself that way.’ He usually adds: ‘I know I’m a young man, still learning.’

So young that if he defeats Hrgovic he will have come within two months of Tyson’s record as the youngest heavyweight champion. ‘I did have an ambition to be that man,’ he says. ‘But honestly it was only in the back of my mind. More important is how I develop.’

In this hard old game which is wearying of the faux-murderous ranting, table throwing and foul language – followed by brotherly love at the final bell – he is a quiet breath of fresh air. It is the pace at which Itauma is developing, at 21, which is the cause for real concern among the heavyweight fraternity.

Atlas speaks to his all-round abilities: ‘It’s not only the southpaw KO punch but the fast combinations, the balance, the reading of an opponent which gets him into position for maximum effect.’

Itauma’s trainer has no need of a pistol to encourage hard work on those qualities. He convinces by persuasion and reports: ‘Moses is a fast and eager learner.’

The young man himself attributes his professionalism and determination to his parents and how they brought him as a three-year-old from the small town of Kezmarok in Slovakia to the British naval port of Chatham. He credits his Nigerian father for his physical strength and his Slovak mother for his will-power. That blend exposed them to the Eastern European racism which obliged them to immigrate to the UK. Moses was the last of them to make the journey, waiting with an aunt while his parents scouted the land on England’s south coast and then sent for him to join them and his two brothers.

The pair clashed on the eve of a fight that could see Itauma become the second youngest heavyweight world champion

The gratitude of the family is to be seen by the Union Jack hung on the walls of their home. In return, the UK has acquired a working family and a potential world heavyweight champion. Perhaps even the undisputed heir to Oleksandr Usyk, more of whose vacated alpha-belts will come into Itauma’s sights if all goes well at the O2.

Not that Hrgovic should be taken at all lightly. At 34 the man from Zagreb is in his prime and until Moses came along was the most avoided heavyweight on the planet. He has frequently been passed over for deserved world title shots, while being fobbed off with ‘final eliminators.’

To their credit several of our heavies have risen to the challenge of the most highly rated fighter in Croatian ring history. He has mopped up Joe Joyce and cult figure Dave Allen.

The only defeat of his 21 fight career was inflicted by Daniel Dubois in one of those elimination bouts but he was ahead on points when he suffered the deep cuts which forced the eighth round stoppage. Notably, as it comes to Itauma, he has withstood the big punching of both Dubois and Joyce. As well as the renowned KO power of Chinese giant Zhilei Zhang.

Itauma, who has not come close to losing in his first 14 professional fights, knows Hrgovic will not roll over easily and declares himself ‘prepared for this one to go as long as it takes.’ But he does add: ‘I know that people don’t come to see heavyweights box to points decisions.’

The humorous Croatian has tweaked the Moses nerves by saying: ‘It will be good for his boxing soul when I give him the experience of a first defeat.’ Itauma’s unruffled answer: ‘Mike Tyson used that to rattle his opponents but it didn’t do them much good.’

Since 15 of Hrgovic’s 20 victories have been knock-outs the blood lust will be rising in a packed O2 in anticipation of a slugfest. As well as expectancy of confirmation that this Moses is on a journey to the undisputed crown.

That would require him making a successful first title defence against Cuban slugger Frank Sanchez, who was paid to step aside from his mandatory right to be in one of the corners this Saturday.

After that, fans, how about a good old-fashioned British barn-burner against the winner of the Dubois-Fabio Wardley rematch for the WBO belt? With whichever gladiator still standing going on to mop up the other two titles vacated by Usyk. The WBC and WBA held respectively by Germany’s Agit Kabayel and Russia’s Murat Gassiev.

Promoter Frank Warren may switch the order by saving his two youngest prodigies from fighting each other until they have bagged all the alpha belts between them. Which would keep them apart until late next year.

The prospect of Itauma coming out top of that pile would have seemed premature until he obliterated America’s Jermaine Franklin inside five rounds this March. Now the bookies quote him as the favourite against all-comers.

Hrgovic should not be taken lightly with the Croatian having been the most avoided heavyweight on the planet, who has deserved more shots at world titles

By the time all that is done and dusted, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua might have settled finally their longstanding differences so that one or other could provide a cross generational Wembley extravaganza. For which Itauma might still be just 22.

Teddy Atlas would expect nothing less than Itauma crushing AJ or The Gipsy King. Albeit by way of a variation on the Tyson theme. He explains: ‘Moses brings other dimensions. Movement. Positioning. Patience when needed if he doesn’t stop ‘em in the first round. And his KOs usually come from combinations. When he sees an opening he throws a lot of leather. He is a more complete boxer. But Mike is still boxing’s most pure one-hit knock out puncher.’

Hrgovic will provide the most severe test yet of Itauma’s finishing power and his punch resistance. If he passes, we may well be witnessing the start of something very big indeed.

Might even Oleksandr The Greatest of his generation have seen Moses coming when he dropped all those belts?

*Itauma v Hrgovic will be televised live on DAZN pay-per-view

Sports.title: Red Bull to keep Dutch GP driver line-up for Monza with Hadjar still injured
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar will sit out this weekend's Italian Grand Prix at Monza as he recovers from a wrist injury he sustained during Formula 1's summer break. As a result, Liam Lawson will once again replace him at Red Bull and Yuki Tsunoda slots back into the Racing Bulls car.

Hadjar sustained a wrist fracturing during a boxing session during the summer break, forcing him to watch the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort from the sidelines on 21-23 August. Racing Bulls regular Lawson deputised for the Frenchman in the Red Bull RB22, with reserve driver Tsunoda being recalled to run Lawson's vacant VCARB 03 alongside rookie Arvid Lindblad.

Red Bull had been hopeful Hadjar would be ready for a return to competition at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix, but also didn't want the 22-year-old to take any undue risk as he recovers from his injury.

Yuki Tsunoda, Racing Bulls Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

Both Red Bull-owned teams have now confirmed they will field unchanged driver line-ups in Monza.

"Liam will drive alongside Max at the Italian GP in Monza, while Isack continues to make encouraging progress," a Red Bull statement read. "The team is closely monitoring his rehabilitation and will take no unnecessary risks with his return to competition and wishes him a speedy recovery."

Both Lawson and Tsunoda impressed on their stand-in roles in the Netherlands, with Lawson guiding his Red Bull to seventh from eighth on the grid. Tsunoda just missed out on points in 11th, with both drivers sticking close to their respective team-mates on one-lap pace.

Meanwhile, the team's other reserve driver Ayumu Iwasa will replace Verstappen for opening practice, fulfilling one of the team's four mandated rookie sessions this season.

Sports.title: Ferrari to bring upgraded engine to Italian GP under ADUO
Sports.content:
Ferrari will introduce an upgrade to its Formula 1 power unit at this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix with it permitted under the Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities system.

This year, F1 introduced the ADUO system, which grants manufacturers extra opportunities to improve their engines should they be lagging behind on performance, with results taken every quarter of a season.

Red Bull was contentiously named as F1’s benchmark and because Ferrari is deemed to be over 4% adrift on power, the Italian marque is granted two upgrade tokens.

“We are introducing an updated power unit as part of the development opportunities available under ADUO,” said team boss Fred Vasseur.

“It represents a step in the right direction and as we know, this year is very much about marginal gains.

“Monza is a demanding circuit and the field is extremely close. Our priority will be to execute every aspect of the weekend as well as possible from Friday onwards.

“We want to draw extra motivation from the passion of our home crowd and give our tifosi a strong weekend.”

Frederic Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

It is understood that the upgrade will add 15bhp to the Ferrari engine, and this will halve the deficit to the Mercedes power unit, which is believed to be the strongest complete package despite the ADUO results.

This is something that has held Ferrari back in 2026 considering its chassis is on a par, if not better, than that of the championship-leading Mercedes outfit, which leads the Scuderia by 87 points.

Ferrari is also set to run a Michael Schumacher-inspired livery this weekend to mark 30 years since the seven-time world champion made his debut at the squad with whom he won five titles.

“Monza is always a very special weekend for Ferrari,” added Vasseur, whose team is searching for its first Italian GP win since Charles Leclerc in 2024.

“Racing in front of our tifosi gives the whole team incredible energy and this year there will be an additional emotional dimension as we celebrate Michael Schumacher and the legacy he has left in our company.

“His relentless pursuit of improvement, attention to detail and strong belief in teamwork are values that remain key to us today.”

Sports.title: Red Bull signs key Aston Martin engineer as Lambiase replacement
Sports.content:
The Red Bull Formula 1 team has confirmed it has hired long-time Aston Martin engineer Tom McCullough to replace McLaren bound Gianpiero Lambiase as head of racing.

Lambiase will join McLaren in 2028 to become its chief racing officer, reporting into team principal Andrea Stella. The Briton is currently serving a dual role at the team as Max Verstappen's race engineer, dovetailing those duties with a more overarching "head of racing" position.

As previously reported, Verstappen's former performance engineer Tom Hart has decided against a move to Williams to take over the race engineer role starting in 2027. The Milton Keynes squad has now also found a successor for Lambiase as head of racing in the shape of Aston Martin man McCullough.

"We're delighted to welcome Tom to the team at the beginning of 2027 and look forward to the wealth of experience and expertise he will bring to the role," the team shared in a statement.

Gianpiero Lambiase is set to depart Red Bull by 2028 at the latest. Photo by: Kym Illman / Getty Images

McCullough was a long-time servant of Aston Martin through its Force India and Racing Point days, performing the chief race engineer role for four seasons before becoming its performance director, a job which he held until the end of the 2024 season.

As part of a restructuring of the team in early 2025, McCullough's duties were taken on by previous team principal Mike Krack. McCullough was shifted to non-F1 projects at Aston Martin Performance Technologies in a senior leadership role, which he is now set to vacate.

The 50-year-old, who started his career at chassis builder Reynard, also served spells at Sauber and Williams.

Sports.title: McLaren to deliver rotating rear wing at Italian GP but calls it H-wing
Sports.content:
McLaren will introduce the H-Wing, its own version of the rotating rear wing, at this weekend's Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix.

McLaren had been working on its own interpretation of the rotating rear wing, which flips 180 degrees between cornering mode and straight mode, after seeing Ferrari introduce its own version during winter testing.

The Woking team first brought a prototype to the Austrian Grand Prix, but decided against trialling it in free practice after encountering an issue in the garage. It subsequently ran a revised example in Hungarian GP FP1 with a view to introducing it at low-drag, high-speed circuits later, when the concept should help reduce drag on the straights.

Monza is the first such opportunity, and McLaren has now committed to introducing the H-Wing on both cars.

The name for the device is not a Star Wars reference, but a nod to the letter H in the Etihad logo that adorns the rear of the MCL40's rear wing. The letter H runs along the centreline where the H-Wing's straight mode actuator is positioned.

McLaren's new wing features an innovative actuator Photo by: Marcel van Dorst / EYE4images / NurPhoto via Getty Images

It follows a tradition set by the team's famed F-duct in 2010, which was named after the F in Vodafone along the nose where the duct was installed.

"This weekend, we have brought what we believe is needed to be competitive, including a new low-drag rear wing specification, including the first use of our H-Wing, alongside some small aerodynamic and low-drag options that we will evaluate before deciding the final specification for qualifying," said McLaren's technical director Neil Houldey.

"Overall, we know there is still more performance to unlock from the MCL40, both through maximising the package we already have and through further upgrades planned for the races ahead.”

McLaren will also run a tweaked livery at Monza and at next week's Spanish Grand Prix to promote its partnership with cryptocurrency company OKX.

Sports.title: Haas rules out switch to 2027 development as VF-26 updates coming in Monza
Sports.content:
After starting the 2026 Formula 1 season strongly, Haas admits that it has been overtaken and out-developed by its rivals this year. However, team boss Ayao Komatsu and driver Oliver Bearman both remain hopeful that it can catch back up with the pack “soon”.

Haas has traditionally started the season strong, and continued this tradition in 2026 when it picked up points in the first three races – including a fifth-place finish for Bearman in the Chinese Grand Prix. However, as the season progressed, the team has been caught by its rivals as it struggles with an inconsistent car and a slower upgrade rate compared with midfield teams like Alpine and Racing Bulls.

“2025 was really the first year for us, or one of very few years, where we seemed to have good pace throughout the year,” Bearman explained ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix. “We actually improved our relative performance as the year went on.

“Now, 2026 is more of what we've seen from Haas in the past, of starting incredibly strong with a really quick car as a base, but not being able to improve like the others have.

“Quite frankly, we've been overtaken right now. We are the 10th-best team. It really hurts, myself and all the others. We were working really hard to make that not be the case, but that's the reality of where we are right now.”

Case in point, the team has not scored points since the Monaco Grand Prix in June when Esteban Ocon managed to bring his car home in ninth. Since then, the team has struggled with inconsistency – which has impacted its ability to extract the most from the 2026 car.

Ayao Komatsu says Haas will not pivot all its resources to 2027 just yet Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

However, team principal Komatsu is hopeful that Haas will soon be able to uncover solutions to the issues it is facing.

“So, the last two years, I think we proved to ourselves and the outside world that we can develop the car. We've got the people, the technical department is functioning,” Komatsu said ahead of the Zandvoort race.

“For us to have any remote chance of keeping up with the others, because of the size of our team, everything has to be perfect. But that's just not realistic in anyone's life. And the Montreal upgrade wasn't perfect. Some bits worked, some bits made the car faster, but some bits wasn't perfect. Actually, [it] made the drivability more difficult as well.

“So, we're learning from those lessons. And what's the objective for the rest of the season? For me, it's the same as the last two years. We've got to prove to ourselves that we can identify the key issues, we can solve the issues and then put it on the car to move forward.”

As a result of the struggles, Komatsu said he is now fielding questions about when Haas will give up on its 2026 challenger and switch focus to next year. This, Komatsu explained, is not an option for the team and it will instead work to unlock the performance of the VF-26 - a move that will benefit the team in the long run.

“If you say, OK, fine, ‘26, we started well, but tail off, it's the first year of regulation. Fine, let's move on, start '27. We haven't solved the fundamental issue. If we do that, it doesn't give confidence to people,” the Japanese engineer explained.

“They've got to believe in themselves. One of the main driving factors in the way they're tackling now, together as a team, is the confidence and togetherness they've gained from the last two years. That's why we are developing out of it.”

Oliver Bearman is hopeful that Haas will have an upgraded F1 car "soon" Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Haas will bring upgrades to Italian GP

To develop its way out of the problem, Haas will bring new parts to the VF-26, which the team confirmed would arrive this weekend in Monza for the Italian Grand Prix.

"This weekend, we’re bringing another upgrade package to the car," Komatsu explained in a statement shared by the team. "So again, it’s critical we maximise our practice time, evaluate our data comprehensively, and strive to keep pushing in the midfield."

However, despite the positives that these upgrades could bring, Bearman warned that new parts don't always equate to a jump forward on track.

“We have new parts coming,” the Briton said. “But we're very sceptical in some ways. We have discrepancies in a race like Budapest. We have discrepancies of downforce equivalent to the size of an upgrade. If I have the car that I had in Spa, here [in Zandvoort], it's like putting an upgrade on the car.

“An upgrade, I don't know how much it costs, but many millions. If we can figure out how to get our car to work, it's for free. If we get the upgrade but it doesn't perform, then it's like not getting it. There's many factors at play, it's a big challenge.”

Looking ahead to the next race in Italy, Bearman believes Haas could at least move a step up to be the ninth best team on the grid. Despite a radical overhaul of the Aston Martin AMR26 in recent weeks that has seen it jump off the back of the pack, the Briton says Haas should have an advantage over the British outfit in Monza.

“We expect to beat [Aston Martin] in Monza, where it's a power track,” Bearman said. “But in Hungary, they were faster than us, or at least more consistent. Those are the facts in terms of that. That's where we are.

“It really hurts to be sitting here saying that, but that's the case.”

Sports.title: How Ferrari can "push until the end" with F1 2026 upgrades, and why it will
Sports.content:
Ferrari will "push until the end" of the 2026 Formula 1 season with car upgrades, team principal Fred Vasseur confirmed, as he shrugged off suggestions the team will have to slow down its development because of cost cap limitations.

Ferrari has rolled out an impressive number of incremental upgrades to its 2026 challenger, the SF-26, which have kept the squad in second place in the constructors' championship and allowed Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to clinch a grand prix win each thus far.

That upgrade push will continue at its home race this weekend in Monza, where Ferrari is expected to introduce smaller aerodynamic improvements alongside its second engine update following the latest ADUO ranking.

Read Also: Formula 1 Ferrari to deliver upgraded F1 engine at Italian GP

The field is becoming incredibly closely matched on performance, especially on circuits where the 2026 power units make less of a difference. Mercedes, McLaren and Ferrari were all covered by one tenth in sprint qualifying in Zandvoort, and three tenths has routinely become the difference between pole and the third row of the grid.

That's why teams who are able to continue bringing performance to the car until late on can still make a solid push in the championship, but they have to balance cashing in their wind tunnel development against the constraints of the cost cap and resources required for the 2027 car project.

Speaking exclusively to Autosport, Ferrari chief Vasseur has revealed the Scuderia will continue its relentless upgrade push, and it has no issues with the cost cap.

"The strategy is that we will continue to push until the end," Vasseur said. "We have a plan. We have no issue with the cost cap, we are following the plan and will continue like this.

Photo by: Marcel van Dorst / EYE4images / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"It's true that you have different strategies. You have McLaren coming each three or four races with a big package on the car, and we are more trying to bring upgrades each race but much smaller. But at the end, in terms of cost, it's the same.

"What is challenging, probably, is that we are still developing with 11 races to go, and I think a crash like Max [Verstappen] in Zandvoort is huge in terms of cost cap [for Red Bull]. It's difficult to anticipate the number of crashes that you could have until the end of the season."

While Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull have all rolled out significant updates, Mercedes has been lagging behind, with its next major package coming at October's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and it has seen its rival teams close the gap as a result in recent weeks and months.

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff claimed the team "hasn't got the money to put developments on the car" beyond what is currently planned, but he did suspect the likes of Ferrari would have to slow down their rate of development given the number of items they had already introduced.

Read Also: Formula 1 McLaren rejects Mercedes claim it cannot afford aggressive upgrades in F1 2026

Vasseur didn't want to comment on Mercedes' upgrade strategy without fully understanding its approach, but he did lift the lid on how Ferrari has been able to bring so many improvements to the car efficiently, something that had raised eyebrows in the paddock.

"I don't want to speak about Mercedes because I don't understand, but with McLaren it's a bit linked to how you develop in the wind tunnel and the capacity of production," the Frenchman said.

"We found our best approach by almost bringing upgrades each race. One week it's mechanical, one week it's aero, and we are continuing like this. It's fitting with our capacity of production, with our wind tunnel capacity, and it's going well.

"Now, if McLaren want to do things differently, it's because they have good reasons to do it. The set-up of the teams is different; the configuration is different. But at the end of the day, over a season we are almost following each other in terms of development."

Sports.title: Mario Andretti and Jacky Ickx: A friendship that has endured for almost 60 years
Sports.content:
Mario Andretti and Jacky Ickx were remarkably versatile even by the standards of their generation, competing and succeeding across multiple disciplines. Having won some of the biggest prizes in motorsport between them, both can look back on their journeys with immense pride.

But competition was only one part of the story, and the relationship Andretti and Ickx built stands out from the rest in motor racing.

So, when the two joined Motorsport.com on a video call for a special double interview, it felt like two old friends had been reunited. The pair always got along well when they were team-mates at Ferrari in Formula 1 and the World SportsCar Championship. But it’s remarkable how, six decades after they first met at the Mexican Grand Prix in 1968, their admiration and affection for each other remain undimmed.

“You have to explain to me how you stay in such good condition, because you look good,” Ickx said of Andretti.

“I understand, yesterday you won [IndyCar’s Freedom 250] and you finished on the podium. You have many reasons to smile. We hope at Genesis to be like you.

“You are amazing, my dear Mario. It brings me some emotions to think that what we did more than almost 60 years ago - yes, almost 60 years ago.

“You are the most famous driver - the celebrated, the iconic Mario Andretti. I had the fortune to share with you, it was yesterday, I believe, 1972, in a Ferrari 312 PB. So thank you very much.”

Andretti, clearly touched by Ickx’s praise, simply replied: “No, thank you. You were the best.”

Endurance exploits ​brought them together

Jacky Ickx, Mario Andretti, Ferrari 312 PB Photo by: Rainer Schlegelmilch / Getty Images

When you see that kind of admiration from the pair, it’s easy to understand why they formed such a formidable pairing on track. It was in 1971 when they first shared a garage, teaming up at Ferrari for a double programme. Even as reliability held them back in F1, both scored a win each, with Andretti - who wasn’t even racing full-time - driving the 312B to victory on his debut outing for Enzo’s squad.

It was in sportscars, though, that their partnership really flourished. Their similar physical dimensions already made life easy for Ferrari’s designers, but it was ultimately mutual respect and understanding that turned them into such a formidable pair. Ickx, for instance, famously let Andretti qualify the car according to the American’s preference.

As a result, Ferrari dominated the 1972 season, with Andretti and Ickx winning four of the 11 races together, including Daytona, Sebring, Watkins Glen and Brands Hatch. Had Ferrari not skipped Le Mans after concluding its F1-derived engine wasn’t fit for a 24-hour contest (that year's Daytona race was reduced to six hours), the pair would most certainly have been among the victory contenders at the legendary La Sarthe.

Andretti admitted that sharing a car in endurance racing brought him and Ickx together, laying the foundation for a friendship that has lasted to this day.

“Long-distance racing taught me a lot,” he said. “You're sharing the moment with someone else to do the same thing.

“There's no bigger pleasure when you're in victory lane together with your partner. The ones that have accomplished the same thing for you - and with you.

“We all depend on each other to minimise the mistakes - and make no mistakes - to be able to bring it home.

“You're sharing your victory in a different way when you're driving in long-distance races. We're both in the same seat during the race at one time or another and we're both experiencing exactly the same thing. That's something that brings you together.

“Jacky, specifically, from the long-distance racing factor, I did most of my long-distance races with him. That's why I said he's my best buddy, my best team-mate.”

Still chasing the same goal

Jacky Ickx, Genesis Magma Racing Photo by: Genesis

Following his stint with Ferrari, Ickx went on to become one of the most successful names in sportscar racing history, winning Le Mans six times. He also triumphed in the Spa 24 Hours and Bathurst 1000 before turning his hand to rally raid and winning the Dakar Rally on his third attempt.

Andretti, likewise, accomplished almost everything he set out to achieve, winning marque races such as the Indy 500 and the Daytona 500 and claiming the championship in both Formula 1 and IndyCar.

Both may have long retired from active competition, but the passion for motorsport still burns brightly in their 80s. Andretti, besides being the patriarch of one of America’s biggest racing dynasties, works as a director for Cadillac’s new F1 team. Ickx, meanwhile, serves as a brand ambassador for Genesis Magma Racing, and recently sampled the GMR-001 at Paul Ricard.

Their lives may now be separated by geography - Andretti remains based in Pennsylvania while Ickx spends a significant amount of time in Africa - but the distance has done little to weaken their connection. If anything, they continue to follow each other’s careers and genuinely want to see the other succeed.

“I'll be watching with interest,” said Andretti. “I wish you guys all the very best. Whatever your endeavours are, maintain your objectives and always go for the sky.”

“I wish you to enjoy life in your projects,” Ickx adds. “We are in very good company. We are lucky to still be active, to be in good health.

“We are very lucky, Mario. I keep in mind these days the years we have shared together, where we have shared long-distance racing.

“Of course, I follow you in your championships, F1, IndyCar, NASCAR, Midget.”

Mario Andretti, Jacky Ickx, Ferrari 312 PB Photo by: David Phipps / Sutton Images via Getty Images

As the call drew to an end, both Andretti and Ickx bid each other goodbye. They could have spent the hour trading stories about their past glories, but instead, the conversation repeatedly returned to the time they had shared together on and off the track.

“You have been a real friend and such a talented driver,” concludes Ickx. “I was tempted to say I love you, but you're not supposed to say that.

“Mario, stay safe, please,” he adds. “Stay safe. And thank you very much for your friendship.”

Sports.title: The underlying upgrade that boosted McLaren's performance jump
Sports.content:
McLaren’s win in Zandvoort, their second in a row after Budapest, highlighted a key point: the updates introduced on either side of the summer break did more than restore the aerodynamic load the car had been missing. They also enabled the team to take a decisive step forward.

At the Barcelona Grand Prix, for instance, McLaren’s strengths had already begun to emerge, and the same was true at Spa, where the car appeared in its most convincing form. The faster and longer the corner, because absolute speed alone is not the sole factor, the more competitive the car becomes. The latest upgrades delivered the extra downforce required to turn the car into the benchmark through those sections.

The effectiveness of these developments surprised even McLaren, as the performance shown in the high‑speed sections exceeded internal expectations.

Yet another factor behind the Zandvoort victory went somewhat under the radar: the debut of the new front wheel rims, a detail that McLaren technical director of engineering Neil Houldey had already hinted at ahead of the weekend.

McLaren wheel cover comparison Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

“We introduced a small change to the rear section of the floor to generate a bit of extra load, along with some minor tweaks to the rear brake ducts. We also have new front wheel rims, which will help us build more temperature in the tyres. These updates are not significant in terms of lap time, but they do make us slightly more competitive”, Houldey said.

Why is this detail so interesting? After the race, team principal Andrea Stella noted that both Budapest and Zandvoort were high-downforce circuits that naturally suited the car's characteristics better than other tracks. However, looking back at Monaco, where the team hoped to fight at the front and repeat previous successes of last year, McLaren and struggled ended outside the podium positions.

The reason for those struggles went beyond cornering speeds and circuit characteristics. While Monte Carlo gives teams greater set-up freedom with fewer compromises, the car suffered from a lack of downforce and from difficulty generating temperature in the front tyres, which reduced overall grip. This limitation had already emerged earlier in the season, most notably in Australia and China, where the car experienced pronounced graining, while in Japan, where graining was not an issue and the new asphalt improved the overall grip, the MCL40 gained its first podium of the season.

One of the concerns heading into the Zandvoort weekend was the possibility of front‑axle graining, although it ultimately proved to be minimal for everyone. The real challenge was getting the tyres into the right temperature window, even over a single lap. That became clear in the final Q3 attempt on Saturday, when Lando Norris secured pole position, while other teams, struggled to bring the tyres up to temperature and needed an additional lap.

Aston Martin 2026 wheel comparison demonstrates a difference between the front and rear to manage temperatures Photo by: Gianluca D'Alessandro

This is where the topic connects with the updates introduced in the Netherlands. With wheel rim development open once again this season as part of the rule changes, teams have gained a powerful tool for managing tyre temperatures and operating pressures. The internal cavities of a custom rim design, that some teams call “pockets”, allow engineers to passively control air exchange and thermal transfer to the tyre.

At Zandvoort, McLaren focused specifically on this area to retain higher temperatures within the rim structure and, in turn, transfer that heat more effectively to the tyre. This is why only the front rim, manufactured by long‑standing partner Enkei, was updated, accompanied by a more closed wheel cover designed to limit the cooling effect of ambient airflow as it strikes the assembly and to reduce drag.

The rear rim remained unchanged because rear‑tyre degradation was already a key factor throughout the weekend, as seen during the sprint and the race. In that area of the car, the priority was to keep temperatures under control in the traction phases and the high‑speed sections rather than adding more heat. Strong gusts caused the cars to slide through the high‑speed corners, where additional downforce becomes critical, as well as through the key traction zones on the exit of the slower corners.

Sports.title: Social Media: Norris forms junior team LN4Fusion to race in F3 and potentially F2 | Brief
Sports.content:
Lando Norris has formed a new racing team under the name LN4Fusion which will compete in at least three categories next year.

The reigning world champion will enter his new team in the Formula 1-supporting Formula 3 series. It will also compete in the Formula Regional European Championship and Italian Formula 4. Norris raced in the same series, or previous equivalent categories, during his ascent to F1.

Norris said he is also looking at entering the team in two other series: Formula 2, the leading feeder championship, and British Formula 4.

“I was lucky enough to achieve my dream and now I want to help others achieve theirs,” said Norris.

“Built with people I trust, people who’ve experienced all levels of motorsport and know exactly what it takes to win. The goal is to become the leading junior single-seater team. We’ll be on the grid in Italian F4, FREC, F3, and are working on a place in British F4 and F2.

“That’s not all. We’ve also created the LN4 Legacy Programme to fund and support talented young drivers who might otherwise not get the opportunity. Giving them the support they need on and off track to have the best chance of success.

“To see this go from an idea to something real is incredible. Huge thanks to everyone who has played a part in making this happen.

“[I’m] excited for what’s to come. See you on the grid in ’27.”

Sports.title: ‘Dad was driving angry’: Jacques Villeneuve on his father Gilles’ fatal crash | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Jacques Villeneuve said he was close to tears as he watched footage from a new movie on the life of his father Gilles.

“Villeneuve: Rise of a Legend” (trailer below) will have its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival on September 19th. The film tells the story of the future F1 driver’s early racing exploits, leading up to his hiring by Enzo Ferrari.

“Watching the trailer, it was difficult to hold back the tears,” said Villeneuve, who won the world championship in 1997.

“I love that it focuses on the early years, the years no one but our family knows about. Most biopics focus on when someone’s in their prime, and they tend to rush through or gloss over how they got there. They give the audience what they already know, whereas this film shows the building blocks.”

Jacques was 11 when his father died in a crash during qualifying for the 1982 Belgian Grand Prix at Zolder. He had fallen out with his Ferrari team mate Didier Pironi two weeks earlier, believing the team had issued orders for them to hold position with Villeneuve leading.

The 1997 world champion now has seven children of his own and has explained the circumstances of their grandfather’s death to them.

“Our four-year-old, Gilles, is really into racing,” he said. “He’s the same age I was when I first believed I would become a racing driver.

“It’s always difficult to know, but it seems to be inside him. He relates a lot to his grandad. He knows the full story. He understands his grandad passed away because he was racing angry.

“He understands death. It’s important, I think, to be able to handle these things so you don’t have a big shock when you’re 60 or something.”

Villeneuve said he managed the risks of racing more successfully than his father did. “I’ve never really raced angry, but my upbringing was different to my dad’s,” he said. “The fact that I was in boarding school and ski-raced a lot meant I paid the price very quickly when I made a mistake.

“I’m able to calculate risk better than he did. I know the risk-to-reward ratios. When I was racing in F1 there weren’t many crazy drivers anymore, which made me look a little bit crazier than I actually was.

“But this thing about driving angry, it’s something I’ve come to understand much more recently. In part, that’s the result of talking to guys like Alain Prost, guys that raced against my dad. They have so many amazing stories, and it’s given me a different picture of who my dad was and the situation he was in. It’s helped me connect some dots.”

He described watching some of his father’s most famous races, including some of his six grand prix victories.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I was there when he won the 1978 Canadian Grand Prix. I was on the podium with my grandparents, and I was wearing a winter ski coat because it was freezing.

“I remember when he won the [1981] Monaco Grand Prix. I was sitting in the grandstand by the swimming pool with my grandparents. I remember talking to myself: ‘Come on, you’ve got to win this…’

“I remember Dijon [Villeneuve’s famous battle with Rene Arnoux during the 1979 French Grand Prix]; I was watching that on TV at a house just outside the track.

“I also have a vivid memory of sitting in the Bosch Kurve grandstand at the Osterreichring in Austria. I could be left alone in the grandstand all day just watching the cars drive by.”

However he was not at Zolder on the weekend his father was killed. “At that point we didn’t go to races anymore,” he said. “We’d moved to Monaco and we were really lagging behind at school.”

“My mother hadn’t gone to that race either. I remember walking back from school, getting home and then the phone ringing and my mother picking up. It was a very emotional moment.”

Sports.title: Temple of Speed or Cathedral of Clipping? Eight talking points for the 2026 Italian GP | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Will Formula 1’s new engines ruin Monza’s high-speed spectacle? Will Isack Hadjar return? Eight talking points for this weekend’s race.

Cathedral of Clipping?

Formula 1’s disastrous 2026 regulations have left its cars with power units which are woefully inadequate for the challenge of racing on the world’s fastest and most demanding circuits.

Those in F1 prefer language which lays the blame for the series’ current predicament more on the venues than the regulations. “Monza is an energy-poor track,” Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff noted in their pre-event press release, “you spend much of the lap asking everything from the power unit and don’t have many opportunities to charge the battery.”

Whether you blame a circuit which has stood for over a century or the FIA’s rules governing the new cars which race on it, the fact remains Monza will be the most extreme challenge for the latest generation of cars. The FIA has set the lowest harvesting limits of the season in a bid to reduce the notorious ‘super-clipping’ and drivers will have few chances to deploy energy around the lap. The ‘Temple of Speed’

Expect to see a lot of ‘towing’ in qualifying. Don’t expect to hear much from F1 Italian CEO Stefano Domenicali about the problem as he gazes across the stadiums packed with fans, most of which likely purchased their tickets long before the 2026 cars hit the track, and tells himself they don’t know or understand what ‘clipping’ is.

Ukraine’s appeal over FIA’s boost to Russia

The FIA’s sudden decision to soften its stance on Russia in the wake of its invasion of Ukraine will be challenged in its own Court of Appeal. F1 drivers previously spoke out against the war when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, but since then the FIA has tightened its rules on drivers making political statements.

Is the Formula 1 paddock happy with the FIA’s decision to help Russia burnish its reputation while it continues to kill Ukrainians and is accused of targeting other European nations?

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Ferrari or Antonelli?

Andrea Kimi Antonelli arrives at Monza with a 59-point lead over Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton. So who will get the loudest cheers?

It goes without saying that huge portions of the Italian crowd will be hoping for a Ferrari victory. But will the fans at Monza also take Italy’s new driving talent to heart – particularly now he’s in such a strong position in the championship?

Penalty gives opportunity to Antonelli’s rivals

Antonelli’s hopes of becoming the first Italian to win the Italian Grand Prix in 60 years have already suffered a blow as he will have to change his power unit this weekend, meaning he will start closer to the back.

That hands a useful opportunity to Hamilton as well as George Russell, who is also 59 points adrift.

McLaren ready rear wing upgrade

Another driver hoping to make inroads into Antonelli’s points lead is Lando Norris, the winner of the last two grands prix. He lies 83 points behind the Mercedes driver.

The good news for Norris is McLaren intend to race their new rear wing configuration, which it calls the ‘H-wing’ in reference to a sponsor.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Ferrari’s ADUO engine boost

Ferrari are expected to introduce their latest engine specification this weekend. The upgrade is allowed under F1’s new Additional Development Upgrade Opportunity regulations which are intended to balance the performance between the combustion engines.

With another high-speed circuit (sorry, ‘energy-poor track’) coming in three weeks’ time, it could prove a well-timed boost for Hamilton and Charles Leclerc.

Will Hadjar be back?

At the time of writing, Red Bull are yet to confirm whether Isack Hadjar will return to action this weekend following the wrist injury which prevented him from competing at Zandvoort.

Red Bull can hardly fault the job Liam Lawson did as his stand-in two weeks ago and it would be a surprise if they turned to anyone else. This would likely mean another call-up for Yuki Tsunoda to replace him at Racing Bulls: the team has tested Red Bull Junior Team member Nikola Tsolov since the last race but the Formula 2 championship leader does not have enough superlicence points to race in F1.

Update: Hadjar to miss Italian Grand Prix, Lawson and Tsunoda continue as substitutes

Will Hadjar get his podium back

Hadjar is also waiting to learn whether he will regain the third-place finish he scored in Monaco. The FIA Court of Appeal met after Zandvoort to hear Red Bull and McLaren’s arguments against the stewards’ decision to cancel Pierre Gasly’s two pit lane speeding penalties but a decision may yet take days or even weeks to emerge.

Sports.title: On This Day: Collins hands his car – and the championship – to Fangio | Brief
Sports.content:
70 years ago today Peter Collins surrendered his car to team mate and championship rival Juan Manuel Fangio during the Italian Grand Prix, in a remarkable gesture which ensured Fangio beat him to the 1956 world championship.

The Ferrari pair went into the final race of the season with Fangio on 30 points, eight ahead of Collins, who was tied with Maserati’s Jean Behra. Fangio’s steering arm broke 19 laps into the race and Luigi Musso, in another Ferrari, refused to hand his car to his team mate (as he had at the season-opener in Argentina).

Collins was running third when he pitted on lap 36, saw Fangio’s predicament, and handed over his car. Had Collins continued, with both Musso and Stirling Moss hitting trouble later in the race, he likely would have won it and beaten Fangio to the title.

Instead he and Fangio shared second place in the race and the latter took the title by three points from Moss. Fangio went on to win a fifth world title the following year, though Collins was killed in a crash in 1958.
