A woman from Amstelveen has contracted a rare form of meningitis from with the West Nile virus, the local health board has confirmed.

The 39-year-old woman is the fourth person known to have been infected with the virus in the Netherlands this year but the first to develop meningitis, which occurs in around 1% of cases.

West Nile virus is transmitted by mosquitos, but previously was caught by people who travelled abroad.

The public health agency RIVM said his year’s cluster of cases in humans, horses and birds show the diseased is now established in the Netherlands.

A week ago the RIVM confirmed that a man had died in hospital in Utrecht from West Nile fever after being infected locally. A woman in Drenthe died from the same illness, but she caught the virus while travelling.

The RIVM will publish an update on the current cases later this week. The agency stressed that the risk of serious illness or death is very low, with 80% of people reporting no symptoms at all.

Another 19% experience mild symptoms such as fever, headache, stomach ache and diarrhoea, as well as occasional skin rashes and swollen lymph nodes.

World.title: Police investigate threat video linked to Overasselt attack
World.content:
A video has surfaced on social media of masked men threatening an attack on Jan G. Jr, a resident of the property that was assaulted by armed men in Overasselt, Gelderland on Tuesday morning.

The video, which police have said they are investigating but has not yet been verified, shows four men in balaclavas, three holding automatic weapons. One reads out a statement in a heavy Spanish accent, accusing Jan G. Jr of stealing 1,283 kilograms of cocaine and two transport trucks.

“You have 12 hours to give the goods back and contact your ‘Belgian friend’”, the man reads, “after that we don’t want our goods anymore, but we promise we are going to kill everyone you love.”

The veracity of the video is still being analysed but it did not surface online before today, according to broadcaster NOS.

The video matches what Telegraaf and Het Parool have reported: that the shooting, in which more than 30 armed men killed a man and fired on police, was a gangland score settling.

Speculation has also been made that the attack was linked to drugs baron Jos “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers, who is wanted in both the Netherlands and Belgium for narcotics trafficking and other offences, and is suspected to be behind a drugs bust in Spain this year – the largest single shipment capture ever recorded.

Leijdekkers’ lawyers have released a statement denying he had any involvement in the incident, telling news service ANP he “firmly distances himself from the unfounded accusations being repeatedly made against him.”

Many residents in Overasselt want the family associated with Jan G. Jr gone. They told NOS they had lived through repeated trouble at the property and hoped the council would step in, with one saying they wanted the family out for good so people no longer had to live in fear. Most would only speak anonymously, saying they feared repercussions.

World.title: Cabinet set to postpone asset tax reform again to 2029
World.content:
Plans to reform the Netherlands’ asset tax system are likely to be delayed for another year as a result of the draft budget deal agreed at the weekend.

The cabinet had hoped to bring in a new mechanism for taxing assets, savings and investments to replace the fictional “box 3” interest rate by 2028.

But junior finance minister Eelco Eerenberg now looks set to withdraw the bill from the Senate to address criticism of the replacement system from opposition parties. If the vote is postponed it is unlikely that the bill can become law before 2029.

The previous system was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2021, when it ruled that taxing unrealised assets on a flat rate, based on the notional average annual return, violated the European Convention on Human Rights.

The rate was initially charged on all wealth above a basic threshold, regardless of whether they were invested in deposit return savings or high-risk investment vehicles with potentially much higher returns.

It also did not take into account overall market performance, so investors still paid tax on their assets even when they made a loss.

Capital gains

The new system planned to tax actual returns by making them submit details of all their savings and investments with their annual income tax return, which would add to the administrative burden.

But right-wing opposition parties want the government to introduce a capital gains tax, which investors pay on the money they make on their assets when they sell them.

In the meantime the cabinet has introduced an interim box 3 system with different fictional rates for deposit savings, investments and debts, which change every year to reflect market performance.

However, savers can claim a refund if they can show their actual returns were lower than the fictional amount, while not being required to pay more tax for higher returns.

The “best of both options” approach is estimated to cost the Dutch treasury some €2 billion a year.

World.title: Dutch central bank moves gold out of US and Canada
World.content:
The Dutch central bank (DNB) has moved about 86 tonnes of gold out of the United States and Canada to London, saying the reserves can be sold faster there in a crisis.

DNB said the transfer took place between March and August this year, and amounts to more than a quarter of the roughly 313 tonnes it had held in New York and Ottawa combined.

London is the world’s main trading centre for physical gold, and the bank said metal stored there is quicker to deploy than gold held in the US or Canada. It framed the move as part of wider work on “crisis readiness” amid growing geopolitical tension.

Most of the gold came out of the underground vault in Manhattan. Around 59 tonnes was sold in New York and bought back in London, which avoided melting down the bars and risking a loss of quality. A further 27 tonnes was physically shipped from the US and Canada to the DNB vault in Zeist, with the same quantity moved on from Zeist to London.

The share of Dutch gold held in New York has fallen from 31.3% to 18.5%, and Canada’s from 19.7% to 18.5%. London now holds the largest single share at 32.1%, up from 18.1%, while 30.8% remains in the Netherlands.

“We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” DNB president Olaf Sleijpen said.

DNB has repeatedly warned about Dutch reliance on the US since Donald Trump returned to the White House, though it has said it is not worried the US would seize the reserves. The Netherlands held 612.4 tonnes of gold, worth €72.2 billion, at the end of 2025.

World.title: Ex-ministers and diplomats urge tougher action against Israel
World.content:
More than 230 former Dutch ministers, ambassadors, diplomats and civil servants have called on the cabinet to take far tougher measures against Israel, including a full arms embargo and the suspension of the European Union’s trade agreement with the country.

The appeal comes as the Netherlands prepares to enforce its ban on settlement goods on September 22.

That measure led Israel to expel two Dutch officials from the US-backed Gaza ceasefire centre last week. The signatories say steps of this kind fall far short of what the situation demands.

Those who signed include former Amsterdam mayor Job Cohen, former foreign minister Jozias van Aartsen, former Rotterdam mayor Ahmed Aboutaleb, former development minister Jan Pronk and former defence minister Joris Voorhoeve.

According to NRC, the signatories held office for the Labour party (PvdA), the Christian Democrats (CDA) and the right-wing liberal VVD.

In the letter, the group calls for a complete arms embargo, the suspension of the EU-Israel trade agreement, and an investigation into possible involvement in international crimes by Dutch nationals and by Israelis living in the Netherlands who have served in the Israeli army.

The Netherlands already restricts some military exports to Israel. The signatories want measures that, in their words, match the scale of the violations taking place.

One of the signatories, former diplomat Angélique Eijpe, who left the foreign ministry over its stance on Gaza, said government policy had barely shifted. “We had cautiously hoped the Jetten cabinet would choose a different course,” she told broadcaster NOS in Dutch. “We see steps that mainly have a symbolic impact but do not bring about a change in behaviour.”

It is not the first such appeal – some of the same figures called for international intervention in Gaza a year ago, following a similar call earlier in 2025.

Eijpe said the group did not expect the letter to change policy overnight. “But the situation is so serious that we consider it necessary to keep putting it on the radar,” she told NOS.

World.title: Drummer Alex van Halen given knighthood in home city of Nijmegen
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Alex van Halen, one of two Dutch brothers who founded the US rock band Van Halen, has been given one of the Netherlands’ highest civil honours.

The 73-year-old drummer was made a knight in the Order of the Netherlands Lion after being nominated by his home city of Nijmegen.

The city said it had recognised Van Halen for his distinctive drumming style, calling it “powerful, dynamic and precise.”

Van Halen, who flew from the United States to receive the honour at a ceremony in from the mayor of Nijmegen, Hubert Bruls, said he was “very grateful”. He also signed the book of the city.

“I think institutions like this are important in people’s lives because it adds a dignity and a gravity to what we do,” he said.

“Whether it’s actually deserved or not, that’s another question. But we can live up to it.”

Nijmegen to Pasadena

Alex and his younger brother Eddie started the band in 1970, eight years after the family moved from Nijmegen to Pasadena in the United States.

Their best-known hits were Jump and Runnin with the Devil, distinguished by Eddie van Halen’s virtuoso performances on guitar.

Originally Eddie wanted to be a drummer while Alex played guitar, but the brothers swapped roles by the time they formed their first band in school, The Broken Combs. They were also classically trained pianists.

In 2019 part of the Hunnerpark was temporarily renamed Van Halenplein and a mural was painted in honour of Eddie van Halen.

The band Van Halen stayed together until Eddie’s death in 2020 at the age of 65.

World.title: Dutch woman living in Nepal found alive after surviving floods
World.content:
The Dutch foreign office has made contact with a woman living in Nepal who had been reported missing in the wake of last week’s devastating floods, which have killed more than 1,100 people.

Foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen said there had been “good news” as he spoke to reporters during a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

The woman is one of three Dutch nationals who were known to be in Nepal when a glacier in the Himalaya region collapsed last Wednesday, causing water and mud to surge down the Bhote Koshi river and wipe out villages in the Rawusa border region with Tibet.

She was in the Himalaya region when the disaster struck, but has reached the Nepalese capital Kathmandu, where she contacted the foreign ministry.

A spokesman said the government was still “very concerned about the fate of the two other Dutch nationals”, 29-year-old Christiaan Berghuis from Nijkerk and 51-year-old Maaike Moolhuijsen from Haarlem.

They were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred Tibetan mountain, when the floods hit. The group of 80 pilgrims were believed to be in an immigration office that was in the path of the floodwaters.

World.title: Cheap Chinese parcels to the Netherlands fall 46% after EU levy
World.content:
The number of small parcels arriving in the Netherlands from outside the EU fell by 46% in July and August compared with the previous six months, according to customs figures presented to parliament. It is the first clear sign that a new €3 import charge is changing the flow of cheap goods from China.

The drop was revealed by Eelco Eerenberg, the junior finance minister responsible for customs, during a debate in parliament on Tuesday.

Around one million such parcels were arriving in the Netherlands each day before the change, 80% to 90% of them from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.

Since July 1, a new EU-wide charge of €3 has applied to parcels worth up to €150 sent from outside the bloc, which were previously exempt from import duties. The fee is levied per type of product rather than per parcel, so an order containing several different items can be charged more than once.

Customs officials say online retailers are already changing how they operate, moving away from sending millions of individual packages and instead importing goods in bulk to store in warehouses inside the EU before shipping them on to shoppers. The same shift has been seen in France and Belgium.

“The figures give a first indication that fewer loose parcels are going straight to the consumer,” Nanette van Schelven, director-general of the Dutch customs service, told broadcaster NOS, “which makes it easier for us to check whether products are safe.”

A single large shipment is easier to screen for unsafe or banned goods, she said, than a constant stream of separate parcels.

The Dutch share

The charge raised about €134 million in import duties in July alone, of which roughly a quarter went to the Dutch treasury. Customs duties are collected as an EU revenue source: member states keep a share to cover the cost of collection and pass the rest to Brussels.

The Netherlands had drawn up plans for a national surcharge of its own on cheap parcels but dropped them in January, choosing to rely on the EU charge after France and Belgium shelved similar schemes and Brussels brought its levy forward.

World.title: Polish drone plant fire “undoubtedly” arson and likely ordered by Russia, says Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. There is now “no doubt” that a fire this week at a drone factory in Poland was caused deliberately, says Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who also suggested it was carried out on behalf of Russia. World.title: Polish court orders Catholic diocese to compensate child sex abuse victim and priest to apologise
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A court has ordered a Catholic diocese in Poland to pay 550,000 zloty (€128,250) in compensation to a woman who suffered sexual abuse as a child at the hands of a priest over four decades ago. It has also ruled that the priest himself must publish an apology to his victim and admit his guilt. The ruling, which can still be appealed, represents one of the largest compensation orders ever issued against Poland’s Catholic church, which has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations of clerical child sex abuse, as well as of negligence by bishops in dealing with such cases. Iwona Dudzik-Osińska, who has allowed her name to be published, was first raped in 1981 at the age of 12 by a priest, who has only been named so far as Father Jan and is now 76 years old, in the city of Kielce. The abuse continued for a period of three years, she revealed to the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. In 2007, Dudzik-Osińska decided to report the crimes to prosecutors, but was told that the statute of limitations had expired. In 2019, after the release of a major documentary on sex abuse in Poland’s Catholic church, she also informed Jan Piotrowski, the bishop of Kielce, of what she had suffered. Dudzik-Osińska said that the bishop was sympathetic but told her he could not meet her request to provide church funds to pay for therapy. However, she later received a bank transfer (for an amount that has not been revealed) from Piotrowski’s personal account. Meanwhile, Father Jan was suspended by the diocese of Sosnowiec, where he had been working since the 1990s, banned from contact with children, and brought before an internal church court. A spokeswoman for the Sosnowiec diocese confirmed to Gazeta Wyborcza that, in 2023, the church court removed Father Jan from public exercise of priestly ministry (though he remains in the priesthood) and ordered that he must reside at a location designated by the bishop (which has not been publicly revealed). In the meantime, Dudzik-Osińska launched a civil case against the church, demanding 900,000 zloty in compensation and an annual lifetime payment. The case lasted over four years, but in July the district court in Kielce issued a ruling, which is only now being reported. It ordered the Kielce diocese to pay the victim 550,000 zloty. Moreover, Father Jan must send a personal apology to Dudzik-Osińska in which he admits to sexually abusing her, and also publish such an apology and admission of guilt, under his real name, in a local newspaper, reports Catholic magazine Więź. The ruling can still be appealed by any of the parties involved. A spokesman for the diocese, Paweł Ścisłowicz, told Gazeta Wyborcza that they would only decide on further steps once the court had sent the justification for its decision. Dudzik-Osińska’s attorney, Michał Sochański, celebrated the ruling as “one of the first of its kind in Poland” and said that it “reflects an extremely important trend in case law that can offer hope to those sexually abused by clergy many years ago”. “Institutional mechanisms for resolving cases of sexual abuse in the church have proven insufficient for victims, but fortunately the court system remains an option,” he added. “Justice may come very late, but this verdict demonstrates that it is not unattainable.” A Catholic diocese has been ordered to pay compensation to a man sexually abused as a child by a priest. The victim was treated as an “accomplice in the sin of adultery” at a church trial that acquitted the priest, who was later convicted by a state court https://t.co/IHay5h56SG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2022 Poland’s Catholic church has in recent years faced a growing number of claims of sexual abuse by clergy and of negligence in dealing with the issue by bishops. The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Holy See announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”. Meanwhile, the Polish church has introduced new rules intended to protect children and other vulnerable people from abuse,held meetings with victims, and apologised for its neglect in dealing with such cases in the past. A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers. It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026 In 2018, a court in the city of Poznań ordered the Society of Christ, a Polish Catholic congregation, to pay 1 million zloty in compensation as well as lifelong monthly payments of 800 zloty to a woman who had been abused by one of its priests as a child. In 2022, the Catholic diocese of Toruń was ordered by a court to pay 600,000 zloty in compensation to a man who was sexually abused for almost a decade while serving as an altar boy. Last year, Bielsko-Żywiec diocese was ordered to pay 400,000 zloty to another victim, who is also seeking a further 20 million zloty in compensation from the archdiocese of Kraków A court has begun hearing the largest-ever compensation claim against Poland’s Catholic church by a victim of clerical sexual abuse. World.title: Poland grants Ukraine permission to search for remains of Ukrainians massacred by Polish partisans
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. The decision marks the latest step towards reconciliation between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Following a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv has also granted Poland permission to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists. On Tuesday, Ukrainian deputy culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi announced that the Polish authorities had granted a permit for a Ukrainian group to conduct exploratory work in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. The search aims to uncover the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by the Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), a major underground resistance movement that emerged in Poland during the German occupation of World War Two. Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population, was attacked by a Peasant Battalion unit on 10 March 1944, with some estimates suggesting around 300 civilians were killed. Among those who died was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa), Poland’s largest armed resistance movement, also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń. According to estimates, they killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Dariusz Kopciowski, the conservator of monuments in the Lublin province where Łasków is located, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that a permit for exploration work in Łasków had been granted. The issue had recently begun to cause tension, with Ukrainian media reporting last week that Ukraine has been waiting over a year for permission to carry out searches in Łasków. By contrast, Kyiv has granted permission for Poland to conduct such searches on its territory. Those Polish efforts are focused in particular on finding and exhuming the remains of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards those massacres as a genocide. However, Ukraine strongly rejects that label and also points to the fact that Polish partisan units killed Ukrainian civilians during the war. Poland, in turn, argues that many such incidents were acts of reprisal for the massacres carried out by Ukrainians. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine introduced a moratorium on search and exhumation work on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). The UPA led the Volhynia massacres but is still celebrated by many in Ukraine for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Last year, following negotiations with Poland, Ukraine lifted that moratorium and again began issuing permits for searches and exhumations of Polish victims on its territory, a number of which have already taken place. Last Sunday, Verbytskyi attended a funeral ceremony for 55 Polish massacre victims, around half of them children, whose remains were recently found and exhumed in a former Polish village located in what is now Ukraine. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, as well as those moves towards reconciliation, there have also been regular clashes between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, in particular following President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision in May this year to name a military unit after the UPA. That triggered strong protests from Poland, whose president, Karol Nawrocki, stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Poland has also expressed concern over a new national pantheon being established by Ukraine. It has warned that, if figures associated with the massacre of Poles are included, that could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poles eating more meat but drinking less alcohol
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, the latest data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show. The average person in Poland ate 82 kilograms of meat in 2025, which was 7.5% more than a year earlier. It also marks an increase of 15.7% since 2015 and 22.7% since 2005. Likewise, consumption of eggs rose 8.5% in 2025 to an average of 218 per person. The increases have come amid rapidly rising incomes, which make such products more affordable. A separate GUS study earlier this year showed that the proportion of Poles who cannot afford to eat meat at least every other day fell from 8.2% in 2015 to 3% in 2025. By contrast, vegetable consumption has changed little, with the average Pole eating 108 kg in 2025, compared with 107 kg a year earlier and 110 kg in 2005. However, consumption of potatoes, a starchy staple of the Polish diet presented by GUS separately from other vegetables, has fallen sharply over the longer term, despite a slight increase last year. The average Pole ate 96.5 kg of potatoes in 2025, down 23.4% since 2005. Meanwhile, alcohol consumption last year continued its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. In 2025, the amount of wine drunk per person, at 4.9 litres, fell even more, by 9.3% year-on-year. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. A 2023 study by ProVeg, an NGO, conducted in partnership with the University of Copenhagen and Ghent University, found that Poles were the most carnivorous among ten European countries surveyed. Three quarters of Poles (74%) said they ate meat frequently, compared to an average of 62% across all countries. Italians and Spaniards (both 69%) were the next biggest meat eaters, while Germans (45%), Austrians (48%) and the Dutch (53%) were the least likely to eat meat frequently. Meanwhile, 7% of people in Poland said they were either vegan (2%), meaning consuming no animal products at all, or vegetarian (5%), meaning they do not eat meat or fish. That was just below the European average of 8%. In terms of what kinds of meat are favoured by Poles, GUS’s most recent such breakdown, from 2017, showed that pork was most popular, with the average Pole consuming 39.8 kg that year, followed by poultry (26.kg) and beef (2.3 kg). Poland's first company to produce cultured meat – which is grown in a lab from animal cells without the need to raise and kill livestock – has received a state grant to support its work. From the start of the new school year, which began today, school canteens are expected to serve meat no more than twice a week, offer fish at least once per week, and offer a plant-based option at every meal. They should also limit fried food to no more than twice a week, use seasonal and locally sourced products, and include fruit and vegetables with meals. A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B. has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding that the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com/DlOn5GvyL5 — Elżbieta Raczyńska (@_eraczynska) August 25, 2026 Acting mayor Stanisław Kracik said that an inspection of the street carried out after the accident had not shown any problems with the existing signage or need for traffic-calming measures. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. It comes after a crash on Saturday in which four men died after their car was filmed driving at dangerously high speeds https://t.co/OSRvyPAtVA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2023 The police also claimed that Kraków is “one of the safest cities” in Poland, with 768 road accidents per 100,000 residents this year, compared to over 1,000 in some other cities. However, TVN points out that the same statistics show that, this year, Kraków has had 71 accidents per 100,000 inhabitants in which someone was injured or killed, compared to 28 in Katowice and 27 in Warsaw. Road safety in Poland has improved dramatically, with the country recording the EU’s largest decline in road deaths between 2019 and 2024. However, its overall number of road deaths in relation to population is still above the EU average. Road deaths have fallen by 35% in Poland since 2019, which is the largest decline in the EU. World.title: Polish student accused of planning Islamist terrorist attack on Christmas market to stand trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The suspect, a 19-year-old Pole, had become "infatuated with Islam", say the security services https://t.co/N4WDVZdlai — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 After news of Mateusz W.’s detention emerged, KUL suspended his student status. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents.
