World.title: Romanian Customs Authority launches new X-ray scanner at Constanța Port
World.content:
The Romanian Customs Authority announced that it put a new X-ray scanning system into operation at the Constanța Port. The equipment will allow non-intrusive inspections of freight vehicles and gives both sectors of the Black Sea port access to the same type of scanning technology.

The system produces higher-quality images and will be used to inspect vehicles selected through risk analysis, in accordance with the EU Customs Code.

It was purchased through an EU-funded project to equip border customs offices with scanners for vehicles and containers and establish a National Customs Image Analysis Center. The project forms part of Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) reforms aimed at modernizing the customs system and introducing electronic customs services.

Once integrated into the national analysis center, the scanners will allow customs images to be monitored and analyzed in real time, improving the coordination of inspections.

According to the authority, the technology will help detect illicit shipments and attempted customs fraud while reducing waiting times at border crossings. It is also expected to support more targeted interventions by operational inspection teams.

Constanța is the largest port on the Black Sea and one of the main entry points for goods into the European Union’s customs territory. The authority said equipping the entire port with modern scanners would strengthen controls at the EU’s external border while helping maintain the flow of cross-border traffic.

World.title: Croatia Sentences Bosnian Citizen for Glorifying Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Mural of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade. Photo: EPA/ANDREJ CUKIC

A Croatian court has handed a suspended prison sentence to a Bosnian national found guilty of glorifying the late convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

Police from the Korenica Border Police Station announced on Tuesday that they had filed a misdemeanour charge against a 43-year-old over social media posts in which he glorified Mladic. According to police, the man posted photos, symbols, songs and texts on social media that “publicly honoured and expressed gratitude to a person convicted of war crimes”.

Mladic was convicted by the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. He died aged 84 in a UN jail in The Hague on August 26.

In the posts, among other things, the man thanked Mladic for “freedom” and said “he will never be forgotten”. The police stated that such content caused agitation and distress among citizens and so constituted an offence under the Law on Misdemeanours Against Public Order and Peace.

Following an investigation, the 43-year-old was brought before a court, which sentenced him to 15 days in prison but suspended the sentence.

The man had been living in Korenica as a foreign worker with a temporary residence permit.

Such cases are not uncommon in Croatia.

On August 28, police arrested 31-year-old Serbian influencer, Marko Stojkovic, in Split after he displayed tattoos depicting Draza Mihailovic, a Serbian World War II collaborator with the Nazis who is considered a war criminal in Croatia. He was charged with disturbing public order and peace as well as violating the Anti-Discrimination Act.

“By publicly displaying several inappropriate images tattooed on his body, he disturbed public order and peace and, with the aim of causing fear and creating a hostile and humiliating environment, violated human dignity and caused public unrest,” Split police announced, adding that his behaviour also violated the Anti-Discrimination Act.

The court sentenced Stojković to 15 days in prison. Following the conclusion of the proceedings, he will be expelled from Croatia and banned from re-entering the country for the next five years.

World.title: Serbia’s Grief Over Mladic’s Death is Neither Honourable Nor Dignified
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

On August 27, I received a push notification on my phone saying that Ratko Mladic had died.

In Serbia, where denial of war crimes has become part of official policy, and where everyone is now waiting for elections to be announced, I knew we would likely miss this opportunity to deal with the past in a dignified and responsible manner.

If it is true that the past is the story we tell ourselves about ourselves, then our story perfectly explains what is keeping us trapped.

World.title: Serbia NGOs Condemn Push to Allow Construction on Fire-Damaged Land
World.content:
Two non-governmental organisations, Transparency Serbia and the Renewables and Environmental Regulatory Institute, RERI, on Wednesday criticised newly adopted law amendments that may allow construction on sites where forest has been destroyed by wildfires.

The amendments to the Law on Planning and Construction, adopted by parliament on August 31, allow for the construction of public infrastructure facilities, or facilities for which a public interest has been established.

“All of this took place during the horrific and unprecedented wildfires that engulfed Deliblatska Pescara (Debilato Sands), the largest sandy area in Europe, an invaluable reservoir of biodiversity that is a protected area of exceptional (Category I) and national importance, as well as a Special Nature Reserve,” the organisations said in a press release.

The amendments stipulate that “forest land where the forest has been damaged or destroyed by fire” retains the designation assigned to it by the planning document in force prior to the fire.

But they also state that an exception to this rule allows a change of land use where it is necessary to implement a project for which a public interest has been established, or for the construction of public infrastructure facilities.

Transparency Serbia and RERI also noted that the provisions concerning construction on forest land damaged by fire were not included in the original draft law submitted by the government to parliament but were introduced through amendments adopted at a session of the parliamentary committee.

This further reduced the transparency of the legislative process, they said.

“The lack of transparency in the authorities’ handling of these legislative amendments, rather than reassuring an alarmed and concerned public, has instead opened the door to further suspicions regarding the future fate of the land affected by the fires,” their press release added.

More than 3,500 hectares of Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve in northern Serbia were impacted by severe wildfires in August. There have been active wildfires in other parts of Serbia. The wildfires affecting the Deliblato Sands and other areas have burned around 13,920 hectares, according to Copernicus data as of 26 August.

World.title: Kosovo President’s Election Jeopardised by Party’s Inner Divisions
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku at a press conference on Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Six MPs from the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, will not follow the decision of the party’s leadership on a joint presidential candidate with the ruling Vetevendosje Movement, potentially jeopardising a possible end to Kosovo’s political crisis and prompting yet another election.

The six have been named as Avdullah Hoti, Hykmete Bajrami, Arben Gashi, Armend Zemaj, Kujtim Shala and Janina Ymeri.

“They are causing irreparable harm to the entire process and – inevitably and unnecessarily – driving the country toward snap elections,” LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku told the media on Tuesday.

“This position is detrimental to Kosovo and to the LDK. Any future elections triggered by this refusal – given that the candidate was excellent – will have electoral consequences that consolidate absolute power and will impact the LDK itself,” he added.

On Monday, following a meeting between Vetevendosje and LDK leaders Albin Kurti and Abdixhiku, the latter announced Bekim Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and former diplomat, as their joint pick for the presidential post.

But soon after, former PM and LDK MP Avdullah Hoti went on Facebook to warn that he does “not support this candidacy for President of the Republic of Kosovo – not for personal reasons but based on a political and institutional principle”, hinting at the divisions within the LDK.

Acting PM Kurti told the media on Tuesday evening, after Abdixhiku’s announcement, that a fresh election now looked more likely.

“After three rounds of elections [since February 2025], it appears there is a desire, will and an interest to head into a fourth election in less than two years,” he said. He added that a new meeting with Abdixhiku was needed.

In the last elections, in June, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the next-placed Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, which won 22 seats. The LDK came third with 18 seats – but only 12 of these would now vote for the chosen president.

Vetevendosje has claimed it can call on 62 votes to form a new government, again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

But in the presidential election, Sejdiu must win at least 80 MPs’ votes in the first two rounds. In a potential third round, he would need a simple majority of only 61 votes.

The announcement of the joint presidential candidate was a move to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since the parliamentary elections in June. Parliament has yet to be inaugurated, as the parties have not agreed on the next president. Without an agreement, new elections seem inevitable.

Amid the institutional logjam, the provisional speaker, Avni Dehari, from Vetevendosje, refused to resume the inaugural session that started on August 6.

Vetevendosje also refused to submit a name for the new speaker, first demanding an agreement with the other parties on the new president.

World.title: ‘This Is How We Lived Here’: Documenting 16 Years in Hungary Under Orban
World.content:
Those who stayed

The vast majority, of course, stayed in Hungary and adopted different survival strategies.

A journalist working for Hungary’s public service broadcaster confessed to Varadi that now he feels he was a coward. He was “only” responsible for cultural content, did not have to do political reporting, but he was one of the hundreds who helped operate what many now refer to as “a factory of lies and propaganda” on state channels.

“I never crossed a professional red line myself,” he justifies in the interview, but goes on to admit that he earned a good salary that afforded him and his family a comfortable life.

While many talk about intimidation, self-censorship and adaption to the system, some stories prove that courage did sometimes pay off. A man who worked on development projects in a provincial town described the mounting pressure he felt from local authorities to award projects – and the public money that came with them – to Fidesz-aligned companies. Yet he did not bow, and decided to maintain strict application criteria. He was prepared to be fired, but to his surprise nothing happened. There were no reprisals.

The conversations often take a turn and raise questions about individual or joint responsibility. “Many people ask the question how could this all happen to us? And above all: why did we let it happen?” Varadi says.

Did Hungarian society simply follow the century-old patterns of making compromises, adapting and succumbing to pressure in order to survive, as was done under the rule of the Turks, the Habsburgs and the Soviets?

“One thing is for sure: there were no guns pointed at people’s heads,” Peter Kreko, director of the Budapest-based Political Capital, tells BIRN.

Kreko, a social psychologist, finds it perhaps most surprising that Orban managed to keep his grip on power for 16 years without resorting to violence, primarily through the manipulation of information. “This was a perfect ‘information autocracy’,” he says.

Kreko believes people always had a choice, and this was especially true for those working for the state media or the public administration. But many followed what historian Timothy Snyder has described as ‘anticipatory obedience’: trying to figure out what is expected of them and behave accordingly.

When it comes to conformism or adaptation, Kreko says, Hungary is not very different from its regional peers, but it is certainly true that Hungarian society has a historical tendency to bow to authoritarian leaders.

“What we see is that many people were afraid, felt intimidated,” is how Varadi explains it. Many feared negative consequences if they spoke up. Many sacrificed their right to free speech for their comfortable lives. And by doing so, many became accomplices of the system.

Stefano Bottoni, an Italian-Hungarian historian researching Central European modern history, points to the general lack of solidarity and mistrust in Hungarian society. “There were no institutions people would have trusted. The most common channel to rebel against the system was to write angry Facebook posts,” Bottoni tells BIRN.

He believes stronger trade unions, something like Solidarity in Poland in the 1980s, would have helped build critical communities, but they are virtually non-existent in Hungary. “We helped weaken the resilience of the system, believing that we don’t need those institutions, we will figure out a survival method all by ourselves,” he says.

Varadi shares this analysis: “Many people felt powerless and left alone. When the teachers went on to strike there was virtually no solidarity from the society.”

World.title: ‘Marine Landfills’: The Garbage Choking Greece’s Seas
World.content:
Last year, on his annual visit to Corfu, Giorgos Kontarinis photographed sun loungers, a pedalo and various other objects on the seabed off Imerolia, a village on the north side of the island.

A keen diver, he took another look this year.

“I went swimming to the spot where I had found the rubbish last summer, wanting to see if anyone had taken the trouble to pick it up,” said 59-year-old Kontarinis, a photojournalist at the leading Greek press photo agency Eurokinissi.

“I was shocked when I saw the same sight again.”

Such a sight is becoming increasingly common in tourist resorts across Greece.

“We’re talking about marine landfills,” said Giorgos Sarelakos, head of the volunteer environmental organisation Aegean Rebreath.

Since 2017, Aegean Rebreath has organised seabed clean-up operations in over 60 areas across the country; it was also the initiator of the Blue Municipalities Network, the first network composed of local municipalities for the protection of the marine environment.

Plastic makes up most of the waste, according to George Papatheodorou, Professor and Director of Oceanus-Lab at the Department of Geology, University of Patras, Peloponnese.

Worse still, large parts of the Greek seabed remain “essentially unexplored”, he warned.

World.title: Demirovski: Macedonian Ammo Maker Untouched by Scandals in Serbia
World.content:
At roughly six o’clock on the morning of July 22, 2024, there was a knock at the door of a 36-year-old weapons engineer in Serbia.

Identified by Serbian authorities by the initials M.O., the man was in bed with his wife, sleeping. His two children were also asleep. His wife got up and opened the door. Police officers in balaclavas stormed inside, accompanied by Serbian security agents, and pinned M.O. to the floor.

The same night, two other weapons engineers, 64-year-old D.L. and 63-year-old D.M., were also arrested.

All three men had previously worked for the state-owned arms manufacturer Krusik. They were suspected of supplying confidential information on Krusik’s production of 120-mm mortar rounds to a company in neighbouring North Macedonia for which they had also done work - ATS Group, owned by Shefshet Demirovski.

It was not the first time Demirovski’s name had surfaced in a case of alleged industrial espionage in Serbia. In 2019, prosecutors accused him of bribing a former employee of Serbian ammunition producer Prvi Partizan to supply him with confidential specifications concerning production machinery.

The 2024 arrests underscored the intensity of competition between defence manufacturers in the Balkans, where Serbia boasts one of the biggest military industries, supplying battlefields across the world.

As global demand for arms and ammunition from the Balkans has increased, so too has the rivalry.

Enter Demirovski, about whom there is scarce publicly available information.

Backed by the state and boasting close ties with Turkey, the 50-year-old businessman has built one of North Macedonia’s most ambitious private defence manufacturers producing small-calibre ammunition.

“God, I wish we had more people like Sheki in this country,” a former government official told BIRN, referring to Demirovski by his nickname.

Demirovski’s alleged activities in Serbia, however, reveal a less savoury side to his success, as well as possible ties to the country’s criminal underworld.

Demirovski did not respond to questions sent to his official email address and via Viber, though the Viber messages were registered as ‘seen’.

World.title: ‘Polish Annexation’ Hoax Campaign Spotlights Czech Disinformation Vulnerability
World.content:
A podcast interview with investigative journalist Lukas Valasek for Seznam Zpravy on Monday laid out a recent well-organised, large-scale disinformation campaign that pushed the notion Poland was preparing to invade and annex a small border area with its southern neighbour around the twin towns of Ciezyn/Tesin.

“It is the first ever operation of this scale,” assessed Valasek. “If we understand this whole thing as a test from a potential Russian actor on how the Czech Republic will respond to a wave of disinformation, then I think that the Czech political scene, and especially the government, did not quite pass.”

The campaign last week relied on paid Facebook ads, AI-generated images, a fake website mimicking Czech Radio’s iRozhlas.cz, as well as fake social media accounts of both ordinary citizens and top officials, including Czechia’s ambassador to Poland.

The apparent goal, most have deduced, was to spark fears of a land grab and property seizures while stirring up historical grievances between the two EU and NATO countries linked to a controversial 1958 border treaty between Poland and then-Czechoslovakia.

According to Czech security expert Bohumil Kartous, the campaign bore all the hallmarks of a Russian-backed hybrid operation, exploiting “a fragment of truth” – the lingering, albeit relatively minor Czech-Polish border dispute – to place it “in a completely different context of fear over losing property”.

“The goal is precisely to trigger a dispute within this pro-Ukrainian coalition,” according to Kartous.

It appears to have mostly missed the mark. Poland was fastest to respond on August 25, with Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski quickly dismissing the claims of imminent annexation as absurd and orchestrated. On August 26, as a symbol of Czech-Polish unity, Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted an image of friendship between the countries’ most famous cartoon characters, the Polish dog Reksio and the Czech mole Krtek, captioning: “Reksio and Krtek have known this for a long time, Poland and Czechia are true friends.”

But over the border the response took longer and was more muddled, with finger-pointing now underway to determine who was to blame for these failings. It took several days for the Czech Foreign Ministry to unequivocally reject “the spread of false information about alleged Polish territorial claims to the Czech Republic”.

Czech President Petr Pavel also weighed in: “This is a targeted provocation. And I’m very glad that people are not listening to this provocation on either side of the border,” going on to assure that “Poland is one of the Czech Republic’s closest and most important partners.”

Czech hesitancy

Yet late last week, Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis lashed out against his intelligence services, saying he had only heard about the ongoing hoax campaign through the media.

On Monday, he again pointed the finger at the Office for Foreign Relations and Information (UZSI) and blamed Czechia’s envoy in Poland, Bretislav Dancak, for the failed response.

Although evidently failing to drive a wedge between Prague and Warsaw, security experts said such a campaign could be used to test both Polish and Czech responses to hybrid threats and influence ops.

Highlighting the decision to entirely scrap the Strategic Communications Department (Stratkom) shortly after taking office, on top of reducing the number of ministerial experts focused on disinformation, many argue the Czech government only has itself to blame.

“If, by chance, there had still been any strategic communication of the state, analysts would have caught [the disinformation campaign] long before and the top representatives of the state could have communicated it,” argued former Stratkom chief Oldrich Bruza. “At least we have our Polish brothers.”

Opposition politicians, too, have accused the government of bringing this upon itself. “We have repeatedly warned about this,” said former foreign minister Jan Lipavsky. “For ideological reasons, the government is liquidating the state’s capacities for combating disinformation and influence operations at the very time when someone is using them against the Czech Republic.”

Hints of Russian involvement abound, but officials have so far refrained from unequivocally accusing Moscow of being behind the operation. Intelligence services in both Poland and Czechia are still investigating the matter.

But in Prague the finger-pointing continues. “We don’t need a Strategic Communications Department,” argued Prime Minister Babis. “We have [intelligence] services here that are supposed to work for the state, for the people and for the interests of the state.”

While failings at the top were evident, the response from the local population did not disappoint, with social media quickly flooded with montages of Reksio and Krtek as long-time chums, nipping in the bud any fears of cross-border animosity.

World.title: This Map Shows Just How Hot Croatia Has Been This Summer
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – This map shows just how hot Croatia has been this summer, with drought and unstable rainfall causing serious agriculture issues.

The State Hydrometeorological Institute (DHMZ) has published an analysis of temperature and precipitation amounts for summer 2026. Index reports that the data shows that almost the whole of Croatia had an extremely warm summer, while parts of the country, especially the east and part of central Croatia, were markedly dry. The mean seasonal air temperature during the summer was noticeably higher than the average for the reference period 1991–2020. According to DHMZ data, deviations of the mean temperature ranged from 1.8 °C in Daruvar and Makarska to as much as 3.3 °C at Puntijarka and Zavižan.

an extremely hot summer for croatia

According to the percentile distribution, summer 2026 has so far been extremely warm across almost the entire territory of Croatia. The only exceptions were Varaždin and Daruvar, where the summer was classified in the very warm category. The DHMZ map shows that very large temperature deviations were recorded throughout the country. In addition to Puntijarka and Zavižan, where the temperature was 3.3 degrees above normal, in Parg, Senj and Gospić the deviation amounted to 2.9 °C. In Osijek the mean summer temperature was 2.8 °C above normal, in Dubrovnik 2.7 °C, and in Zagreb, Bjelovar and Pazin 2.4 °C above the average. Percentiles at numerous stations were very close to the maximum values. In Osijek, at Puntijarka, Zavižan and in Dubrovnik they amounted to 99.9, which shows how unusually warm the summer was in relation to the climatological normal.

droughts caused serious issues for eastern and central croatia

DHMZ also published data on precipitation amounts. Deviations relative to the 1991–2020 normal ranged from only 24.7 percent in Gradište, where 51.2 millimetres of rain fell, to 119.2 percent on Rab, where 193.5 millimetres were measured. The most pronounced precipitation deficit was recorded in the east of the country. Gradište and Slavonski Brod had an extremely dry summer. The map shows that in Gradište only about a quarter of the usual summer precipitation amount fell, while in Slavonski Brod around 37 percent of the normal was recorded.

Very dry conditions were recorded in Osijek, Daruvar and Parg, as well as in the western part of central Croatia, i.e. in the area of Zagreb, Puntijarka, Sisak and Karlovac. In Zagreb and Karlovac around 51 percent of the usual precipitation amount was recorded.

rainfall along most of the coast was relatively normal

It was also dry in the vicinity of Križevci, Ogulin and Gospić, at Zavižan and on Lastovo and Vis, i.e. at the Komiža station. In the rest of Croatia the precipitation amount was within normal limits. This also applies to a large part of the Adriatic, including Rijeka, Senj, Zadar, Šibenik, Split, Makarska and Dubrovnik. Thus, summer 2026 has been one of exceptional temperature terms across all of Croatia, while the distribution of precipitation was considerably more uneven, with a particularly pronounced drought in the east and in part of central Croatia.

World.title: Kaljski dialect Officially Declared Protected Cultural Asset of Croatia
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – The Kaljski dialect from Kali has officially been declared a protected cultural asset of the Republic of Croatia.

The Kaljski dialect, spoken in Kali on the island of Ugljan, has officially become part of Croatia’s protected intangible heritage. By decision of the Ministry of Culture and Media dated the 26th of August, this specific island speech has been entered into the Register of Cultural Assets of the Republic of Croatia under the designation Z-8010. Morski reports that the Kaljski dialect is a distinctive speech that belongs to the Central Chakavian dialect of the Chakavian dialect group. In its explanation, the competent ministry particularly emphasised its unique linguistic structure, as well as the invaluable role it plays in preserving the local identity, rich history, customs and everyday life of the residents of Kali.

This prestigious recognition is the result of many years of effort and dedication by the entire local community. Side by side in the preservation and promotion of the indigenous expression are the “Srdelica” Kindergarten, the Kali Branch School and the parent “Valentin Klarin” Primary School, with strong support from the Kali Public Library, numerous local associations, the Tourist Board and the Municipality of Kali itself.

The particular value of this linguistic story lies in contemporary projects aimed at documenting and transmitting the speech. As part of the Kalipedia project, an extensive online dictionary has been created that today numbers around three and a half thousand words enriched with authentic audio recordings. At the same time, through the Kalamra project, free speech recordings of residents of all generations have been recorded and digitised, while the “Kualjska besida” initiative systematically encourages children and young people to creative and literary expression in their native Chakavian. With the official acquisition of the status of a cultural asset, concrete protection measures have also been secured. In the coming period, detailed documentation, scientific research and the lasting transmission of the Kaljski dialect to new generations will be carried out, with the continued active engagement of the entire local community.

World.title: Around 78,000 People Were Registered as Unemployed in Croatia in July
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – Approximately 78,000 people were formally registered as being unemployed in Croatia back in July, which is a figure that is 0.1% less than in June.

Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that Eurostat estimates that 13.5 million people were unemployed across the EU back in July, of whom 11.3 million were in the Eurozone. According to a report by the European statistical office Eurostat, the unemployment rate in the Eurozone and the European Union remained more or less entirely unchanged in July compared with June, while it slightly decreased in Croatia. Specifically, it stood at 6.4 percent across the Eurozone and 6.1 percent at EU level. Compared with the same month last year, the unemployment rate rose by 0.1 percentage points.

Furthermore, Eurostat estimates that 13.5 million people were unemployed across the EU in July, of whom 11.3 million were in the Eurozone. Looking at the situation on a monthly basis, the number of unemployed people fell by 41,000 across the EU, while it remained unchanged in the Eurozone. As for Croatia specifically, the unemployment rate back in July stood at 4.3 percent, which is 0.1 percentage points lower than it was in June and half a percentage point lower than in the same month in 2025. Around 78,000 people were registered as formally unemployed in July, which is 1,000 fewer than the previous month and 8,000 fewer than back in July 2025.

Countries with a lower unemployment rate than Croatia were the Czech Republic (3.3 percent), Poland (3.4 percent), Malta and neighbouring Slovenia (both 3.5 percent), Bulgaria (3.6 percent), Cyprus (3.9 percent), and Germany and the Netherlands (both 4 percent). The highest rates were recorded in Finland (10.5 percent), Spain (10 percent) and Sweden (8.7 percent). For Croatia, Eurostat also publishes quarterly data on youth unemployment. In the second quarter of 2026, that particular rate stood at 16.4 percent, with around 19,000 young people registered as formally unemployed.

World.title: Jadrolinija Extends Sailing Season for High Speed Zadar-Ancona Line
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – Jadrolinija has decided to extend its sailing season for the high speed Zadar-Ancona line until September the 6th.

Jadrolinija has stated that for its very first season of operation, the high speed Zadar-Ancona line has achieved positive results and great interest from passengers on both sides of the Adriatic. Poslovni reports that Croatia’s largest ferry company, Jadrolinija, will extend the first season of the high speed Zadar–Ancona line until the 6th of September due to excellent passenger interest.

“Jadrolinija has extended the sailing season for this line until the 6th of September, with additional trips on Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays, as well as promotional ticket prices. For adults the ticket costs 80 euros while children aged 3 to 12 travel for 40 euros,” Jadrolinija stated. They recalled that they introduced the high-speed Zadar–Ancona line this year as a new international connection that brings the Croatian and Italian sides of the Adriatic coast closer and enables travel between the two cities in approximately four hours on the vessel Jelena, which has a capacity of 400 passengers.

The strong interest from passengers on both sides of the Adriatic and the good response confirms the importance of fast, simple and direct connections between Croatia and Italy outside of air travel. It also confirms the Zadar-Ancona line’s potential for the further development of tourist and transport links between the two coastlines.

Back in 2025, Jadrolinija carried 12.6 million passengers, which is on a par with the previous record year and confirms stable demand, as well as 3.8 million vehicles, which is two percent more vehicles than the previous year. The growth and trend of these operational indicators are also accompanied by positive financial results. Jadrolinija’s fleet now comprises 58 vessels with an average age of 27.8 years, which is below the European average of around 33 years. Fleet renewal remains the company’s most important strategic project.

World.title: Has the Much Anticipated Croatian Robotaxi Failed?
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Has the Croatian robotaxi story ended? It has been revealed that Mate Rimac’s Verne may need to return 89.7 million euros if it is determined that the project has indeed failed.

The company Verne, which has been engaged in developing the much anticipated robotaxi project, is prepared to return 89.7 million euros in advance payments drawn from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan if the evaluation of what has been achieved so far in the project shows that the contracted obligations have not been fully met. “The company is prepared to return all funds,” Verne said in its announcement.

an ongoing procedure

The Verne project, partially financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), officially ended on the 31st of August, but the key part of the procedure is still to come, the final evaluation that will show whether all contracted obligations have been fulfilled. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the company has stated, as touched on above, that it is prepared to return all funds if the competent authorities determine that the objectives have not been fully achieved, according to the announcement. The company has so far drawn 89.7 million euros in advance payments from the NPOO project, while it has raised more than 140 million euros from various private investors.

The Verne robotaxi project has therefore formally ended, but the procedure is not finished. Within one month, Verne must submit a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that documentation, the competent authorities will carry out the final evaluation and determine what of the contracted obligations has actually been fulfilled.

what we know so far

The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, testing has been carried out, and regulations have been adopted. “The project ended on the 31st of August. The company is now submitting, within one month, a report on all activities carried out, costs incurred and final results achieved. On the basis of that report, the competent authorities will make the final evaluation of the project, i.e. an assessment of what has been successfully fulfilled in the project,” Verne stated.

According to the company’s claims, some of the objectives have already passed the verification of the competent institutions. The delivery of all prototypes of fully autonomous electric vehicles envisaged by the project has been verified, appropriate testing has been carried out, and regulations governing autonomous driving have been adopted. However, three remaining objectives still need to receive a final assessment, and the outcome of the project will largely depend on them. These are: the issuance of 50,000 free vouchers for rides in fully autonomous vehicles to persons with disabilities, the production of fully autonomous electric vehicles adapted to the needs of passengers with disabilities, and the establishment and operational readiness of specialised infrastructure.

multiple amendments have already been made

“In the implementation of the project so far, the competent institutions have verified that all verification prototypes of fully autonomous and electric vehicles have been successfully delivered, that appropriate testing has been carried out, and that regulations on autonomous driving have been adopted,” the company stated. They add that the public will be informed after the competent authorities complete the procedure of assessing the success of the project.

The main result of the project, for which Project 3 Mobility was approved 179.5 million euros from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, was supposed to be a fully autonomous electric vehicle of the fifth level of autonomy. That objective did not change even after multiple amendments to the contract and extensions of deadlines. The Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure particularly emphasised this back in April, when the last annex to the contract was signed.

The fifth level represents the highest level of autonomy. Such a vehicle does not need a driver and is not limited to predefined areas or driving conditions. Neither Verne nor any other company in the world has a vehicle of that level of autonomy today.

there are still many unknowns in the story

As Mate Rimac revealed recently, the fact is that Verne has, in addition to EU funds, also attracted more than 140 million euros in private funds. The robotaxi is already driving the streets of Zagreb. Uber is a strategic partner, and Pony.ai is the technology partner. Verne will be the owner of the fleet and the operator of the service, Pony.ai will provide the autonomous driving solution, while Uber will integrate the service into its global ride-hailing network, which will be an additional option alongside the Verne application. Together, the companies are building a commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb, and over time also in additional European and international markets, with plans to expand to a fleet of thousands of autonomous vehicles in the coming years.

“It’s difficult even to determine precise deadlines for when this will become a profitable business. It’s a kind of adventure, but all partners see potential in it. It will be a great story, but realistically it will take quite a lot of time. It wouldn’t be particularly serious to forecast now when this will be a sustainable business model,” was Rimac’s answer to the question about the profitability of the robotaxi business itself.

World.title: Petition Launched After Removal of Lokrum Nudist Beach
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – A petition has been launched by dissatisfied local people following the removal of a favourite Lokrum nudist beach.

The decision to remove the signs marking out the way to a favourite Lokrum nudist beach has sparked a wave of reactions among residents of Dubrovnik. Morski reports that after the signs were taken down, a group of people decided to take concrete steps and launched a petition calling for a solution that would allow the long-standing practice to continue.

“With this petition, we wish to encourage those responsible to find a legal framework for the lawful continuation of the tradition of naturism on the island of Lokrum. Back during the mid-1960s, with the establishment of the Lokrum Reserve, signs designating a swimming area for nudists were put up by the institution above the cliffs on the eastern side of the island of Lokrum.”

As a reminder, the public first learned about the removal of the signs from a reaction by Professor Igor Legaz, who confirmed on the 26th of August that the signs pointing to the Lokrum nudist beach had been removed, noting that the nudist beach in that area had operated contrary to the applicable regulations.

“This concerns a stretch of coastline about 300 metres long, characterised by a series of large natural stone slabs, which has been under general use since yesterday. For that reason, I thank the Management of the Lokrum Reserve and the director for the step they have taken, because that ‘special-purpose beach’ on the island of Lokrum had in any case been established contrary to the provision of Article 80, paragraph 2, point 2 of the Maritime Domain and Seaports Act,” Legaz said.

While part of the public welcomes the alignment of the situation on the ground with the Maritime Domain Act, the initiators of the petition emphasise the historical and cultural significance of that section of the coast and appeal to the competent institutions to find an appropriate model that would allow the lawful retention of the naturist tradition on the beautiful island of Lokrum.

World.title: September Sea Temperature Records Broken in Split and Komiža
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – The September sea temperature records have been broken in both Split and Komiža, with strong warmth still beating down on the Croatian coast.

The sea was unusually warm along a large part of the Croatian coast on the first day of September. According to DHMZ data, at 14:00 yesterday, the temperature measured in Split was 28.0 degrees, in Komiža 28.2 degrees, and near Dubrovnik it also stood at 28.2 degrees. Index reports that the sea is even warmer on Mljet. In Malo jezero at 2 p.m. as much as 30.2 degrees was measured, in Veliko jezero 29.9 degrees, while on the open sea near Mljet the temperature was 28.8 degrees.

september records have been broken in split and Komiža

Data from both Split and Komiža is particularly interesting. According to the DHMZ bulletin for September 2025, the previous absolute September maximum in Split was measured at 27.3 degrees, measured on the 2nd of September 2015. In Komiža, the record was also 27.3 degrees, set on the 2nd of September 2024. Yesterday afternoon’s 28.0 degrees in Split is therefore 0.7 degrees higher than the previous September record, while Komiža with 28.2 degrees exceeded the old record by as much as 0.9 degrees. These are operational DHMZ data, so the final values will be confirmed after data processing. For comparison, during the whole of September last year the highest measured value in Split was 25.0 degrees, and in Komiža 24.6 degrees. Even in the very warm September of 2024, the maximum recorded in Split was 27.0 degrees. The average sea temperature in Split that September was 24.0 degrees, a full 1.7 degrees above the climatic average for the period 1991–2020.

a mere 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that particular station

Yesterday afternoon’s 28 degrees in Split is only 1.4 degrees lower than the absolute record for that specific station. In Split back on the 15th of July 2024 a temperature of 29.4 degrees was measured. Values from Mljet should not be directly compared with the long-term series from Split and Komiža. Malo and Veliko jezero are measured by automatic sensors and aren’t part of the same long-term series of the four stations – Rab, Split, Hvar and Komiža – that DHMZ uses in monthly analyses of September sea temperatures. Surface sea temperature at the classic stations is measured approximately 30 centimetres below the surface.

World.title: Croatia Records Modest Tourism Growth in First Half of 2026 as EU Nights Rise 1.7%
World.content:
September the 2nd, 2026 – Eurostat reports that Croatia has recorded modest tourism growth throughout the entire first half of 2026, as EU overnight stays rise.

Over the first six months of 2026, tourist accommodation establishments across the European Union recorded 1,321 million overnight stays, a 1.7% increase compared with the same period in 2025 (1,299 million nights), according to official data released by Eurostat on 1 September 2026. Eurostat reports that while the EU as a whole continued its recovery and expansion, growth was highly uneven across member states. The strongest increases were recorded in Ireland (+14.6%), Malta (+9.9%) and Slovakia (+5.9%). Nine countries registered declines, with the sharpest falls in Cyprus (–7.7%) and Romania (–6.7%).

Croatia, long one of Europe’s leading tourism destinations, registered only a mild increase of approximately 0.5% in overnight stays during the same period. This placed the country near the bottom of the group of member states that still achieved positive growth, just ahead of Finland and the nine countries that recorded outright declines.

international visitors drive the numbers up

Foreign (non-resident) tourists accounted for 48.9% of all overnight stays in the EU in the first half of 2026. Nights spent by international visitors grew by 2.5%, nearly three times the increase recorded by domestic guests (+0.9%). Dependence on foreign visitors varies dramatically across the bloc. Malta (95.2%), Cyprus (92.6%) and Luxembourg (87.7%) recorded the highest shares of foreign overnight stays, while Germany (18.5%), Poland (19.8%) and Romania (23.0%) remained heavily reliant on domestic tourism.

Croatia’s modest 0.5% growth comes against a backdrop of strong overall EU performance and particularly rapid expansion in several smaller markets. The figures cover the traditionally quieter first half of the year, before the peak summer season. Full-year results will depend heavily on performance in July, August and the shoulder months of September and October. Eurostat’s data underlines that while tourism demand in Europe remains resilient, competition for visitors is intensifying and growth is no longer automatic even for established destinations.

World.title: Estonia's defense minister resigns in national defense procurement scandal
World.content:
The National Audit Office's criticisms of the activities of the EDF and the Center for Defense Investments are serious enough that the defense minister should resign, Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) said.

Pevkur told ETV news show "Aktuaalne kaamera" that he will resign as defense minister.

He said a leader must have the stature and courage to take responsibility even when the responsibility is not personal, if doing so serves the broader goal of defending the country.

"As defense minister, I of course have to recognize that I am responsible for the entire area under my ministry and if you are now waiting for that big answer, then, of course, a leader must have both the courage and the stature to take responsibility as a matter of political responsibility, even when there is no personal responsibility. I will take that responsibility and the prime minister will have to find a new defense minister," Pevkur told "Aktuaalne kaamera."

"Although the minister does not count socks and ammunition or conduct contract negotiations, the National Audit Office's criticisms, primarily concerning the activities of the Defense Forces and the Center for Defense Investments, raise the question of political responsibility. I therefore believe it is right to take political responsibility today for the entire defense sector and hand over the defense minister's baton at a time suitable for the prime minister," Pevkur wrote in a social media post published at the same time as his "Aktuaalne kaamera" interview.

"I do so with the firm knowledge that we have made the right decisions to strengthen national defense. Estonia is better defended than ever before," he added.

"I sincerely thank everyone who has worked over the years for Estonia's national defense — members of the Defense Forces and Defense League, officials, the defense industry and our allies. I would especially like to thank Kaja Kallas and Kristen Michal for placing their trust in me and inviting me to serve as defense minister in their governments. Estonia's security is not a one-person project. It is our shared responsibility," Pevkur wrote.

Pevkur had served as defense minister since 2022.

It emerged Wednesday that Estonia had sought to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to Indian companies that had never previously sold a single shell.

Magnus-Valdemar Saar, then head of the Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), said that no major decisions were made without the approval of Defense Ministry leaders. In addition to Minister Hanno Pevkur, then-Permanent Secretary Kusti Salm was also aware of the matter during negotiations on the first contract, while the new permanent secretary, Kaimo Kuusk, was subsequently kept informed.

Pevkur told "Aktuaalne kaamera" that he had indeed not read the contracts, but confirmed that RKIK had brought the contracts to him.

Asked why he had not read the contracts, Pevkur said the defense minister is not responsible for dealing with such details.

"The defense minister does not conduct contract negotiations; the defense minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defense minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine. The preparatory work for contract negotiations and finding contracting partners is RKIK's responsibility," Pevkur said.

Earlier that day, a special Riigikogu committee discussed the confusion surrounding accounting in the defense sector. The hearing was prompted by a consolidated report from the National Audit Office that highlighted problems in the defense sector.

Toomas Uibo, chair of the Estonia 200 parliamentary group; Social Democratic Party Chair Lauri Läänemets; and Isamaa Chair Urmas Reinsalu all publicly said that Pevkur should resign.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) on Tuesday called a Cabinet meeting for Thursday morning, at which he will ask the auditor general to provide an overview of the lack of clarity surrounding defense-sector accounting.

Michal said that while he did not believe the defense minister was personally at fault over the questionable transactions in the defense sector, that did not rule out taking political responsibility. In his view, Pevkur could have made the decision himself after Thursday's meeting.

World.title: Who is Estonia's new President Ülle Madise and what does she think of life?
World.content:
On Wednesday, Estonia's parliament elected 51-year-old lawyer and longtime Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as the new president of the Republic of Estonia. The public, however, knows relatively little about the new head of state and her views on life in Estonia.

A graduate of the University of Tartu's School of Law, Madise has had a distinguished career in Estonia's state administration, heading several government bodies and carrying out major reforms over the past 30 years. In the early 2000s, for example, as head of the Ministry of Justice's legislative policy department, she helped introduce Estonia's online voting system and several years later, as head of the secretariat of the Riigikogu Constitutional Committee, she helped transpose European Union legislation into Estonian law.

A lawyer known for her clear manner of speaking and extensive knowledge who became one of Estonia's best-known constitutional law experts through her media appearances, Madise caught the attention of President Toomas Hendrik Ilves, who hired her as his legal adviser in 2009. During the so-called Ice Cellar process, many noticed how heavily Ilves relied on her and Madise came to be regarded as the president's right-hand woman.

"It was entirely understandable that she would be there because the issues were constitutional and legal. At the time, there were major protests against the government's actions. So of course you bring your legal adviser along as your right-hand person," then-President Toomas Hendrik Ilves recalled, confirming Madise's influence within his office.

Ülle Madise and "Pealtnägija" host Kristjan Pihl in a rowboat. Source: "Pealtnägija"

In January 2015, Madise was chosen as Estonia's first female chancellor of justice. She is now in her second term and has held the position for 11 consecutive years. One indication of her standing in society is that as early as fall 2016, when the presidential election failed to produce a winner through several rounds of voting in parliament and ultimately in the Electoral College, Madise's name was also floated as a possible candidate.

Ilves said he already believed at the time that Madise would make a good president, although in his view she was still too young for the office then. Madise herself said she was not yet thinking about becoming president at the time.

Madise defends the Constitution and human rights, but she also speaks out boldly on matters of political choice. She has criticized excessive government bureaucracy, the Police and Border Guard Board's use of license plate recognition cameras and government agencies' desire to snoop through private individuals' banking data. Former State Secretary Taimar Peterkop said some of the sharpest disputes within the government took place during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Because Madise was quick to defend fundamental rights and freedoms, many were left with the impression that she was opposed to vaccines. That perception was reinforced by an episode involving a mask — or, more precisely, the absence of one. A photo from spring 2021 shows her posing alongside President Kersti Kaljulaid who was wearing a mask. Asked by a journalist why Madise was not wearing one, she replied: "Because I can't be a hypocrite. Before that, we'd spent an hour and a half talking without masks, eating and laughing. Neither of us had symptoms or COVID."

Ülle Madise at the first meeting of Kaja Kallas' third government at Stenbock House, with Taimar Peterkop to her right. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Madise said this did not mean she considered Kaljulaid a hypocrite. "No, I'm not criticizing anyone. People have different convictions and, indeed, the photographer told me to put on a mask as well, but I said I didn't think it was appropriate in that situation because it could also give people the impression that a surgical mask helps under COVID restrictions or protects against COVID. A surgical mask does not prevent the spread of the coronavirus. That has been established."

According to Madise, her character simply does not allow her to go along with things like that.

"I saw those people who thought, for example, that they didn't need to get vaccinated or that they could go out while showing symptoms of illness as long as they were wearing a surgical mask. And then you have to explain that if you have symptoms, you must not go out because the person across from you could have cancer or could be someone who dies because of you. /…/ So that was one aspect of it: It was simply my duty not to go along with the power of that symbol and I certainly don't criticize anyone who felt it was a sign that could help keep society's awareness of the danger high."

Peterkop, who worked closely with Madise at the time, recalled being pleasantly surprised by her empathy. "How she noticed when someone was having a hard time and how she helped that person — I've experienced it myself. I've seen it with others as well: She supported my colleagues, the employees of the Government Office. She would go and talk to them directly and, so to speak, lift their spirits when she saw that someone had become discouraged during those difficult times. So empathy, which is in short supply in our society today, is something I think she possesses to an above-average degree," Peterkop said.

Despite Madise occasionally delivering fairly devastating assessments of Estonia's political culture and the quality of legislation coming out of the Riigikogu, politicians from both the coalition and the two major opposition parties rallied behind her with surprising unanimity this summer.

Ülle Madise's husband is EU Court of Justice judge Lauri Madise who is based in Luxembourg. Given both his reserved nature and his work in Europe, he may take on a role somewhat similar to Georgi-Rene Maksimovski who accompanied Kersti Kaljulaid on official state visits and to Independence Day receptions but otherwise largely stayed out of the public eye.

Ülle Madise and husband Lauri Madise. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

Madise said her husband is very supportive of her. "My husband supports me very much, just as I support him, so we always try to have each other's backs. At the same time, I think that's entirely reasonable. Nowadays, both people in a marriage can choose their own careers and of course that means making compromises. We've made those compromises, so I hope it will work out, yes," Madise explained.

Asked by a journalist what kind of president Estonia would be getting in her, Ülle Madise replied: "Health and life permitting, I believe a dedicated and hardworking one, while also being down-to-earth. And I have no intention of giving up my belief that we need much more lightness, humor and creativity, so I doubt I'll be overly serious."

Madise declined to criticize the work of previous presidents. "I wouldn't want to say anything that could come across as criticism of anyone and I would say that, in my view, every president has been the right person in the right place at the right time. And I think the president being elected now should try to reduce the areas where people come into conflict with one another," Madise said.

Peterkop believes Estonia will get a good president in Ülle Madise. "Ülle Madise has a very strong academic background. She is a constitutional expert — I think Estonia's most prominent constitutional expert — so she knows very well what the president's role is intended to be," Peterkop said.

Madise said people will be able to count on her as president if a political force that comes to power begins attacking judges, the free press or civil servants, for example. "It's too early to say what I would do, but I have some ideas," she said.

Madise said she is not afraid of the future. "I'm not in the habit of being afraid and fortunately it seems that we're once again in the kind of turbulent situation where I have the opportunity to be one of those at the helm," Madise said, laying out her vision: "That Estonia will be able to choose a path that allows Estonia to remain the kind of place where it's the coolest place to live and to be and where Estonia is still Estonia. That life within Estonia is peaceful and safe, that we have enough other countries prepared to defend us and deter those who might want to attack us from outside. I believe it is possible to steer these processes in such a way that Estonia's future is bright, that this is a place where people want to live."

Turning to Estonia's foreign and defense relations, Madise said international law and defense relations between countries are not a British gentlemen's club, but rather an arena where everyone looks out for their own interests.

Ülle Madise after being elected president on September 2, 2026. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

"Estonia also has to look out for itself. Estonia can do that by being smart and shrewd and by having very good and powerful allies. That means, of course, maintaining good cooperation with the United States, but also aligning ourselves very clearly with the European Union," Madise emphasized.

Toomas Hendrik Ilves said Ülle Madise also has a good sense of humor. Asked to recall a funny incident, Ilves said: "There have been many. For example, I really liked it when my colleagues once gave me an Allar Jõks hairstyle to put on my head. They'd actually ordered it and brought it in."

Madise relieves stress by exercising, taking walks or joking with her husband, among other things. "Just yesterday we were discussing our godson's training. It was great and we were saying what a handsome young man he is."

Madise understands that in the near future there will be plenty of people offering advice on what she should be like and suggesting things she ought to change about herself.

"I really have heard that I should somehow be prettier and more polished, but to be frank, I am exactly who I am and I don't think I can change that much, nor do I think I need to change that much. When serving as president, you do have to be presentable and proper, but I think that as soon as a person allows themselves to be redesigned into someone else and starts speaking the way people think is appropriate, it becomes artificial. It doesn't come from the heart and it hasn't been thought through," Madise said.

"I don't know how to do that, I won't do it and I don't think I'd be any good at it," she added.

Ülle Madise. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

World.title: Ministry: Publishing officials' vacation data would infringe privacy
World.content:
Current law does not allow government agencies to publish information on officials' vacation periods and their temporary substitutes on institutional websites, because vacation data constitute sensitive personal information, the Ministry of Justice says..

The Ministry of Finance asked the Ministry of Justice whether, under the Public Information Act, agencies may publish vacation information together with the name of the substitute official. The goal, the ministry said, would be to inform the public about an agency's work arrangements and ensure efficient, low‑bureaucracy communication with state and local authorities. At the same time, any change must respect data‑protection principles and safeguard officials' privacy.

However, the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Digital Affairs concluded that the current Public Information Act does not provide a clear legal basis for publishing vacation periods online. Vacation status is personal data, and active disclosure on a government website constitutes an intrusion into private life. For such processing, lawmakers must define both the purpose and scope of disclosure.

The ministry noted that agencies may still publish information on whom to contact when the usual official is unavailable. In such cases, the focus is on ensuring continuity of service, not revealing personal details about an official's private life. Many agencies already publish substitute contacts without specifying the reason or duration of the absence.

Links to vacation documents of officials in the public database of state employees. Source: Screenshot

If agencies were to systematically publish vacation periods, durations and substitutes, a specific legal basis would need to be added to the law, clearly defining the purpose and timeframe of disclosure. The ministry emphasized that effective communication with the public can often be achieved through less intrusive means — for example, by publishing only substitute contacts or general unit contact details, without indicating vacation dates.

Another option would be to require officials to designate a substitute during vacation and include that information in automatic email replies. This way, individuals contacting the agency would know whom to approach, but the official's vacation period would not be publicly visible.

The Ministry of Justice concluded that although it would be possible to legislate the publication of vacation periods, the same goal — improving communication with agencies — can be achieved with less privacy‑intrusive measures. Therefore, amending the Public Information Act is not necessary.

In practice, information on Estonian public officials' vacations and their substitutes can be found in the RTIP public documents registry of the civil service portal.

World.title: Half marathon champs postponed over bomb scare now to take place in Tartu
World.content:
The national half marathon championships which had been due to take place in June will now be held in Tartu in October.

The original race was set to take place in Narva on June 6 and were canceled over a bomb scare which turned out to be a false alarm.

The Estonian Athletic Association on Wednesday announced that this year's Half Marathon Championships will take place in Tartu as part of the Tartu City Marathon event. The half marathon will start at 11 a.m. on October 3.

The championships will determine the Estonian champions in the men's and women's categories. Leonid Latsepov and Liis-Grete Hussar were crowned Estonian champions in the men's and women's categories the last time the race was held in Tartu, two years ago.

The Narva City Run half marathon was canceled after a suspicious bag was found along the route. June 6, 2026.in Narva on Saturday. June 6, 2026. Source: Dmitri Fedotkin/ERR

The planned Estonian Half Marathon Championships were canceled shortly before the start after authorities received a tip about a suspicious bag.

The small bag was found abandoned on a park bench. After examination by the bomb disposal squad; the Rescue Center announced the bag contained personal items and was not a danger.

World.title: Paul Aron to get Alpine F1 drive again, this time at Monza
World.content:
Estonian racing driver Paul Aron will get another Formula One opportunity this week, driving for Alpine in first practice at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza at the weekend.

Aron, 21, is this season a test and reserve driver for the BWT Alpine F1 Team, seen as a stepping stone to a full F1 career. He already took the wheel in practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix this season.

"I'm excited for the first free practice session with the team this weekend," Aron said in a team statement. "I'm grateful to the team for giving me the opportunity to get back behind the wheel again so soon.

F1 NEWS



Estonian driver Paul Aron will take part in the first free practice session in Italy with Alpine. He will replace Pierre Gasly in the cockpit. #F1 #ItalianGP #Alpine pic.twitter.com/M8yRy6QHY4 — Sport Chronicle (@SportFilesF1) September 2, 2026

"I was delighted with my session in Budapest and hope to build on that here, especially by helping the team with our upgrade package, which I have driven with in the simulator," he went on.

"It will be a busy weekend, as I'll be in the simulator in Enstone on Friday evening to help the team further fine-tune the setup before returning on Saturday," the Estonian continued. "I'll give it everything to hopefully contribute to a successful weekend for the team."

Aron made his first official practice appearance of the season for Alpine at the Hungarian Grand Prix in July, where he took part in Friday's free practice.

Alpine's starting drivers are Pierre Gasly (France) and Franco Colapinto (Argentina); Aron deputized for Colapinto in Hungary and is now filling in for Gasly in Italy. The team is French, though based at Enstone in Oxfordshire, England, and traces its DNA back as far as the Toleman team of the early 1980s, which became Benetton and subsequently Renault.

This year's Italian Grand Prix weekend starts this Friday with the race on Sunday as per tradition. There are still another nine races left in 2026, with Kimi Antonelli (Italy) topping the drivers' table for Mercedes with 242 points, over his teammate, Britain's George Russel, and seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari), both on 183 points.

No Estonian has yet raced full-time in F1 even as its northern neighbor, Finland, has had several down the years, three of them becoming world champions.

World.title: Estonia's top defense officials point finger at predecessors
World.content:
At a Riigikogu special committee hearing, the Defense Ministry blamed procurement problems on the Estonian Center for Defense Investments, which in turn blamed its former director. The EDF acknowledged lacking a modern inventory system.

On Wednesday morning, a Riigikogu special committee discussed disarray in the defense sector's accounting. The hearing was prompted by a National Audit Office summary report that identified major problems in the defense sector.

It also emerged Wednesday that Estonia had sought to buy artillery shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to Indian companies that had never previously sold a single shell. Instead of military materiel, Estonia received repeated promises and the dispute is now in court.

The National Audit Office criticized the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), which is responsible for procurement, for failing to provide it with the contract for the €70 million shell deal despite repeated requests. RKIK said the contract had been sent on June 5. The National Audit Office maintained that it had not received the contract and the hearing failed to establish which side was correct.

RKIK was also unable to comment on the terms of the contract at the hearing because of a confidentiality clause.

Urmas Reinsalu (Isamaa), who chaired the hearing, asked Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) why the contract had not been made available to the National Audit Office.

"I can't recall all the details right now, but as far as I know, some of these contracts simply contain confidentiality clauses agreed with suppliers. Perhaps RKIK can clarify that better," the minister replied. He stressed, however, that in his view, the National Audit Office must be given access to the contracts.

Reinsalu noted that advance payments had been made to a company that had not previously produced ammunition and asked whether the contracts had reached the defense minister in writing and whether the decisions had been documented in writing.

Defense Ministry Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk replied that procurement is RKIK's responsibility and that RKIK also assesses the risks. "Advance payments don't go before the minister for a decision. That's not how it works," he added.

Reinsalu asked whether the Cabinet had also been informed of the risks associated with the intermediary contracts.

Pevkur said the Cabinet had discussed aid to Ukraine in broader terms.

"How to implement the million-round initiative and how to use foreign donors to purchase equipment for Ukraine — implementation of all of that was handed over to the Estonian Center for Defense Investments, which negotiated with the European Commission and donors, agreed on the financing terms and then searched the global market for materiel," Pevkur said.

When Reinsalu again asked whether the minister's position was that no memorandum on the risks had been presented to the Cabinet, Pevkur replied that this was part of RKIK's ordinary business operations. Reinsalu took this as a no.

Kuusk added that information about the contract that had gone sour had also been shared with the Internal Security Service (ISS) and that officials had been in contact with the ambassadors of the countries connected to the contract. "When it became clear that this wasn't producing results, RKIK was instructed to terminate the contract and go to court," he said.

Reinsalu asked how the problematic companies had come into contact with Estonia.

"We trusted the Estonian Center for Defense Investments. The ministry gave the general instruction that assistance needed to be found for Ukraine," Pevkur said.

Pevkur: The minister does not pick contractors

The defense minister confirmed that he had not personally read the problematic contract. The permanent secretary, for his part, stressed that negotiations are RKIK's responsibility.

"We contacted the Internal Security Service (ISS) when delivery deadlines had been missed across the board and the RKIK leadership at the time kept saying that they would still get it done, that the contracts would be fulfilled despite the delays. That no longer inspired confidence. Negotiations over the substance of these issues are RKIK's responsibility," Kuusk said.

Pevkur stressed that the defense minister does not decide who contracts are signed with.

"The minister's decision-making meeting takes place every two weeks. RKIK provides an overview there and it also provided updates on aid to Ukraine. Of course, it reported who contracts were being signed with and what was being procured for Ukraine. This was always agreed with Ukraine and the European Commission as well. These were three-way arrangements. The information presented at the minister's decision-making meeting was who the contractual partners were and what was being procured. It was provided for information purposes," Pevkur said.

The defense minister confirmed that he had been informed of heightened risks related to aid for Ukraine, but said the ministry's position was that those risks had to be mitigated.

"There were no additional risks with the vast majority of partners. Those deliveries reached Ukraine without problems. The delivery from this partner might also have arrived, but the goods they supplied were not of sufficient quality and those goods are still being held pending resolution," Pevkur said.

Kaimo Kuusk told Eesti Ekspress that while the company did deliver some components to an intermediary warehouse, the goods were not of sufficient quality. "The shipment was completely lacking in essential components," Kuusk said. "An artillery round requires a fuse, a propellant charge that ignites in the gun barrel and a primer. Without any one of these components, the round is unusable. Estonia rejected the incomplete shipment," the weekly wrote.

Because RKIK has undergone personnel changes, its current leadership is unable to comment on the problematic deals.

RKIK's current director general, Elmar Vaher, told ERR in an interview that former RKIK director general Magnus-Valdemar Saar bears responsibility for the failed €70 million shell deal.

Estonian Defense Forces lack a modern inventory management system

The hearing also revealed that the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) lacks a modern inventory management system.

The National Audit Office has criticized the Defense Forces over problems with inventory records both in previous reports and at Wednesday's hearing.

Chief of Defense Lt. Gen. Andrus Merilo told the hearing that the EDF has more than 200 million items subject to inventory checks, but insisted there is no issue with whether the items actually exist.

"What can improve the situation are technical solutions that we don't have today. Inventory management and everything else is very much done manually. We don't have the kind of system used by companies with highly advanced warehousing operations because our core mission isn't inventory management, but carrying out military tasks. Once those systems are introduced, things should improve," Merilo said.

Auditor General Janar Holm noted that the inventories conducted by the Defense Forces do not provide sufficient assurance that the items are actually there. Holm stressed that the Defense Forces has been entrusted with a large amount of money and said he did not want to hear the issue dismissed as a "pointless" accounting problem.

"I have never said that accounting is pointless," Merilo replied. "At the same time, I don't accept that after 34 years of service, I'm now hearing suggestions that I have somehow siphoned off money or that the entire Defense Forces has done so. Once again, the supplies exist and are in the possession of subordinate units."

The chief of defense said much of the confusion was related to paperwork. "So I won't allow this to be framed in a way that suggests we don't know where the money is or that money has disappeared when it comes to the Defense Forces," Merilo said.

The auditor general replied that, in that case, the Defense Forces must provide that assurance.

Merilo stressed that Defense Forces personnel are not professional accountants, but said the organization is working to recruit people with the necessary expertise.

World.title: Court issues mostly suspended terms in conscription‑evasion scheme
World.content:
Harju District Court ruled Wednesday that Andrei Vesterinen, Janika Butkevitšus and Armylaw OÜ were guilty of fraud and submitting false information to the Defense Resources Agency (KRA). The court did not find evidence of document forgery or use of forged documents.

The court sentenced Vesterinen to two years and eight months in prison. One month and four days must be served immediately. The remaining two years, six months and 25 days will not be enforced if Vesterinen does not commit a new intentional crime during a three‑year probation period.

The court sentenced Janika Butkevitšus to two years and four months in prison. The sentence will not be enforced if she does not commit a new intentional crime during a three‑year probation period.

The court also found Armylaw OÜ guilty and imposed a fine of €12,000. The fine will not be enforced if Armylaw does not commit a new intentional crime during a one‑year probation period.

Vesterinen must pay €4,824.75 in procedural costs, Butkevitšus €3,519.89 and Armylaw €3,279.28. The defendants must also compensate victims' legal costs totaling €5,414.88. The court granted the civil claims filed by the victims.

According to the charges, Armylaw board member Vesterinen and employee Butkevitšus offered legal services on social media and the company's website in 2021–2022 that promised clients they could "legally" avoid conscription.

Prosecutors said clients were misled and instructed to submit false address information to the population register, forged and used falsified address notices, and changed contact details to prevent KRA from reaching them. They also provided false information about language skills in misdemeanor proceedings to delay cases.

The scheme caused financial losses totaling €16,224.99 to ten victims.

The court found that Vesterinen promised on Armylaw's website and in personal communication with clients that he offered a service allowing them to be released from military service obligations on a legal basis and in a legal manner. He also repeatedly used the slogan "100% guarantee" that clients would not have to enter military service. Based on this, various people — including victims and witnesses — turned to Armylaw for help, believing they were guaranteed a legal way to avoid conscription.

The court found that the instructions given by Vesterinen and Butkevitšus through Armylaw were not lawful. Their actions were aimed at violating norms set out in the Military Service Act and avoiding legally established military service obligations. Their instructions also met the elements of submitting false information to an administrative authority. Their legal guidance misled clients and created the need for further legal assistance.
