The former prime minister believes these events shed more light on one of the points in the letter he received, which referred to “supporters” such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili.

“Now the picture is clear to me, and I have received answers to all my questions: why did the first point of the letter say that ‘such supporters as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili’ raise serious doubts and cause significant damage to the interests of the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze team” Gharibashvili writes.

In another part of the letter, the former prime minister criticises Mamuka Mdinaradze, saying that his mistakes led not only to his removal from office but also to his departure from politics.

Gharibashvili stresses, however, that in his view, Mdinaradze’s departure from politics will not make up for the damage he believes Mdinaradze and Irakli Kobakhidze caused to the country, its people and the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Gharibashvili also writes that questions remain in society about the deaths of other people during the period when Irakli Kobakhidze and Mamuka Mdinaradze were leading the country.

Context

The first corruption charge against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was brought in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising illicit income on a particularly large scale. A second charge – accepting a bribe on a particularly large scale – was brought on August 24, 2026.

Gharibashvili made his first statement from prison on August 17. In a Facebook post, he wrote that a letter had been sent to him on the orders of Bidzina Ivanishvili [oligarch, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party] and that it “left him no choice” but to confront the “evil that insults his dignity”.

Gharibashvili published his second letter from prison on August 19. In it, the former prime minister claimed that the aim of his arrest was his political destruction and said he had initially decided against legal action to avoid confrontation with the authorities.

According to Gharibashvili, he was forced to fight back.

Gharibashvili also said he received a letter from Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. He said that on the same day he explained his position to Mdinaradze and again confirmed that he had no intention of returning to politics.

News from Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan versus Western media: Why were different reports labelled a single ‘information campaign’?
World.content:
Azerbaijan and foreign media

Four separate reports about Azerbaijan have appeared in international media: a TVP World programme by Poland’s public broadcaster on political repression, an Independent report on the conditions in which Ali Karimli is being held, a BBC analysis of political prisoners, and a Guardian review of a documentary about Karabakh.

Baku responded with two official statements. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Poland’s ambassador over the TVP World programme and handed him a protest note. In a separate statement, the Media Development Agency described the other three publications as possible elements of a single “targeted information campaign”.

However, when examined individually, the reports clearly differ in their subject matter, format and main sources.

TVP: international success and domestic repression

The central question of the TVP World programme “Peace in Azerbaijan comes with repression”, broadcast on 26 August, is why Azerbaijan’s political space continues to shrink despite Baku’s growing international influence.

The programme discusses the arrests of journalists from AbzasMedia, Meydan TV and Toplum TV, as well as criminal cases against opposition figures, activists and researchers. Presenter Benjamin Lee and İPEK Centre deputy director Türkan Bozkurt discuss oil revenues, the transfer of power within one family, the legitimacy Ilham Aliyev gained from victory in Karabakh, relations with the West and the position of national minorities.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry described the programme as biased and the presenter’s conduct as provocative. Since TVP receives state funding from Poland’s budget, the Azerbaijani side linked the programme’s content to the Polish government’s position and described its broadcast as an “unfriendly act”.

The Independent: conditions of Ali Karimli’s detention

The British newspaper’s 30 August report focuses on a narrower issue. The family and lawyers of Ali Karimli, the detained chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, say he has no access to safe drinking water, ventilation, adequate sleep, outdoor exercise or reading materials. A Human Rights Watch representative says the authorities have not presented convincing evidence to the public in his case. The UK Foreign Office confirms that it has raised the issue with Azerbaijani authorities.

The article’s emotive headline highlights the family’s claim that authorities are trying to “break” Karimli. The report also describes the charge against him as “treason”. Officially, however, prosecutors have charged him under an article concerning actions aimed at the violent seizure of power and the forcible alteration of the constitutional order. This is a specific point on which Baku could request a correction.

The newspaper also says it contacted Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry for comment but received no response.

BBC: figures and the case of Igbal Abilov

The Russian Service of the BBC’s article “Why is Ilham Aliyev stepping up repression?”, published on 31 August, focuses not on Ali Karimli but on Talysh researcher Igbal Abilov, who received an 18-year prison sentence.

The BBC analysed lists compiled by the Institute for Peace and Democracy from 2021 to May 2026. It concluded that the number of political prisoners had more than tripled, while the average prison sentence in politically motivated cases reached about 12 years in 2026. The article also examines the cases involving AbzasMedia, Radio Azadliq and Toplum TV, as well as the trials of researchers Bahruz Samadov and Igbal Abilov.

The fact that the calculations rely on lists compiled by a single human rights organisation may be open to debate. However, the BBC explains its methodology in detail, includes Ilham Aliyev’s position that he denies political persecution, and says it contacted the Penitentiary Service for comment but received no response.

Who is restricting access to the official position?

The MEDİA Agency accuses foreign news organisations of failing to seek Azerbaijan’s official position. However, in February 2025, the BBC closed its Baku bureau on the Foreign Ministry’s instructions. The bureau had operated in the country since 1994.

The Foreign Ministry cited the principle of reciprocity and the lack of a legal basis for the bureau’s operation. When authorities restrict the work of local bureaus and government agencies leave journalists’ requests unanswered, foreign news organisations have to rely more heavily on lawyers, relatives and experts based outside the country.

The information landscape that Baku describes as one-sided may therefore partly result from the authorities’ own media policies.

The Guardian: a review of a film about Karabakh

The Guardian article is not a political investigation. It is a short review of The Black Garden, a documentary by director Alexis Pazoumian. The film explores the wartime experience of Karabakh Armenians through the stories of two children and a young soldier who lost a leg.

The review’s introduction says Karabakh Armenians fought against “countless military campaigns” by the Azerbaijani army. However, it does not mention the First Karabakh War, the occupation of Azerbaijani territories, Azerbaijani internally displaced people or other aspects of the conflict. The reviewer also acknowledges that the film lacks a broader political and historical context.

Baku can reasonably criticise this one-sided presentation. However, expecting a film critic to seek comment from the Azerbaijani government would mean applying standards associated with news journalism to a piece about culture.

What do the different reports have in common?

What the four publications have in common is not any proven coordination between them, but the fact that the picture of Azerbaijan they present differs from the government’s official narratives.

TVP and the BBC question the authorities’ arguments about domestic stability and the legitimacy of criminal prosecutions. The Independent raises concerns about the conditions in which a particular detainee is being held. The Guardian, meanwhile, presents the Karabakh war primarily through the experience of the Armenian side.

The reports therefore cover different subjects, but within a single week they touch on three sensitive areas for the Azerbaijani state: domestic political control, relations with international partners and the historical narrative surrounding Karabakh. Baku sees them as part of a single attack not because their content is similar, but because all four diverge from the international image that the Azerbaijani authorities seek to project.

Is the “information campaign” proven?

The MEDİA Agency statement does not specify which facts in the reports are incorrect, nor does it provide evidence that could indicate coordination between the news organisations. At the same time, it claims that the authors did not attempt to establish Azerbaijan’s official position.

However, The Independent says it sent a request for comment to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry. The BBC quotes the president’s position and says it also sought comment from the Penitentiary Service.

A separate response to each report would have been more convincing. In the case of the Guardian, the authorities could have pointed out factual inaccuracies in its account of the historical context. For The Independent, they could have provided a documented response to the claims about the charges against Karimli and his conditions of detention. The BBC could have received alternative data on the criteria for including people on political prisoner lists and on sentencing statistics. TVP could also have been asked to give the Azerbaijani side a right of reply on air.

Grouping all the reports together in a single statement and presenting them as a politically motivated campaign erases the differences between them. Moreover, the absence of specific rebuttals does not end the debate. Instead, it creates the conditions for further reporting.

The confrontation here is not simply a conflict between “Baku and Western media”. The main problem is that the state places verifiable factual errors, editorial assessments, statements by human rights groups and even a film review in the same political category. This approach does not weaken the criticism. On the contrary, it creates the impression that different news organisations really are acting as a united front.

Although the agency said it intended to take “necessary measures”, it did not specify whether this meant seeking corrections and a right of reply, filing an official complaint or taking other steps.

Azerbaijan and foreign media

World.title: Georgia’s central bank explains how new transfer restrictions for people over 60 will work
World.content:
Georgia’s central bank on new rules for older customers

Georgia‘s central bank has clarified that new restrictions on electronic transfers for people over 60 will not apply to regular payments and transactions.

The new rule applies only when a bank or other payment service provider suspects that a customer may be the victim of fraud.

Under the National Bank’s new regulation, if a person over 60 makes an electronic transfer of more than 500 lari and the bank suspects that the transaction may be linked to fraud, it will suspend the transfer for 48 hours.

When does the rule apply?

According to the National Bank, all four conditions must be met for a transaction to be suspended:

The user must be over 60;

The transfer must exceed 500 lari;

The bank or payment organisation must detect unusual spending or behaviour by the customer;

The payment must involve activity that carries a high risk of fraud.

In other words, being over 60 and making a transfer of more than 500 lari are not, by themselves, enough to trigger a suspension.

For example, if a 65-year-old regularly pays 700 lari in utility bills each month or transfers money to a family member, the transaction will not be automatically suspended.

The situation changes if, for example, the same person is suddenly asked to transfer a large sum to an unknown account and their behaviour within the banking system appears suspicious. In that case, the new protection mechanism may be triggered.

What can the bank do?

If all four of the above conditions are met, the bank or relevant payment service provider will suspend the electronic transaction for 48 hours.

During this period, the bank must contact the customer and explain in simple terms why it considers the transaction suspicious and what risks it may involve.

The final decision then rests with the customer.

If the customer decides they still want to transfer the funds, they must confirm this to the bank, and the transaction will go through.

Why did the central bank introduce the rule?

The National Bank of Georgia says the measure aims to protect vulnerable customers, particularly older people, from fraud.

The idea is simple: if a fraudster convinces someone to make an urgent transfer, the 48-hour pause gives them additional time to consider whether they really want to go ahead with the transaction.

According to the National Bank, a similar approach is used in other countries, including the US, Canada, Brazil, the UK and EU member states.

The new rule therefore does not ban people over 60 from making bank transfers. Instead, it temporarily suspends transactions that appear suspicious based on a number of indicators. This gives customers another opportunity to reconsider their decision before falling victim to fraud or losing their money.

Georgia’s central bank on new rules for older customers

World.title: Tajikistan’s retail trade gains strong momentum in 1H2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The retail trade turnover in Tajikistan reached 38.3 billion somoni ($4.15 billion) in the first half of 2026.

According to data from the Interstate Statistical Committee of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), retail trade turnover in Tajikistan increased by 35.9% in constant prices from January through June 2026 compared with the same period of 2025.

In June 2026, retail trade turnover grew by 48.7% in constant prices compared with June 2025, while increasing by 12.4% compared with May 2026.

For comparison, retail trade turnover in Tajikistan increased by 5.1% in the first half of 2025 compared with the same period of 2024.

Furthermore, in June 2025, the indicator decreased by 5.1% year-on-year and by 8.3% compared with May 2025.

The Trend’s analysis indicates that Tajikistan’s retail trade sector accelerated significantly in the first half of 2026, pointing to stronger consumer activity and an expansion in domestic demand.

The sharp improvement compared with the previous year suggests that retail trade has become a more significant contributor to economic activity. The particularly strong year-on-year growth recorded in June also indicates that the sector maintained its momentum toward the middle of the year.

The monthly increase in June further points to an expansion in consumer spending during the period. At the same time, the sustainability of this trend will depend on household income growth, price dynamics, employment conditions, and the availability of consumer goods.

The acceleration in retail activity may also support related sectors, including wholesale trade, transport, logistics and services, while providing additional opportunities for businesses operating in Tajikistan’s domestic market.

World.title: Pro-stadium opinion piece by public servant had input from Devils footy club
World.content:
Less than two months before a final vote in parliament on the Macquarie Point stadium, Tasmania's coordinator-general, John Perry, entered the public debate.

The senior state service employee's intervention came in the form of a 3,000-word opinion piece published in Tasmania's major daily newspaper, The Mercury.

Mr Perry attempted to quantify the broader economic activity that would potentially stem from the state's then-promised $875 million spend.

His predicted economic return was more than six times greater than the government's own estimate.

"Can we really afford for the State not to make that investment?" he wrote.

The Macquarie Point stadium passed Tasmania's upper house in December, two months after John Perry's opinion piece was published. (Supplied: Cox Architecture)

The main role of Mr Perry's office is to attract private investment into the state.

But his public commentary on the stadium, prior to a parliamentary vote, prompted questions about whether he adhered to principles in the State Service Act to be "apolitical" and "impartial".

What was not known at the time was the extent of the role other interested parties played in helping to shape and promote Mr Perry's work, well before it was publicly released.

Emails obtained by the ABC — provided by his overarching department nine months after they were requested under right to information laws — show that draft copies of the piece went through a range of hands, including one of the main stakeholders: the Tasmania Devils AFL football club.

Football club involved in state servant's 'awesome work'

The piece came out in October 2025, but two months earlier, the football club was already involved in Mr Perry's work, emails show.

He was carrying out his own economic analysis on the stadium, sending Tasmania Football Club's marketing manager, Kathryn McCann, a "draft iteration of the narrative".

John Perry: As you can see, the narrative still needs a lot of refinement, further tidying and tweaking. Kathryn McCann: It's looking very useful. Want to make a time in the next week or so to regroup on this (awesome) work?

A month later, Mr Perry presented his modelling and analysis to the football club's senior executives and chair.

Kathryn McCann praised John Perry's stadium work multiple times during its development. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The next day, he wrote to Premier Jeremy Rockliff suggesting he would seek approval to publish an opinion piece on his modelling, "as I expect is required as a public servant".

No formal approval could be found under right to information laws; neither the government nor the Office of the Coordinator-General responded to a question about what form the approval was given, and if advice was sought.

State servant wanted to 'counterbalance' public commentary

As the piece developed, Mr Perry described his intention in multiple emails as being "to counterbalance the 'we can't afford the stadium'" commentary.

He sent a draft to Ms McCann, and two drafts to Master Builders Tasmania chief executive officer Jenna Cairney, who is a former communications director for the premier and past Mercury editor.

John Perry: Very keen for your thoughts and suggestions. Jenna Cairney: This is looking really really great. I'll have another stab of it overnight to try to get that first section down to a reasonable size for a large talking point/oped in the newspapers.

Ms Cairney wrote that she had "whipped up" a media release "for a news lead", while Ms McCann suggested incorporating further information — the content of which was redacted — and offered to assist in distributing it to media outlets.

A media release was ultimately not included, but the ABC understands it was pitched to media outlets as being fully Mr Perry's own work.

Jenna Cairney (left) was asked to provide feedback on multiple drafts of John Perry's opinion piece. (ABC News)

The Department of Premier and Cabinet (DPAC) also had a request.

The government was due to release its formal response to a scathing Tasmanian Planning Commission report on the stadium.

DPAC wanted Mr Perry's piece to be released to coincide with this.

Suggestion to brief 'key' upper house members

Three days before it was released, Mr Perry sent a draft copy to DPAC and the premier's office.

It included mark-ups and Ms Cairney's "general approach for releasing" it to the media.

Jeremy Rockliff was questioned about the opinion piece in parliament last year, but did not say when approval was given to John Perry. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Mr Perry also mentioned to Mr Rockliff's chief of staff that he would offer to brief "key" upper house members on his economic analysis.

At the time, the stadium looked set to pass the lower house with Labor's support, but the government needed the vote of at least three additional upper house members.

Briefings by department staff relating to bills are typically extended to all upper house members, rather than selected members; the ABC asked what was meant by "key" members and if it was appropriate for a state servant to make this political suggestion.

Neither the government nor the Office of the Coordinator-General responded to this question.

The suggestion for Mr Perry to brief these members appears to have originated with the Tasmania Football Club, emails show.

A briefing was not offered, according to at least one of the upper house members whose vote was required by the government.

Government argues Perry acted 'independently'

Mr Perry was questioned in a parliamentary hearing after the piece was published on October 11, saying it had not been requested by the government.

He was asked about who reviewed the work and analysis.

"I had shared internally just before it was released and I provided it the day that it was provided to others," Mr Perry said.

He said he had "sought some input" from people outside of government, and had talked to the football club.

John Perry was questioned about his opinion piece in a public accounts committee in parliament. (ABC News)

Mr Perry provided a written response in which he said he provided the "final version" to "people who have regular contact with the media".

The extent of the involvement of the Tasmania Football Club and Master Builders Tasmania — and the sharing of a draft with the government — was not disclosed in parliament, nor in the piece itself.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Coordinator-General said it had publicly supported other proposals. It is unclear if any of these were publicly funded.

"The office has undertaken various levels of analysis for a number of major investment proposals over the years and, where appropriate, provides official support for a proposal on the record," they said.

"Working collaboratively with relevant stakeholders to ensure timely material that is both to the point and factually correct is vital."

A government spokesperson said the work was done independently and was "in accordance with his duties".

"Attracting investment is what Mr Perry is employed to do," they said.

"Mr Perry independently undertook this work to assess how the stadium might impact Tasmania's economy."

Economic analysis faced scrutiny

The content of the opinion piece was also heavily scrutinised at the time.

Mr Perry argued the stadium would generate "at least $220.9m per year in new economic activity" at a cost of $44.5 million to finance the debt, a benefit of $4.97 for every $1 spent.

He wrote that other public commentary on the stadium had "questionable inclusions and startling omissions", and his office told the ABC his piece aimed to "address misinformation".

While being based on different methodologies, it was a vastly different figure to the government's estimate of 69 cents of benefit for every $1, and economist Nicholas Gruen's estimate of 44 cents per $1.

Independent upper house member Ruth Forrest described it as "when economic spin masquerades as analysis".

Dean Winter questioned John Perry's opinion piece, including how he reached a much higher level of economic benefit than other analyses. (ABC News)

Labor's Dean Winter was also critical, despite the party being in support of the stadium.

He argued that Mr Perry had double-counted interstate visitor activity and new hotel economic activity, which Mr Perry rejected.

"[This is] a piece of work, an editorial by a senior public servant, that isn't peer-reviewed, is not a cost-benefit analysis, it has double-counted spending," Mr Winter told parliament.

The stadium passed the upper house in December after several remaining independents supported it.

Work to remove about 100,000 cubic metres of soil from the waterfront site started in July.

The government intends to have it completed by the end of 2030, meaning the Tasmania Devils will play at least the first three seasons at Bellerive Oval and York Park.

The overall cost estimate remains at $1.13 billion, but an update could be provided once the construction tender process concludes.

World.title: Insurance delays as Exmouth residents struggle with living conditions
World.content:
Darryl Byatt and his family have been living in a shed for the last five months after Cyclone Narelle significantly damaged their home in March.

The Exmouth resident said he was fortunate that before the cyclone hit the town, 1,250 kilometres north of Perth, he renovated the shed so it was liveable for the short term.

Extensive damage made Darryl Byatt's house unliveable. (Supplied)

"The house was unliveable, the roof came off, the verandah came off and there was extensive damages to plasterboards and flooring," Mr Byatt said.

"We had concerns the insurance might take a little bit of time to process, we just did not expect five months," he said.

Not a unique situation

Cyclone Narelle was a category four system when it passed the coast of Exmouth, damaging homes, business, roads and the airport.

Mr Byatt said an assessment was done of his property by builders sent by his insurance company.

Darryl Byatt's property is still unsafe to live in five months after the damage. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

However, when Mr Byatt received the settlement quote he found a lot of the damage was missing from the report.

He said he questioned the insurer about why items were left out but could not get a definitive response.

"We declined to sign that thinking maybe we can get somewhere quickly and it's now been referred to Australian Financial Complaints Authority," he said.

" It just seems to be an extreme lack of follow-up and communication. "

Mr Byatt said his experience was not unique.

"I have spoken to a few people, there is different people with different insurance companies experiencing the same frustration," he said.

Some of the offered settlements seemed much below the actual repair costs while some cases failed to receive much response.

Several other property owners who had damage during the cyclone are experiencing similar issues. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

Challenging system

Exmouth Shire president Matt Niikkula said anybody with an insurance policy should be looked after.

"The insurance claims are obviously very high in volume and the insurance companies have to step up to the plate," Cr Niikkula said.

"Our expectation is they will look after each and every claim and make sure our community is not left in the dark."

Matt Niikkula says residents with policies deserved to be paid what they were entitled to in a timely manner. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

In the aftermath of the cyclone, the shire helped organise a team of legal aid lawyers to town to offer services not easily accessible in the remote location.

Regional Alliance West lawyer Dempsey Morgan visited Exmouth and said they wanted to ensure locals were aware of the obligations of insurance companies.

"We want to arm them with the knowledge so they know where to go from here," he said.

Mr Morgan said some insurance companies had hired builders from outside the town to conduct assessments and provide quotes.

Dempsey Morgan travelled to Exmouth to offer advice to residents. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

"Those quotes have come back higher than what the properties were insured for and that is leading to cash settlements," he said.

"Once people are accepting the cash settlement, there is a limited amount of funding available for alternative accommodation while works are completed."

A report released from the corporate watchdog, Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), earlier this week found at least 63 per cent of final home insurance claims included a cash settlement.

High volume of claims

Australian Insurance Council's director of Extreme Weather Response Liam Walter said more than 1,100 claims were reported from Exmouth following the cyclone, with more than 600 of them being household claims.

Houses in Exmouth suffered massive damages after Cyclone Narelle. (ABC News)

"I'd like to acknowledge the severity of the incident and the disruption it's caused and that we certainly understand what people are going through," Mr Walter said.

"Certainly the process can take some time and is really dependant on the damage."

He said while the properties with minor damages might have their claim settled, they expected five months waiting period for those with extensive damages.

"In some cases, it could be up to a year before their property is completely repaired," Mr Walter said.

He urged Exmouth locals to submit complaints to attract more attention to their case if they felt the insurers were not communicating appropriately.

"If things are not making sense or if requests are not being heard, then that complaints process is a really critical lever that customers have to kick their claim into a different path of review to try and get those issues resolved," Mr Walter said.

Following Mr Byatt's rejection of the quote, the insurance company has reached back out to him suggesting a re-assessment of his property.

"They said it seems the builders missed some items out of their paperwork and they are asking the builders to do it again," Mr Byatt said.

"We are not sure who missed what, we can't get any answers."

World.title: Warwick Thornton enters Red CentreNATS with 'Michelangelo of the bush'
World.content:
Acclaimed Kaytetye filmmaker Warwick Thornton has a tongue-in-cheek warning about his entry into this year's Red CentreNATS in Alice Springs.

"You probably need a tetanus shot to actually drive it," he says.

But the truth is the Cannes Film Festival Camera d'Or winner, whose landmark films Samson and Delilah and Sweet Country have cemented him as one of Australia's finest directors, has always loved cars.

Bull chasers are stripped-down, short-wheelbase four-wheel-drives, fitted with heavy bull bars, reinforced steel sides and gutted interiors. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Finding and buying them, Thornton then spends hours tinkering away in backyards and sheds across Alice Springs until their engines burst to life and roar.

This year, Thornton is making his Red CentreNATS debut with a beast: a heavily-modified, 1970s Toyota FJ 40 "bull chaser", rebuilt to chase and catch scrub bulls in the harsh Northern Territory outback.

He says his car fixation is linked to his film expertise.

"Where they intersect is in storytelling," he says.

Warwick Thornton says cars have "always been a part of me". (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"Lust and envy and a certain amount of madness is the basis of storytelling.

"There are so many great Australian films about car culture and I was watching that even before I thought I'd be a cinematographer, let alone a director.

"It's always been a part of me."

A Northern Territory icon

The Mad Max-esque automobile is by no means Thornton's prettiest car, but it has been a passion project for about 10 years after he and his son, filmmaker Dylan River, brought it back to Alice Springs from the Top End.

Bull chasers are stripped-down, short-wheelbase four-wheel-drives, fitted with heavy bull bars, reinforced steel sides and gutted interiors, made for tearing through rough terrain.

Bull chasers are a piece of station history, dreamed up out of necessity. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I found it under a big old mango tree, covered in bat shit, rotting — just completely rotting," Thornton says.

In the hulk of rusting metal, Thornton saw the potential to preserve a piece of station history, dreamed up out of necessity.

"These things were built to get in there, give [bulls] a tap with those tyres on the front, or give them a slap on the arse with that big side plate there, and push him out where there would be a bull catcher [with a mechanical arm] waiting," he says.

Warwick Thornton says there have been "many great Australian films about car culture". (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I have such love and respect for this, this would have been flogged."

Amber Driver, who owns Elkedra Station, about 400 kilometres north of Alice Springs, says station workers are still using similar vehicles to muster cattle.

"[They are] quite an iconic part of the Central Australian and also Northern Australian cattle industry," she says.

Warwick Thornton jokes that "you probably need a tetanus shot" to drive his entry into this year's Red CentreNATS, which also has no brakes. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

" While they might look like they're straight out of a Mad Max film, they offer a lot of practical tools when you're mustering wild cattle or even buffalo. "

But unlike most working bull chasers, Thornton and River have installed a shiny new V8 engine in theirs.

'Michelangelo of the bush'

Red CentreNATS is a sister festival to Canberra's Summernats, celebrating all things horsepower with dozens of high-octane events across four days, including burnout competitions, drag races, a street parade and even a mullet-off.

The festival, which begins today, is an economic boon for the town, as more than 50 per cent of the 700 entrants to descend on the Red Centre each year travel from interstate.

A spanking new V8 separates Warick Thornton's bull chaser from the rest of the class. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Festival organiser Andy Lopez says part of the magic is the special permit available across the weekend which allows motoring enthusiasts driving heavily modified cars that aren't usually allowed on the roads to participate.

"This might sound a bit soppy, but in the end, these vehicles are an outpouring of love," he says.

"They represent the personality of not just the owner, but the people behind it and with that comes meaning."

Warwick Thornton describes his bull chaser as "a work of art". (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Although Thornton will not be participating in the street parade — his bull chaser doesn't have brakes because "you don't really need brakes in the bush" — he will be parking it up at the show and shine for all to see.

"It's a work of art, a Michelangelo of the bush," he says.

World.title: Hampshire ditches New Zealand all-rounder after fan backlash
World.content:
Hampshire Cricket has cancelled the contract of Kiwi international Scott Kuggeleijn minutes before he was set to take the field after backlash from supporters.

The 34-year-old fast bowler was named in a social media post as part of the 15-man squad to take on Warwickshire in the County Championship match.

The club had not announced the three-Test player's signing on their social channels.

The presence of the New Zealand international bowler in the squad was met with furious resistance from the club's supporters and some staff members, with reaction including comments of "disgraceful" and "shameful" on social media.

"Having reflected and listened to feedback from our staff and supporters, Hampshire Cricket can confirm that Scott Kuggeleijn will not represent the club," a statement from the club read.

"We value the passion of our fanbase and thank everyone who took the time to share their views."

Kuggeleijn had been signed for the final four games of Hampshire's County Championship season as a replacement for South African Delano Potgieter, who was called up for the South Africa A series against Bangladesh last month.

Kuggeleijn faced a rape charge in 2015 and was acquitted in 2017 after the first trial resulted in a hung jury.

The Hamilton-born player made his international debut after his acquittal in an ODI series against Ireland in Dublin in 2017.

There was backlash in New Zealand when Kuggeleijn was initially selected in the squad, with then-coach Gary Stead forced to defend the call-up.

In addition to his three Test matches, Kuggeleijn has played two one-day matches and 18 T20 games for the Black Caps.

He has not played for New Zealand in any format since the second Test against Australia at Hagley Oval, Christchurch in March 2024, which the Aussies won by three wickets.

Prior to his signing for Hampshire, Kuggeleijn was playing for the Kingsmen in a Darwin T20 league.

He is a regular player in first-class cricket for Northern Districts in New Zealand.

World.title: $12m koala underpass not used in five months
World.content:
Underneath one of south-west Sydney's busiest roads lies the city's first koala underpass.

At 52 metres long, the Glen Lorne crossing cost $12 million and was designed to reduce vehicle strikes and deaths for one of the state's last disease-free koala populations.

Transport for NSW estimates around 10,000 vehicles use this section of road each day.

But since the underpass opened to wildlife five months ago, not a single koala has been recorded using the safe passage.

The Sydney Basin Koala Network says more than 50 koalas have been killed in vehicle strikes along Appin Road since 2022. (Supplied)

That came as no surprise to environmental researcher and policy analyst Colin Salter, who said studies of underpasses in northern NSW and Queensland found koalas rarely used them.

"[These studies] used wildlife cameras within the underpasses themselves as well as outside the structures," said Dr Salter, who also works as WIRES policy lead.

"While there are records of koalas using them, there are not many, and they are infrequent … like one or two detections.

"But the research has also said that there is not enough data, even though there are repeated results from different studies that show there's a low use by koalas."

Colin Salter says there have been few recorded sightings of koalas using underpasses. (ABC News: Simon Avery)

In 2022, researchers from the University of Southern Queensland spotted only one koala and a handful of native animals using crossings under the Toowoomba bypass throughout a 12-month study using camera traps.

This was similar to Southern Cross University's 2021 study, which detected close to 5,000 medium-to-large mammals and goannas using highway underpasses at Port Macquarie and Grafton.

Dr Salter said studies showed it could take a "significant period of time" for wildlife to start using new crossing structures.

Overpasses preferred

Dr Salter said overpasses were a more effective way to protect animals from vehicle strikes.

"There appears to be a preference for overpasses as they are wildlife crossing structures that replicate habitat," he said.

"There's research in Australia, but also internationally, which shows this."

The NSW government told the ABC it knocked back an early proposal from WIRES to build an overpass at Glen Lorne as additional land clearing would have been required.

Dr Salter said although it was a disappointing decision, the underpass could help fill important knowledge gaps.

"The [underpass] is the approach the government has adopted, so we just have to hope it's going to work," he said.

"It provides us with a significant opportunity to monitor the movement of animals on either side of the underpass in the adjacent habitat, but also if they are moving towards and through the underpass.”

Cameras installed at the underpass will be used to improve koala safety and habitat connectivity. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

The box-culvert structure was delivered by developer Stockland, which is building the neighbouring 1,700-home Figtree Hill Estate.

Construction of the crossing was held up while Stockland sought access to Lendlease-owned land on the opposite side of the road.

The Sydney Basin Koala Network (SBKN) said BioNet data showed there had been six koala strikes and five deaths during the delay period, which Stockland described as "regrettable".

SBKN said 66 koalas have died on Appin Road since July 2022.

More Appin Road underpasses

Environment Minister Penny Sharpe (centre) describes the completion of the Glen Lorne koala underpass as "historic" and "really important". (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Stockland is now due to build another Appin Road underpass near the Beulah Nature Reserve.

NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said she wanted to avoid the delays that left the Glen Lorne crossing almost a year behind schedule.

Stockland is to deliver Glen Lorne and Beulah underpasses while the state government will build Ousedale. (Supplied: Transport for NSW)

"Sometimes delays happen. I still think this is absolutely worth it," she said.

"Hopefully the lessons that we have learnt here will see works sped up.

“I understand why people are concerned about it as it is a precious koala population."

The developer has told the ABC it has secured a land access licence with Lendlease to facilitate Beulah's delivery and that environmental applications would be lodged in the coming months.

The final Appin Road underpass, Ousedale, is a Transport for NSW project slated for the end of 2027.

Glen Lorne koala underpass at Noorumba Reserve is supported by around 3km of koala exclusion fencing along both sides of Appin Road. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

World.title: Sydney's gangland war marks another tragic chapter
World.content:
The brazen murder of an underworld figure's suspected business associate possibly marks the sixth innocent victim of the city's sprawling gangland war in just over a year, and the second this week.

The man in his 40s, police believe, was "likely" ambushed after picking up children from a nearby school.

Fatally shot in broad daylight at a home with two children inside, he is the 41st murder attributed to underworld violence since shootings began in 2020 over the city's drug trade.

"Tragically, that [mistaken identity] is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by these offenders," Superintendent Simon Glasser told reporters on Wednesday afternoon.

Forensics teams were at the Merrylands West scene on Wednesday night. (ABC News: Digby Werthmuller)

The victim's associate is "very well known to police" and detectives believe the shooting stems from feuding organised crime groups.

The death marks another tragic chapter in the tit-for-tat violence that has been plaguing Sydney for years and continues a disturbing pattern of civilians caught in the crossfire.

Marco Tapia died early on Tuesday morning. (Supplied)

Just a day earlier, university student Marco Tapia died after masked men stormed his Glen Alpine home and shot him dead.

In the wake of Mr Tapia's death and hours before the Merrylands West attack, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said the taking of "innocent life" was "completely unacceptable".

Underworld fugitive Iziah Utai was quick to take to social media to gloat that the attackers: "popped the wrong person, didn't even get the right house".

Iziah Utai's self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel" is openly feuding with the Alameddine crime family, and police believe the two gangs are responsible for a recent surge in violence.

Clumsy crooks and death by association

Gilbert Shino died as a result of multiple gunshot wounds. (Supplied)

The mistakes from bungling hit-men over the last year, police alleged, range from wrong addresses, similar names, appearance or death by association.

Gilbert Shino died in a hail of bullets leaving a Forest Lodge pub in August 2025 in the company of a "DLASTHR" associate aware of threats to his life.

Beloved entrepreneur Luke Manassa, 21, was allegedly stabbed to death by two teenagers after being mistaken for an in-law involved in the current organised crime conflict.

John Versace, who was killed in a shooting outside his family's Condell Park home. (Facebook)

Similarly, police have made clear that plumber John Versace was anything but a gangster when he was gunned down at his family home in May 2025.

Others like Bankstown mother Thi Kim Tran April last year have been targeted due to their relationships.

Ms Tran was taken, stripped naked in the street and shot in the head by what police allege are the underlings of a Vietnamese crime boss attempting to lure her husband out of hiding.

Thi Kim Tran was killed in April. (Supplied: Facebook)

In February, two men were charged over the alleged kidnapping murder of 85-year-old Sydney man Chris Baghsarian in a case of mistaken identity, with the intended abduction target understood to be a man living nearby.

Several people remain before the courts on that matter.

So worrying is the state of the city's criminal milieu that Premier Chris Minns cancelled some of his plans while on a trade mission in India to receive a briefing on the latest shootings.

Sydney's era of 'disorganised crime' One of the state's top police officers has promised feuding gangs bringing terror to Sydney's streets will not exist "by the time we finish" as police stare down a new era of disorganised crime.

Police Minister Yasmin Catley, at the same press conference, detailed the model being used by crime networks in the city.

"Bringing in people who are just happy to commit a crime without understanding the consequences, and here we've seen again, allegedly, that we have somebody who is [targeted] from mis-identification," she said.

Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook has previously told the ABC Sydney's gangland scene has entered a new era of "disorganised crime" with underworld figures, who are often offshore, putting contracts out for murder and intimidation on the open market.

The jobs are increasingly being accepted by inexperienced young people with devastating and unintended consequences.

World.title: Golfers despair as rabbits damage one of Australia's best courses
World.content:
Plague proportions of feral rabbits invading one of Western Australia's premier golf courses are highlighting widening gaps in Australia's feral animal control measures.

Albany Golf Course, about 450 kilometres south of Perth, is home to the state's oldest golf club and was last year named one of the top 100 golf courses in the country.

The rolling coastal greens attract golfers from across the state, but in recent years, increasing numbers of rabbits have posed a threat to the course's legacy.

Dan Northcott says extra holes have been turning up on the Albany Golf Course. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

General manager Dan Northcott said the damage caused by rabbits was highly visible and repairs were costing him hours in staff time.

"Without doubt, this is definitely the most rabbits we've ever seen," he said.

"They've doubled, if not tripled, over the last two years."

Feral rabbits dig into the course's greens. (ABC Great Southern: Caris Harper)

City of Albany reserves manager Jacqui Freeman said calicivirus and myxomatosis were being used to control rabbits across the city in areas where they were causing environmental or amenity damage.

But Mr Northcott said those controls were losing their effectiveness, forcing him to explore alternatives, including shooting.

Albany gun retailer Cooper Daniels said more people were complaining about the rabbit problem.

Cooper Daniels says shooters tell him feral rabbit numbers are skyrocketing. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

"I'd go out for a night and maybe shoot, say, three or four, and now I'd be able to shoot eight, 10, 12 even," he said.

"A few of the farms I go out to have massive crops, and you just see acres of land getting destroyed by them."

Farmers hit hard

Biocontrols such as the calicivirus, developed in the 1990s and used to replace myxomatosis, developed in the 1950s, have been used by authorities to reduce rabbit populations for decades.

Cranbrook farmer Lewis Miller said resistance to the viruses had contributed to a rise in numbers.

"Growing up on the property, you would see the odd rabbit here or there, but not like the numbers we're seeing now … It's just sort of exploded," he said.

"They've just got this immunity that's built up over time, and their numbers are gradually increasing again."

Lewis Miller says rabbit numbers on his Cranbrook farm are rising (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

Mr Miller said he had about 40 rabbit warrens spread across his 3,000-hectare property, with hundreds of rabbits causing long-term damage to the farm.

"It's a nuisance for sure, just because they're obviously in competition with the sheep that we run on the property," he said.

"Rabbits graze plants basically down to the root system, and once you've done that, you've really sort of hampered the plant for its life."

Lewis Miller says he has about 40 rabbit warrens spread across his 3,000-hectare property. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

'Plague proportions'

The federal government invested $2.6 million into a new rabbit biocontrol study as part of the 2026 budget.

The Australian Invasive Species Council welcomed the investment, but said it could take up to a decade to develop a new virus.

Feral rabbits are most active at dusk and dawn. (ABC Great Southern: Caris Harper)

Senior advocate James Johnston said the country was approaching "plague level proportions" of the animals not seen since the 1990s.

"We are behind the eight ball on rabbit biocontrol in this country," he said.

Trish Fleming says new control measures are needed. (ABC News: Ben Tessler)

Murdoch University wildlife ecologist Trish Fleming said rabbit biology necessitated updated control measures.

"There's substantial work that goes into developing new viruses to introduce as biocontrols for rabbits, and we do need a new one every 10 to 15 years," she said.

"The rabbits breed themselves out of it, so there's always going to be a requirement for us to bring a new one online."

A Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry spokesperson said it was working on the recommendations from the National Rabbit Biocontrol Pipeline Strategy, including developing new tools.

World.title: Aviation authorities to review low flyover at Cape Town rugby match
World.content:
A low-altitude flyover by two Airlink passenger jets before a rugby match at Cape Town Stadium is being reviewed by South African aviation authorities after it drew safety concerns, officials say.

The South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it had obtained flight data recordings and requested additional information from regional carrier Airlink as part of its assessment. A full report with recommendations will be issued once the review is complete.

"It is therefore critical that we interrogate this past weekend's events … to determine if there were any safety concerns which warrant a review," the agency said in a statement.

Airlink has withdrawn plans for another flyover at the upcoming rugby match in Soweto, according to the SACAA, which regulates aviation safety and security.

The flyover ahead of the Springboks and All Blacks match on August 29 drew huge cheers from an estimated crowd of about 56,000, but it also sparked a debate over safety risks after video footage from spectators inside and around the stadium spread online.

Deandra Peters, 25, a pilot and aviation enthusiast attending her first live rugby match, said the spectacle electrified the crowd in the stadium in a way that was difficult to capture on video.

"You can watch the planes fly over, but you can't recreate what it felt like to be inside a stadium full of Springbok supporters absolutely losing their minds," she told The Associated Press.

"The atmosphere was electric — the noise, the pride, the emotion. It was a very uniquely South African moment."

Airlink on Wednesday said the manoeuvrer had been carefully planned and rehearsed and that safety was "the first consideration at every stage of the process." It said each aircraft had three senior captains aboard, with more than 75,000 combined flight hours across the crews.

Earlier this week, Airlink had provided the data from the aeroplanes' black boxes to the civil aviation authority for review.

The SACAA said it would examine flight data to determine whether any safety concerns warranted a review.

The airline acknowledged the enthusiasm generated by the spectacle while also recognising what it described as the "valid questions and concerns" that followed.

"We never intended to become the news or upstage rugby's greatest rivalry," Airlink chief executive de Villiers Engelbrecht said in a statement.

The regulator said the airline had made applications for three flyovers. The most recent one in Cape Town was the second, while the first flyover took place in Johannesburg on August 22. Both were approved in line with the requirements for special air events.

Airlink has withdrawn its application for a flyover scheduled for September 1, over Johannesburg's Soccer City Stadium. The airline said forecast weather conditions were unfavourable for a safe formation flyby. SACAA confirmed that the application had been withdrawn.

South African rugby has a long tradition of stadium flybys at major matches, dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg, when a Boeing 747 swept over Ellis Park before the Springboks faced the All Blacks.

Last Saturday's flyby was unusually low and dramatic, drawing international attention, with some aviation experts later questioning whether the aircraft had left too little margin for error.

Washington: Australia and the US flagged further acceleration of America’s military presence in Australia following a meeting between the countries’ defence ministers – though they stopped short of saying it could mean more US troops stationed in Australia. Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles met US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington on Wednesday (US time), after which the Pentagon announced both leaders had “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases”, among other things. Both sides confirmed US force posture in Australia would increase, with announcements to come later this year. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein That is on top of the rotation of US nuclear-powered submarines through HMAS Stirling near Perth from next year under the AUKUS agreement, which will see as many as 2300 American troops deployed there. Marles confirmed US force posture in Australia was discussed at the meeting, but would not provide details. Announcements would be made at an Australia-US ministerial (AUSMIN) meeting later this year, he said.



“American force posture in Australia is growing. That’s across all the domains,” Marles told reporters. “We think that’s really important in terms of providing deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, providing stability and peace in the Indo-Pacific. That’s very much in Australia’s national interest.” Related Article AUKUS AUKUS makes Australia a nuclear target, top experts warn Force posture expansion could involve additional joint military exercises and upping co-operation on logistics, not necessarily an increase in US troops. In a sign that the administration had not given up its long-standing call for Canberra to increase spending on defence, the Pentagon also said Hegseth “emphasised the need for capable allies to contribute to the collective defence and invest in their own sovereign security”. However, unlike previous occasions, the Pentagon’s summary did not include an explicit request that Australia increase spending to 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product.



Marles said Australia had lifted expenditure four years in a row, and it was among the highest in the region. “We have a good story to tell … we understand the American position, but I think that is a story that is well received.” During a whirlwind visit to Washington, the deputy prime minister also met his US counterpart, Vice President JD Vance, at the White House, and President Donald Trump’s deputy chief-of-staff Stephen Miller. He now heads to the United Kingdom for further meetings about the AUKUS pact. Richard Marles arrives at the Pentagon to meet Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein Marles’ encounter with Hegseth appeared friendly, with the Australian patting his American counterpart on the back as they walked into the Pentagon. It marked a different tone to the diplomatic stoush this time last year, when – amid an ongoing review of AUKUS – the Pentagon initially described their meeting as a “happenstance encounter”.



This year’s meetings came on the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS defence treaty between the US, Australia and New Zealand. A poll this week by the United States Studies Centre found 68 per cent of Australians believed the US would come to their aid if attacked by China, down from 84 per cent in 2023. Related Article Trump diplomacy Hegseth enrages Canada by mocking appearance of female military cadets Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, who attended the meeting with Hegseth and Marles and was previously an AUKUS sceptic, marked the anniversary with a social media post praising the alliance as stronger than ever. “Australia and the United States have taken great strides over the last year and a half to strengthen collective defence and deterrence by denial in the Western Pacific, but we both know we must move faster and do more to meet the moment,” Colby said. The signal that the US intends to keep growing its military posture in Australia comes as a public inquiry into AUKUS, led by opponents of the pact, hears evidence that the deal risks making Australia more of a target.



Asked about that, Marles said the US-Australia alliance provided for peace and stability in the region. “That’s what underpins the security of Australians,” he said. “This work is profoundly important.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

A car has crashed into a Travel Money shopfront in the heart of Perth’s CBD in the early hours of Thursday morning. 9News Perth

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek says young Australians are internalising “scripts” from pornography and playing them out in their own sexual encounters.

Plibersek has long warned of the dangers of the practice of sexual strangulation, and said the government was considering a ban on depictions of choking in pornography following the news a 16-year-old girl had died after a suspected choking act during sex on Sydney’s northern beaches.

Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek. Alex Ellinghausen

She said it was just one example of an “extremely dangerous practice” learnt through porn consumption.

“All of us who work in this area have been told about young men and young women who have perhaps been engaging in sexual strangulation … It can’t be done safely,” Plibersek told News24.

World.title: Binge banks on its new Colin From Accounts replacement, as it unveils 2027 line-up
World.content:
CultureTV & radioStreaming Binge banks on its new Colin From Accounts replacement, as it unveils 2027 line-up Louise Rugendyke September 3, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A wild black family comedy starring Miranda Otto leads Binge’s slate of new local originals, as the streamer seeks to find a replacement for their hit Colin From Accounts. Created, written and starring Rick Donald, and directed by the team behind Colin From Accounts – Trent O’Donnell and Madeleine Dyer – Tough Love is about a hopeless 39-year-old who still lives at home with his mum, but whose life is upended when his mum is diagnosed with cancer. She, meanwhile, is stricken by the fact her three adult children are unprepared for life without her. The cast of new Australian comedy Tough Love (from left) Rick Donald as eldest son Shane, Miranda Otto as mum Kerry, Liz Kingsman as daughter Steph and Hugo Johnston-Burt as middle child Rodney. “It’s a tragic comedy about family and chaos and how that can be incredibly funny, but also incredibly sad,” said the bushy-bearded Donald, who is now filming Tough Love in the leafy Sydney suburb of Roseville Chase, largely while wearing footy shorts, a singlet and a dirty apron. “It [came from] knowing a lot of older kids that failed to leave the nest and how common that is. And that can be for many different reasons, in our case it’s because my role, Shane, he’s just a manchild that’s lazy and just stunted – intelligence-wise and emotionally. “But for some people, they don’t leave because it’s so incredibly hard to buy, and they have to stay with their parents, so there are a lot of reasons why people are staying home, and they’re failing to leave.”







Related Article Australian TV Jonathan LaPaglia has one word for fans boycotting Australian Survivor: ‘Good’ “It’s in the rearview mirror, it’s its own service now,” said Monaghan of HBO Max, adding that Binge had “grown all year”, in large part due to its content deal with US network NBC. “It’s on an upwards trajectory,” he said. “And that is because of All Her Fault. We also have Outlander from Sony, which did phenomenally well. We had a real big surprise with The Other Bennet Sister, which will end the year as one of our top two or three shows, which is wild. “We are building, those shows are doing HBO-level numbers. The biggest day for Colin [episode five from season three, “Druggy Druggy Sex Party”] that was our biggest [audience] day since one of the HBO shows, I’m going to say season two of The White Lotus … I think we’ll end the year in a far better position than people probably anticipated when HBO went away.”

World.title: Perth daycare centre forced to close over asbestos concerns
World.content:
NationalWAChildcare Perth daycare centre forced to close over asbestos concerns Holly Thompson September 3, 2026 — 9:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A daycare centre in Perth’s southern suburbs has been forced to close its doors after asbestos from a nearby demolition site landed in the centre’s garden, impacting the air quality. Parents were notified the centre would be closed on Wednesday morning, pending further testing, after an initial test within the Fremantle Early Learning Centre returned positive for asbestos air fibres. Fremantle Early Learning Centre, the building towards the back, surrounded by development. “An air quality assessment undertaken by SW19 on behalf of the Department of Communities included testing conducted at the centre last night,” an email to parents from the centre said. “As the testing occurred while routine cleaning was underway, the results were inconclusive and further testing is required while the centre is unoccupied.



“As a precaution, we have been asked by SW19 to close the centre today as a precautionary measure. We were informed early this morning that this testing is required. “We sincerely apologise for the late notice of this communication and the inconvenience caused.” It has not yet been confirmed whether the second test returned a positive result. Parents at the centre were told that a lump of asbestos was found in the garden on Monday. The daycare centre is surrounded by a development site, which was formerly community housing.



It is being transformed into a new residential development precinct that will accommodate 700 new homes, including commercial and public spaces. Development WA undertook hazardous materials surveys and engaged a licensed asbestos removal contractor to carry out the removal of identified asbestos before demolishing the site. It has also commissioned an independent environmental hygienist and installed an air monitoring system, including one on the boundary with the daycare centre. Fremantle Early Learning Centre was also provided with advice on the demolition and asbestos removal. A Department of Communities spokesperson said they were a “small fragment containing asbestos was found in an outdoor play area at an early learning centre in Fremantle”.



“The immediate focus is the health and wellbeing of the children who access the centre, staff and their families,” they said. “An investigation is underway to determine how the material was present at the centre, and to ensure any further risks are immediately identified and mitigated.” They said that initial expert advice was that this was a low-risk exposure because the asbestos was bound within cement material and was unlikely to have become airborne. The Department of Communities, managing the incident on behalf of the childcare centre, said the service has been temporarily closed as a precaution and that parents were being informed of any updates.

World.title: ‘Name of the game’: De Minaur adapts to New York deluge with fast win
World.content:
Updated SportTennisUS Open ‘Name of the game’: De Minaur adapts to New York deluge with fast win Marc McGowan Updated September 3, 2026 — 9:19am ,first published 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alex de Minaur had to wait until the fourth day of the US Open to play his first match. Fifty minutes later, he was off court again. New York’s wet weather continues to wreak havoc with the tournament’s first week as Australia’s world No.7, who was supposed to start his campaign on Wednesday (AEST), endured another rain delay before returning to blitz Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri 6-2, 6-2, 6-4. Alex de Minaur finally progressed to the second round after days of rain delays at the US Open. AP De Minaur broke Guerrieri – playing his first grand slam main draw match at age 27 – in the first game of each of the first two sets and appeared poised for a quick passage to the second round until weather intervened. He led 6-2, 4-2 when the chair umpire suspended play, with the delay lasting about two hours before he joined fellow Australians Dane Sweeny, Tristan Schoolkate, Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth as a first-round winner.



De Minaur needed only 99 minutes either side of the latest rain disruption to demolish his left-handed rival, looking sharp with his ball-striking and movement from the outset, albeit with a slight detour in the third set. With the finish line in sight, the three-time US Open quarter-finalist threw in a sloppy service game that he lost to love when trying to push 4-2 ahead. He also slipped 0-30 behind his next time with the Wilson balls before getting back on track to complete his victory. Loading “These tournaments, it’s all about adapting – and that’s the name of the game,” de Minaur said. “There’s too much to play for to let something like this affect you, so I’m glad [about how] I handled it. I’m glad I got in and out, played a relatively clean match, and now I can focus on the next one.



“Because of the rain, there’s nothing you can do about it. You’ve just got to get out there, play your tennis match and, ultimately, if you win enough matches, you’re going to get out on the stadium court. So that’s the mindset.” But several other Australians’ US Open is over. Twenty-year-old wildcard Preston was trounced 6-1, 6-1 in a mere 48 minutes by American Taylor Townsend in her second-round match, hitting only two winners compared to 28 unforced errors. It has been a wet and wild week for tennis fans in New York. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Daria Kasatkina is also out, losing her rain-interrupted first-round clash with Spain’s former world No.2 Paula Badosa that was carried over from the previous day.



Badosa was only two points from victory when the match was paused, and had to stave off two break-back points before clinching a 6-1, 5-4 win on her ninth match point to lock in a showdown with 2024 champion Coco Gauff. Related Article Updated

US Open From GoFundMe to making big bank: Australian’s US Open breakthrough Birrell staged a mid-match fightback against No.18 seed Ekaterina Alexandrova to force a third set, but a double fault on the first point led to her immediately handing the initiative to her Russian rival before eventually going down 6-1, 2-6, 6-3. Pushed out to Flushing Meadows’ back blocks on court 11, after originally being scheduled on the bigger Grandstand stadium a day earlier, de Minaur did not have the fortune of playing on one of the event’s two courts with a retractable roof. The challenges for de Minaur rise steeply from here – beginning in the second round with dangerous Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp, who also advanced in straight sets against outmatched Brit Jan Choinski.



Van de Zandschulp famously upset Carlos Alcaraz in the second round at the US Open two years ago. De Minaur’s projected rivals beyond that are 31st seed Zizou Bergs (third round) and top seed Alexander Zverev (quarter-finals), who needed almost five hours to battle past Italy’s Lorenzo Sonego in the first round. Australia’s Taylah Preston has been knocked out in the second round. Getty Images However, his potential path was made somewhat easier when possible fourth-round opponent, in-form No.12 seed Rafael Jodar, suffered a shock 6-2, 6-1, 6-1 loss to lucky loser Bu Yunchaokete, who entered the draw when Australia’s Thanasi Kokkinakis withdrew with an ankle issue. After a brilliant start to the season, including a second straight Australian Open quarter-final and winning the Rotterdam title, de Minaur has relatively struggled, at least by his lofty standards.



But the US Open has been a happy hunting ground for Australian tennis’ torchbearer, so he will hope to return to at least the last eight again after losing in the third and fourth rounds at Roland-Garros and Wimbledon, respectively. Related Video Video icon 0:50 Demon smashes through to second round His wife, English player Katie Boulter, crashed out with a 6-1, 6-0 second-round loss to Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova. “Of course, it’s difficult,” de Minaur said. “Ultimately, we’ve got each other’s backs no matter what, and we’ve always got one eye out on each other. Obviously, it was a tough day for Katie, and I had to do my best to just focus on my task ahead and get the job done in the best way possible. I’m glad I was able to achieve that today.” Joint (against No.9 seed Elina Svitolina) and Duckworth (Wu Yibing) are also due to play their second-round matches on Thursday (AEST).

World.title: Hottest start to September tipped for this weekend but don’t call it a heatwave
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWeather Hottest start to September tipped for this weekend but don’t call it a heatwave Dominique Tassell September 3, 2026 — 9:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Spring has sprung in Brisbane, bringing with it the possibility of the hottest start to the month this century. While the temperature in the River City is expected to climb to 31 degrees on Thursday, the mercury is forecast to reach 9 degrees above average in Brisbane at the weekend. On Friday, the maximum temperature is expected to stay in the 30s, with a high of 35 degrees predicted for Sunday. Brisbane residents will swelter through four days of hot weather in the first week of September. Courtney Kruk Hot and dry conditions are expected throughout the rest of south-east Queensland.



Bureau of Meteorology senior meteorologist Felim Hanniffy said there was the possibility of four days over 30 degrees in the first week of September, which would be the first time in at least 26 years. Related Article Weather Thirty-three degree Friday to ‘rubber-stamp the change in season’ in Brisbane The last time Brisbane sweltered through 30 degrees for three days in the first week of September was in 2019. “Brisbane’s temperature very much will depend on the sea breeze,” Hanniffy said. “So if the sea breeze comes in, then that could peg it back at a couple of degrees cooler.”



Temperatures are expected to cool off early next week. The average maximum temperature for Brisbane in September is 26 degrees. The spate of hot weather will not be considered a heatwave, as it will not have sustained high temperatures overnight. “To get a heatwave warning, you’d want to have both significantly warm overnight maximums and also daytime maximums as well,” Hanniffy said. “So, this time around the days will be warmer [and] the nights, a little bit warmer, but still there’ll be a little bit of a fresher feel to the early mornings as well.



“But certainly the outlook as we go into the rest of spring are well above average temperatures and certainly increased potential for heatwaves as well.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Your preferences, made simple
World.content:
Sponsored NationalVictoriaLa Trobe University Your preferences, made simple Advertorial for La Trobe University September 3, 2026 — 9:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You’re in year 12, with a lot on your plate: classes, assignments, tests. End-of-year exams are looming. You’re also considering what comes next – maybe further study at uni or TAFE next year. There’s a lot to think about. While you’re focused on the pressures of getting through VCE, planning what and where to study next year, drawing up a list of your preferences can seem challenging and confusing. The first thing to know is that you’re not alone. If last year is any guide, VTAC (the Victorian Tertiary Admissions Centre) will this year manage applications for uni undergraduate and TAFE courses from around 70,000 students. La Trobe University offers VCE students free advice via its Students Hub, regardless of where you want to study.



So, a lot of people are in the same boat. And there are plenty of people, places and resources that can guide you as you plan your next steps. Your school careers adviser can outline how VTAC works and how it will process your application. Fellow students, friends who’ve already gone through the process, and family members can provide support and advice. And there’s a mass of material on the VTAC websites and unis that can help, too. Don’t be daunted The Students Hub at La Trobe University is a good place to start, with free, easily accessible content and handy links that are useful, regardless of what higher education institution you want to get into.



So, don’t be daunted; the process is manageable, with a bit of thought and some basic planning. Central to your VTAC application is listing the courses you’d like to undertake, in order of preference. You can list eight preferences, with your favourite option or dream course at the top. We’ll come back to this. Drawing up your preferences might be easy if you already know what and where you want to study, if you are confident that you’ll meet the entry requirements and you’ve got a clear idea of what you’ll do once you’ve finished study. Or, like plenty of others, you might be uncertain. Either way, the preference list gives you options. As you consider your options, it helps if you draft a plan to guide you through the VTAC process step-by-step, as you look for courses that match what you like and what you’re good at, before you lodge your application.



You can use the course search platforms provided by VTAC and unis. As you draft a list of courses that appeal to you, step two is to consider if you’re likely to meet entry requirements based on your ATAR. The La Trobe ATAR Calculator can help you estimate your ATAR or use your actual ATAR score to find courses that match your interests. It can also help you discover options you might not have thought about. Don’t forget that there are access and equity schemes and scholarships, which could mean you get additional ATAR points if you’ve experienced circumstances that have impacted your education. La Trobe’s ATAR Adjustment Factors Calculator can help you find out what you might be eligible for. Many pathways to success If you think your ATAR won’t get you into your preferred course straight away, that’s not the end of the story. Instead, look at pathways that can move you towards your long-term goal. Pathways are certificates, diplomas or related degrees that can be a way into your dream course at your preferred uni later.



By doing some basic research, and applying a step-by-step approach, the process becomes manageable. You’ll gain confidence as you enter the next stage – listing, reviewing and submitting your preferences. This is where some students get stuck, and where Jemima Bowen, manager in La Trobe University’s student recruitment team, has some key advice. “At the top of your list put the course you most want – your dream course, no matter how competitive – not the course you guess you’ll get into. You won’t be disadvantaged if you aim high,” she says. “Think of your preferences as a wish list rather than a prediction of what you think you’ll be offered.” Aiming high doesn’t mean being unrealistic, so include second and subsequent preferences that give you options that might still get you where you want to go. If you don’t get your first preference, you’ll automatically be considered for your next preferences.



A common misconception is that listing only one preference will improve your chances. “It won’t,” says Bowen. “You should include all the courses you want to study, as well as any pathway options that might apply.” In December, when ATARs are issued, VTAC manages the offer process – matching you with places in courses based on your results and preferences. It then sends out an offer for the highest course for which you qualify. If you miss out in the first round, there are more rounds to come. Along the way, there will be times when you can re-order, add or remove course preferences if you change your mind. Finally, to go back to where we started: remember you’re not alone.



If you’re still unsure about the process, even after you’ve done your research, you can still seek support. At La Trobe you can contact the support hub, where you can talk to an expert, submit questions or engage in online chat to get personalised advice to help you make the best choice for your future. For more information, visit latrobe.edu.au
