World.title: Choose a uni that helps you make an impact
World.content:
Sponsored NationalVictoriaLa Trobe University Choose a uni that helps you make an impact Advertorial for La Trobe University September 3, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Even while you’re focused on deciding what course you’ll study next year, plenty of people will already be asking you: “What do you want to do after uni?” It might be easy to answer if you already have a dream job in mind and the university course that will help you land it. But it’s a big question to throw at you if you’re not sure what you want to do after uni and instead are keeping your career options open. Either way, the world of work is being transformed (just think of the dramatic impact of AI); jobs don’t stay the same, and it’s possible you’ll have more than one career in your lifetime. So, at a time of massive change, how does a uni course set you on a path to achieve your ambition, or open avenues that ensure you can adapt and have an impact in whatever path you take after university? An academic qualification – a diploma or degree – is at the heart of what universities offer and what employers will look at when you apply for a job.



But surveys show employers are looking for more than academic achievement. They prize analytical and creative thinking, resilience, flexibility, leadership and social skills – and the fast-growing demand for skills in AI and technology literacy. Student ‘capabilities’ underpin job-readiness Many of those same skills were mentioned by employers with whom La Trobe University consulted when building its Career Ready Advantage, a program designed to prepare students for the workplace. It’s based on a framework focused on building capabilities – communications and literacy skills allowing you to build relationships, personal and professional skills of leadership and teamwork, and analytical skills that allow you to interpret data. La Trobe University is embedding AI capabilities across its suite of courses and study disciplines.



To shape those skills, the Career Ready Advantage’s integrated package is built into undergraduate courses. It has three components: access to professional learning; support with gaining practical experience in workplaces and community activities; and a career portfolio that showcases your skills, experience and accomplishments to potential employers. Academic courses remain the essential foundation. If you’re in year 12, you’ll need to check universities’ online course guides to see if they offer the range of subjects you’re interested in and if you meet entry requirements. A good place to start is La Trobe’s Year 12 Hub which has handy links to useful resources that will help you navigate application processes. You can also explore La Trobe’s extensive and growing range of course offerings, in diverse disciplines including health, science, engineering, arts, law and IT. A new addition is an Australian first – an honours degree in artificial intelligence engineering. Depending on your lifestyle, you might want to consider if the university offers you flexibility so you can blend online study to your on-campus degree. And depending on where you live, you’ll want to check campus locations. La Trobe, for example, has seven campuses – two in Melbourne, one in Sydney and four in regional Victoria, including its Shepparton campus which has recently had a $20 million expansion.



Another question is: how does a university fill the gap between an academic qualification and all those additional skills that employers are looking for? Embedding industry experience, AI skills La Trobe has responded to this challenge by building practical experience into courses through work-integrated learning. Over half of its bachelor’s degrees already include compulsory industry experience. Students studying healthcare subjects at La Trobe, for example, have a real-world impact while gaining practical experience at the recently opened La Trobe Health Clinic at its Bundoora campus. Vice chancellor Professor Theo Farrell says that by embedding clinical training within a working health service, “we are giving students the confidence and practical experience they need to enter the workforce, while also improving access to care for people who need it most”.



Where industry experience is not compulsory, many La Trobe courses let students choose a placement or industry project as an elective, while multidisciplinary industry projects allow them to apply learning in a simulated workplace, connect with industry professionals, and contribute to solving a problem for an industry or community organisation. With AI reshaping every industry, La Trobe is embedding AI capabilities across all its teaching and learning – not just technology degrees – so students in all disciplines can develop skills and confidence to work with emerging technologies. This integrated approach to academic courses, enhanced by building skills, experience and connections, means graduates can have an impact in a professional workplace from day one. One other thing to consider when looking at university options: remember your uni experience extends beyond the classroom. So, check out student clubs and societies, sport and fitness facilities, and student support services. Becoming part of the student community helps forge networks and enhances the social skills that are in demand in whatever career you choose. Finally, independent evidence of the success of La Trobe’s approach is in the national Employer Satisfaction Survey that measures how well graduates meet employer demand, and La Trobe rates among the top three Victorian universities. A similar survey shows La Trobe’s graduate full-time employment outcomes also rank among the top three. For more information, visit latrobe.edu.au

World.title: WA news LIVE: Car smashes into Perth CBD shopfront
World.content:
A 52-year-old man is in hospital after his car smashed into a shopfront in Perth’s CBD in the early hours of Thursday morning.

It is understood the car reversed into the front of the Travel Money store at the intersection of Hay Street and William Street, in the heart of the city, about 3.30am.

A car has crashed into a Travel Money shopfront in the heart of Perth’s CBD in the early hours of Thursday morning. 9News Perth

Police remain at the scene and the area is cordoned off as people begin to stream into the city on Thursday.

The 52-year-old man, who was the only person in the car, was rushed to Royal Perth Hospital, where he is currently receiving treatment.

World.content:
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek says young Australians are internalising “scripts” from pornography and playing them out in their own sexual encounters.

Plibersek has long warned of the dangers of the practice of sexual strangulation, and said the government was considering a ban on depictions of choking in pornography following the news a 16-year-old girl had died after a suspected choking act during sex on Sydney’s northern beaches.

Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek. Alex Ellinghausen

She said it was just one example of an “extremely dangerous practice” learnt through porn consumption.

“All of us who work in this area have been told about young men and young women who have perhaps been engaging in sexual strangulation … It can’t be done safely,” Plibersek told News24.

World.title: Binge banks on its new Colin From Accounts replacement, as it unveils 2027 line-up
World.content:
CultureTV & radioStreaming Binge banks on its new Colin From Accounts replacement, as it unveils 2027 line-up Louise Rugendyke September 3, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A wild black family comedy starring Miranda Otto leads Binge’s slate of new local originals, as the streamer seeks to find a replacement for their hit Colin From Accounts. Created, written and starring Rick Donald, and directed by the team behind Colin From Accounts – Trent O’Donnell and Madeleine Dyer – Tough Love is about a hopeless 39-year-old who still lives at home with his mum, but whose life is upended when his mum is diagnosed with cancer. She, meanwhile, is stricken by the fact her three adult children are unprepared for life without her. The cast of new Australian comedy Tough Love (from left) Rick Donald as eldest son Shane, Miranda Otto as mum Kerry, Liz Kingsman as daughter Steph and Hugo Johnston-Burt as middle child Rodney. “It’s a tragic comedy about family and chaos and how that can be incredibly funny, but also incredibly sad,” said the bushy-bearded Donald, who is now filming Tough Love in the leafy Sydney suburb of Roseville Chase, largely while wearing footy shorts, a singlet and a dirty apron. “It [came from] knowing a lot of older kids that failed to leave the nest and how common that is. And that can be for many different reasons, in our case it’s because my role, Shane, he’s just a manchild that’s lazy and just stunted – intelligence-wise and emotionally. “But for some people, they don’t leave because it’s so incredibly hard to buy, and they have to stay with their parents, so there are a lot of reasons why people are staying home, and they’re failing to leave.”

We also have Outlander from Sony, which did phenomenally well. The biggest day for Colin [episode five from season three, “Druggy Druggy Sex Party”] that was our biggest [audience] day since one of the HBO shows, I’m going to say season two of The White Lotus … I think we’ll end the year in a far better position than people probably anticipated when HBO went away.”

World.title: Perth daycare centre forced to close over asbestos concerns
World.content:
NationalWAChildcare Perth daycare centre forced to close over asbestos concerns Holly Thompson September 3, 2026 — 9:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A daycare centre in Perth’s southern suburbs has been forced to close its doors after asbestos from a nearby demolition site landed in the centre’s garden, impacting the air quality. Parents were notified the centre would be closed on Wednesday morning, pending further testing, after an initial test within the Fremantle Early Learning Centre returned positive for asbestos air fibres. Fremantle Early Learning Centre, the building towards the back, surrounded by development. “An air quality assessment undertaken by SW19 on behalf of the Department of Communities included testing conducted at the centre last night,” an email to parents from the centre said. “As the testing occurred while routine cleaning was underway, the results were inconclusive and further testing is required while the centre is unoccupied.



“As a precaution, we have been asked by SW19 to close the centre today as a precautionary measure. We were informed early this morning that this testing is required. “We sincerely apologise for the late notice of this communication and the inconvenience caused.” It has not yet been confirmed whether the second test returned a positive result. Parents at the centre were told that a lump of asbestos was found in the garden on Monday. The daycare centre is surrounded by a development site, which was formerly community housing.



It is being transformed into a new residential development precinct that will accommodate 700 new homes, including commercial and public spaces. Development WA undertook hazardous materials surveys and engaged a licensed asbestos removal contractor to carry out the removal of identified asbestos before demolishing the site. It has also commissioned an independent environmental hygienist and installed an air monitoring system, including one on the boundary with the daycare centre. Fremantle Early Learning Centre was also provided with advice on the demolition and asbestos removal. A Department of Communities spokesperson said they were a “small fragment containing asbestos was found in an outdoor play area at an early learning centre in Fremantle”.



“The immediate focus is the health and wellbeing of the children who access the centre, staff and their families,” they said. “An investigation is underway to determine how the material was present at the centre, and to ensure any further risks are immediately identified and mitigated.” They said that initial expert advice was that this was a low-risk exposure because the asbestos was bound within cement material and was unlikely to have become airborne. The Department of Communities, managing the incident on behalf of the childcare centre, said the service has been temporarily closed as a precaution and that parents were being informed of any updates.

World.title: Christopher Luxon defends taking second plane overseas after criticising Hipkins for the same
World.content:
The prime minister is defending the deployment of a second Defence Force plane for his Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) mission, having previously criticised the use of a back-up plane when in opposition.

Christopher Luxon is in Palau for the annual PIF leaders meeting. Both of the RNZAF Boeing 757s have been deployed on the mission, with one staying in Cairns as a back-up.

Luxon said it was a Defence Force decision to take two planes, with 88 people from New Zealand heading to PIF.

"We've taken 14 delegations up here, we've got a lot of people to take home on Sunday as well, and we're taking some home when I go out on Friday as well."

Luxon said connectivity was a big challenge at PIF, and he had talked about the importance of connectivity at the realm leaders' meeting with Tokelau, Niue, and the Cook Islands last week.

"It makes the case for why we need a good, reliable Air Force plane."

Air Component Commander Air Commodore Andy Scott also spoke of the PIF meeting's remote location.

"This important meeting is being held in a comparatively remote location where air services and options are limited, and therefore a back-up aircraft has been positioned to assist if required for any reason."

New Zealand is hosting next year's leaders meeting.

Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Nick Monro

In 2023, the Defence Force sent a back-up plane for then-Prime Minister Chris Hipkins' trip to China.

The back-up plane, which was sent in case the first broke down, was left in Manila. It attracted strong criticism from then-opposition leader Luxon, who said it "doesn't seem a good move" in a climate challenge.

Luxon vowed not to use Defence Force planes to travel internationally if he became prime minister - a promise he quickly reneged on.

The government is currently purchasing two new Airbus A321XLR planes on a lease-to-buy arrangement, to replace the ageing 757s.

The current planes, which were purchased in 2003, are mostly used for transporting cargo around the Pacific. But they have a recent history of unreliability when it comes to prime ministerial travel.

In 2024, Luxon had to fly commercially to Melbourne after the 757 broke down.

He also left a business delegation in Papua New Guinea after a 757 broke down during a refuel stop en route to Japan.

In 2016, Sir John Key was forced to cancel the first day of a trip to India after the 757 broke down in Townsville, while in 2019 Dame Jacinda Ardern flew commercially back from Melbourne after a breakdown.

World.title: Penrhyn port upgrade raises transparency and environmental concerns in the Cook Islands
World.content:
The United States and New Zealand-funded upgrade of Penrhyn port, a former American military base, in the northern Cook Islands has raised concerns about transparency and environmental impacts.

Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown described the port as a "lifeline" for Penrhyn, saying the US$60 million upgrade was one of the largest infrastructure projects in the country's history.

The US and New Zealand made the announcement in Palau this week, promising safer access to the remote atoll and better connections for the rest of the country.

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said the new port project builds on that shared history, but also on the Critical Minerals Framework which sets out how the Cook Islands and the US would work together to look at how the country's critical minerals could be explored and developed, including minerals found on the seafloor.

Penrhyn, also known as Tongareva, has a long-standing connection with the United States. Ewan Smith

World War II connection

Penrhyn, also known as Tongareva, has a long-standing connection with the US.

During World War II, the US forces established a military presence on the atoll. In 1942, an airfield was built on Penrhyn with around 1000 military personnel stationed on the island at the height of the war.

The airfield, which is now known as Tongareva, airport is still in use today. The port, located in the village of Omoka, was also constructed during World War II.

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown, and New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters mark the announcement of the Penrhyn Port Project in Palau. 1 September 2026 Facebook / US Embassy New Zealand

While Penrhyn MP Vaine Wichman has welcomed the project, a Cook Islands landowner and environmental organisation Te Ipukarea Society say they have concerns about transparency.

TIS director Alanna Matamaru Smith told Pacific Waves there was a lack of information on the project.

"Definitely concerned, especially when you've got a major state like the United States having interest in the South Pacific for nodules and deep sea mining," she said.

"Wanting to work in a space that we really don't know too much about, let alone what these nodules will be used for future purposes ... is it going to be for the green tech transition as they say, or is there something sinister at play here where it could be used for military defence purposes?"

A Cook Islands landowner, who RNZ Pacific has agreed not to name, said while she was not opposed to the port being upgraded. However, she said there needs to be more transparency about why the project is being funded.

Cook Is landowner questions investment in Penrhyn port Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

"The people of our Pa Enua (outer islands) deserve a safe, reliable infrastructure and better access to essential services," they said.

"What my concern is the way a project appears to be connected with a much wider critical mineral and geopolitical agenda."

The landowner said that the public needs to see the complete funding arrangements, project agreements, environment assessments and other conditions placed on the people on Penrhyn. She questioned whether there had been public consultations.

But Penrhyn MP Vaine Wichman told Pacific Waves the project had been a long time coming.

Penrhyn MP welcomes port upgrade amid concerns Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

"This kind of activity is not reflected really easily in the decisions that the country makes in terms of significant projects being approved for the small islands like Penrhyn," Wichman said.

She said the need for improved port infrastructure had been raised for nearly two decades.

'Our people deserve something permanent'

Wichman also rejected concerns raised by "these environmentalists" and said the people had been consulted "for many years".

The Penrhyn MP added that the focus on the US and the critical minerals overlooked the needs of the island, which is home to 200 people.

"I just find it sad that a lot of people like these environmentalists go first for something that's not even in the minds of our people, straight away - America, critical minerals - no good," Wichman said.

"No one ever thought to think about all these years while our poor port was being eroded by time and the weather and our people deserve something very permanent."

Wichman also dismissed questions around the timing of the announcement with Brown still serving as caretaker prime minister, saying the government had already been confirmed and there was no need to delay the announcement.

"The fact that it's announced now is just like any day, you know, business as usual. I can't say much for other people, but why hold on to something that's good news for some people?".

Penrhyn MP Vaine Wichman (file image) Cook Islands News

Looking ahead

Wichman said the project should also create opportunities for Penrhyn people to take part in its development and hoped it would encourage those who had left the island to return home.

"I will make sure that our people will be involved, especially in the construction of the infrastructure because we've grown since 80 years ago and we have some of our Penrhyn people working overseas, building other people's wharves and airports, why can't they come home and help build ours?"

The project will now move into a design phase, with the Cook Islands, New Zealand and the US expected to work through the details of the development.

For Penrhyn, the port promises a long-awaited improvement to its connection with the rest of the Cook Islands.

World.title: New Zealand pilgrims narrowly escaped Nepal flash flood
World.content:
More than half a dozen New Zealanders narrowly escaped last week's deadly flash floods on the Nepal-China border after their Auckland-based tour operator decided to cross the border a day earlier.

A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, burying villages.

Eight New Zealanders were among a group of 20 pilgrims who crossed through the Gyirong Port immigration centre just a day before it was completely washed away by the deluge.

Dixit Chauhan, owner of Royale Travels, said he made the decision to take the group across the border one day earlier than planned because previous experience on the pilgrimage had taught him the benefits of acclimatisation before attempting the trip.

The gruelling 53-kilometre pilgrimage around Mount Kailash is undertaken at altitudes exceeding 5000 metres, and pilgrims are advised to spend some time in the area before making a gradual ascent in elevation.

Chauhan's decision to cross earlier than planned to spend time at altitude meant the New Zealanders were safely on the other side of the border when the flash flood struck.

Wire agencies have reported that more than 1200 people have been confirmed dead in the disaster, with another 4200 missing, including five New Zealanders.

Pilgrims stand in front of the Gyirong Port Immigration Building and the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge last month, both of which were washed away in a flash flood last week. Amar Prakash

Chauhan was leading the group on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar.

Mount Kailash is believed to be the resting place of Hindu deities Lord Shiva and his wife, Parvati, and is considered one of the holiest places for Hindus, Buddhists and Jains.

The mountain is also viewed as a "cosmic pillar", a central axis connecting the physical world and higher spiritual dimensions.

It is believed that Lord Shiva sits on the mountain top in perpetual meditation, sustaining cosmic equilibrium.

For that reason, pilgrims are prohibited from climbing to the summit.

Nearby Lake Manasarovar is also considered sacred.

Hindu devotees believe completing the pilgrimage and taking a holy dip in Lake Manasarovar can cleanse a lifetime of sins and help attain moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth.

"We were all shocked by what happened," Chauhan said from Darchen in China's autonomous region of Tibet.

The group had completed its physically demanding walk around Mount Kailash.

"We were initially planning to cross the border on Wednesday when the floods happened but, because this was my second time, I told our operators we need to go a day earlier for the group to acclimatize to the conditions," he said.

Chauhan believed the decision to cross a day earlier was guided by Lord Shiva.

"I think it's not me who saved their lives but Lord Shiva," he said. "It's not my decision but the god's."

Chauhan said the group left New Zealand on 20 August and would return at the weekend.

He said the group was at the Gyirong Port immigration building as well as Rasuwa a day before the flash flood struck.

"We left Kathmandu in the morning [on Monday] and arrived [at Rasuwa] at 5pm and spent the night," he said.

"The next morning [on Tuesday] we left for the border, spent a couple of hours at the building and then crossed the border."

Chauhan said the group only learnt of the flash flood sometime later because it had limited connectivity in the mountains.

Amar Prakash (second from left) at Mount Kailash in July. Supplied

Remembering past visits

Auckland resident Amar Prakash has completed the pilgrimage twice.

Prakash arrived in Nepal in July, circled Mount Kailash and crossed the border from Tibet back into Nepal on 2 August.

"We were devastated and shocked because we have been through that border four times now," he said.

"We just couldn't believe the force of the water, the rubble, everything coming down," he said. "[It] is just heartbreaking."

Prakash said the hotel where they had stayed a few weeks earlier had been washed away and the guide who helped the group in China was missing.

"Without her, our pilgrimage wouldn't have been complete," he said.

Prakash said it took a while for him to fully accept that the places he had walked through just a few weeks earlier were completely gone.

Prakash first went to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar in June last year.

"I was going through a big life event transition in my life, going through divorce. I was at a very low point in life, I guess, and I needed something to sort of help me get back on my feet again," he said.

"It's quite a tough journey to go on because it challenges you emotionally, mentally and physically in all various aspects."

Prakash said the trip genuinely helped him, and he started to see positive changes in his life upon returning to New Zealand.

Inspired, he took some family members, including his parents and a cousin, on the pilgrimage this year.

Prakash said he spent a lot of time in Syabrubesi last year and walked around the bazaars of Rasuwagadhi this year as well.

He said the trip cost him somewhere between $10,000 and $12,000.

Unlike his first trip in 2025, Prakash noticed a significant increase in the number of Tibetan pilgrims this year.

"Because it is the Year of the Fire Horse, one that only happens every 60 years, the number of pilgrims from the China side increased this year," he said.

Pilgrims walk towards Mount Kailash in China's autonomous region of Tibet. Amar Prakash

'We shouldn't let this devastation stop us'

Monark Panchal, another Aucklander, also made the pilgrimage this year.

"It was my long wish to go to Mount Kailash since I was young but somehow it got delayed until this year," Panchal said.

He said the pilgrimage was very tough, and he was asked by his tour operator to train in advance.

"The parikrama (clockwise circumambulation) around Mount Kailash is a tough hike and takes three days to complete," he said.

The walk enables pilgrims to see the mountain from all sides - north, south, east and west.

Panchal said members of the group had to take medicine because of the high altitude.

"Every 20 minutes we had an alarm set just for drinking water," he said.

Panchal said the third day of the trek was the toughest.

There were horses and porters to help pilgrims carry their luggage and provide a ride if anyone needed one, he said.

Panchal said the high altitude, lack of oxygen and tough terrain combined to make the pilgrimage physically demanding.

"When we reached Dolma La Pass, we were more than 5600 metres above sea level," he said.

"If you go up [another] 3000 metres above sea level, you'll be on top of Everest and so you can imagine how tough it must be."

Panchal said the climb down from the Himalayan plateau was equally treacherous, requiring hikers to navigate steep seven-kilometre drop.

He said most pilgrims crossed into Nepal through Gyirong Port because it was the shortest way back.

Panchal said he tried to get in touch with a few people he met during the trip but had been unable to do so.

"We have been trying to reach them," he said. "It's all washed out actually and very sad.

"Since the disaster, I'm really disturbed and a bit stressed thinking about all the people that I know."

Pilgrims travel by horseback on the Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar trek. Amar Prakash

Chauhan, Panchal and Prakash said they were keen to make another trip.

Prakash vowed to return to Mount Kailash next year.

"Nepal is a beautiful country and so is the Tibet side. The journey is a big economic industry for both areas," Prakash said.

"The pilgrimage creates a lot of jobs, creates a lot of money flow within the economy and so I think it's important that, where possible, we should still support and go through this journey because we shouldn't let this devastation stop us [from visiting]."

Five New Zealanders remain missing following the deadly flash flood: Dejan Kuzmic, Shweta Mhatre, Mihir Patel, Kinnari Patel and Suhasini Reddy.

Three hundred and thirty foreign nationals have been rescued, according to an update from the Nepal Tourism Board early Tuesday morning.

No New Zealanders have been included in that number.

RNZ understands Mhatre was also part of the Isha Foundation's pilgrimage, and Sadhguru had previously said two New Zealanders were missing from his trekking group.

Meanwhile, Reddy's family has called on rescuers not to stop searching for the 44-year-old after conflicting reports of her status emerged online.

Reddy's brother, Rajeev, and his wife, Lauren, urged people to keep searching for survivors in a Facebook post.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said on Tuesday there had been no change to the status of the five missing New Zealanders.

"While various information is circulating online of those rescued and recovered, there is still no new verified information on the missing New Zealanders," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Melanesian countries to review Indonesia's status at MSG if no action on West Papua visit
World.content:
Melanesian countries are pushing Indonesia to facilitate a long-requested visit to West Papua by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights or have its membership in their regional bloc reviewed.

A request for the visit was made by Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) countries back in 2019, but it has still not gone ahead, despite ongoing human rights violations in Indonesian-ruled Papua region, known internationally as West Papua.

Frustration has built up among the Melanesian countries in the intervening years that Jakarta has not yet allowed the visit to take place.

Now the members of the Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) say that if a visit by the Commissioner's office is not facilitated by Indonesia in order for a report on human rights issues in West Papua to be produced by their next summit in 2027, then Indonesia's associate member status in the MSG will be reviewed.

The full members of the MSG are: Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia's FLNKS Kanak Movement. The United Liberation Movement for West Papua (ULMWP) has observer status at the MSG, and Indonesia has associate member status.

The West Papua delegation flying the Morning Star flag at the opening of the 7th Melanesian Arts & Culture Festival in Port Vila on 19 July 2023. Twitter.com / @MSG Secretariat

The MSG has issued a statement from the current PIF leaders summit in Palau, saying Melanesian leaders "urged continued engagement with Indonesia to facilitate access by the end of Indonesia's term as President of the Human Rights Council on 31 December 2026".

MSG members requested the bloc's current chair, Fiji, to write to Indonesia to allow the visit of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to West Papua to produce a report on human rights issues in Papua, and to have the report delivered for consideration at the next MSG summit in 2027.

Leaders "affirmed that if these actions are not undertaken the Associate Member status shall be reviewed accordingly at the next MSG Summit in 2027".

They also requested MSG member country embassies in Jakarta to "support appropriate follow-up and engagement on this matter".

Furthermore, the members are considering a proposal for MSG leaders to meet Indonesia's president Prabowo Subianto on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York last this month.

He said the pilgrimage was very tough, and he was asked by his tour operator to train in advance.

"The parikrama (clockwise circumambulation) around Mount Kailash is a tough hike and takes three days to complete," he said.

The walk enables pilgrims to see the mountain from all sides - north, south, east and west.

Panchal said members of the group had to take medicine because of the high altitude.

"Every 20 minutes we had an alarm set just for drinking water," he said.

Panchal said the third day of the trek was the toughest.

There were horses and porters to help pilgrims carry their luggage and provide a ride if anyone needed one, he said.

Panchal said the high altitude, lack of oxygen and tough terrain combined to make the pilgrimage physically demanding.

"When we reached Dolma La Pass, we were more than 5600 metres above sea level," he said.

"If you go up [another] 3000 metres above sea level, you'll be on top of Everest and so you can imagine how tough it must be."

Panchal said the climb down from the Himalayan plateau was equally treacherous, requiring hikers to navigate steep seven-kilometre drop.

He said most pilgrims crossed into Nepal through Gyirong Port because it was the shortest way back.

Panchal said he tried to get in touch with a few people he met during the trip but had been unable to do so.

"We have been trying to reach them," he said. "It's all washed out actually and very sad.

"Since the disaster, I'm really disturbed and a bit stressed thinking about all the people that I know."

Pilgrims travel by horseback on the Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar trek. Amar Prakash

Chauhan, Panchal and Prakash said they were keen to make another trip.

Prakash vowed to return to Mount Kailash next year.

"Nepal is a beautiful country and so is the Tibet side. The journey is a big economic industry for both areas," Prakash said.

"The pilgrimage creates a lot of jobs, creates a lot of money flow within the economy and so I think it's important that, where possible, we should still support and go through this journey because we shouldn't let this devastation stop us [from visiting]."

Five New Zealanders remain missing following the deadly flash flood: Dejan Kuzmic, Shweta Mhatre, Mihir Patel, Kinnari Patel and Suhasini Reddy.

Three hundred and thirty foreign nationals have been rescued, according to an update from the Nepal Tourism Board early Tuesday morning.

No New Zealanders have been included in that number.

RNZ understands Mhatre was also part of the Isha Foundation's pilgrimage, and Sadhguru had previously said two New Zealanders were missing from his trekking group.

Meanwhile, Reddy's family has called on rescuers not to stop searching for the 44-year-old after conflicting reports of her status emerged online.

Reddy's brother, Rajeev, and his wife, Lauren, urged people to keep searching for survivors in a Facebook post.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said on Tuesday there had been no change to the status of the five missing New Zealanders.

"While various information is circulating online of those rescued and recovered, there is still no new verified information on the missing New Zealanders," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Should outside nations be allowed at the Pacific Forum summit?
World.content:
RNZ's Teuila Fuatai in Koror, Palau

The Solomon Islands is asking its fellow Pacific Island Forum (PIF) members to reconsider the presence of dialogue partners at the regional body's annual leaders meeting, RNZ Pacific understands.

The issue was raised at a closed meeting of the PIF on Wednesday morning in Palau, with the Solomon Islands asking members to consider whether the leaders meeting should be separate from the dialogue partners' process, RNZ Pacific understands.

The presence of partners at the annual leaders' meeting has been a contentious issue over the past few years.

Each year, a partners dialogue meeting is held as part of the leaders' meeting week. In total, 21 countries are PIF dialogue partners, with key regional players like the United States, China, Japan and France among them. Taiwan, which also has a delegation in Koror, is a development partner.

However, last year, then-host Solomon Islands banned partners from attending and deferred the dialogue partner meeting to Palau. It was held on Tuesday in Koror.

As interest in the region has grown, the presence of partner delegations, as well as NGOs and observers has increased substantially. The current leaders' meeting was expected to bring 2000 people to Palau.

While interest and investment in the region are welcomed by members, the sheer number of people, countries and organisations now attending the leaders' week has resulted in an extensive list of bilateral meetings and sideline events that sit outside the official PIFs agenda.

Christopher Landau United States Deputy Secretary of State at the opening ceremony of 55 PIFLM in Koror, Palau. 31 August 2026. TMC Palau/Ohanna Rabo Galo

RNZ Pacific understands several delegations from Pacific nations have struggled to keep up with the demands of the week. It is understood that a separate partner process could offer more time for members to speak directly with one another and focus on the PIF agenda.

Despite that, support for the Solomon Islands proposal among the membership is unlikely to be clearcut. The Solomons' decision to stop partners' attending last year divided members.

New Zealand foreign minister Winston Peters made it clear at the time he believed partners needed to be at the leaders' meeting because of the investment role they played in the region - a sentiment he repeated this year. While Sāmoa, represented by previous prime minister Fiame Naomi Mata'afa, and Palau president Surangel Whipps Jnr supported the decision from then-Solomons Prime Minister Jeremiah Manele.

The Solomons proposal also comes as the 18 PIF members have been deliberating on a new partnership structure. The proposed structure would divide partners into two tiers, with the top tier having greater access to member states.

With large delegations from China, the US and Taiwan present, geopolitical competition around the PIF has dominated headlines.

The absences of six leaders, including Solomons Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, has also been reported extensively. Wale had to return home after landing in Koror due to a motion of no confidence in his leadership.

World.title: Maori, Pacific galleries at Auckland Museum to stay shut until 2029
World.content:
Auckland Museum hopes to be free of asbestos by the middle of next year, but the still-closed Māori and Pacific galleries won't reopen until the end of 2029 - four years after the toxic dust was found.

Asbestos was discovered in the Grand Foyer and the adjacent Māori Court and Pacific galleries in May 2025.

The foyer reopened five months later, but work on the other wings continues.

"It is a tricky substance, and we've had some changes of the regulations come upon us as well which has actually lengthened the process, annoyingly," chief executive David Reeves said.

"Under the regulations, we have to assume everything has [been contaminated], each individual item has to go through a cleaning process, and then it goes through an air-disturbance test, and it individually gets certificated as being asbestos free, even though almost all of them were asbestos free in the first place."

Auckland Museum. Auckland Museum

He said roughly 2100 of the wings' 3000 artifacts had been cleaned.

Now staff were dismantling the Māori Court's pataka, a traditional storehouse carved from totara.

"As each of the gallery spaces is cleared, then the building team move in behind," he said.

"We have to get things like the pataka out of there because it's in the way of the scaffolding that has to go up into the roof, so the team over the last couple of weeks have begun dismantling the pataka which is a huge job."

Some exhibits have been cleaned and are back on display. RNZ/ Marika Khabazi

After more than a year without a comprehensive Māori exhibit, Reeves said the museum felt like it needed to fill the void.

Last week it opened Te Ripo o te Moana, a three-year exhibition featuring many of the same objects, now asbestos-free.

"We've got a number of taonga that have come up out of the Māori Court, so there'll be some familiar things people know, as well as some things that haven't been displayed for a very, very long time," Reeves said.

"The Māori collections are the pre-eminent collections of the museum, so we've been really feeling the loss. Not having a focused gallery has been a real loss, so it's great to have it back."

He said the decision was made to open a medium-term gallery as it became clear the asbestos remediation would drag on.

"As soon as the asbestos is all cleared - and we think that'll be in around June next year - we need to start work on the complete renewal of the infrastructure on the ground floor there, so replacing air conditioning systems, lighting, wiring, rearranging some of the flooring and display cases, and then the team will be putting in a brand new and completely refreshed visitor experience as well," he said.

"That, realistically, is going to take up until the centenary of the building which is at the end of 2029. We really felt we couldn't just hold on without any sort of comprehensive Māori content for the visitors for that long."

To aid that work, Auckland Museum was seeking additional funding from either Auckland Council or the central government.

"Those conversations are ongoing, is probably the best I can say there... We are still in conversation, but thus far we're still having to fund it from a deficit and from deferring other projects," Reeves said.

Auckland Council's principal advisor for CCO governance and external partnerships, Trudi Fava, said future funding for the museum would be considered by councillors as part of the next long-term plan in 2027.

World.title: ‘Bigger than football’: Rabbitohs, Roosters to unite for Jai Arrow’s 100th NRL match
World.content:
A historic rivalry between the South Sydney Rabbitohs and Sydney Roosters will be briefly set aside on Friday, as Jai Arrow is honoured for his 100th NRL game.

Arrow, 31, retired from rugby league earlier this year - just two games shy of his hundredth match - as he battles motor neurone disease.

Following his diagnosis, the NRL approved a special one-off rule change that would allow Arrow to reach the milestone with his former club the Rabbitohs; being named as an additional player on the team list and interchange rotation.

The exemption saw Arrow lead the Rabbitohs onto the field at Cbus Super Stadium for his 99th game last weekend, arm-in-arm with teammate Cody Walker, and greeted by a standing ovation.

He was then taken off three seconds after kick-off against the Gold Coast Titans - despite jokingly trying to wave off the call from Rabbitohs co-captain Cameron Murray.

Arrow was then permitted to remain on the bench in his playing kit for the remainder of the match.

Prior to the game, footage from the changing sheds showed veteran coach Wayne Bennett helping Arrow pull up his socks on and lace his boots.

Bennett told Fox League Arrow was first on the team bus - "right up the front".

"I didn't have the heart to tell him that he's just running on, he's not staying on," he joked.

Roosters utility Connor Watson told NRL.com the emotional scenes showed "some things are bigger than football", and when they meet at Allianz on Saturday for Arrow's milestone 100th, everyone would be "there to celebrate with him".

"It's a privilege to be in that moment with him," Roosters prop Naufahu Whyte said.

"I know all us Roosters brothers support him."

Rabbitohs boss Blake Solly told NRL.com the club was grateful for the support from the Titans and the Roosters in accommodating the rule change for the final two games.

"For Jai to be able to add these games to his tally against his former club, and at a game which we believe will be close-to, if not sold-out at Allianz Stadium, will be a fitting tribute," he said.

Before medically retiring at the start of the year, Arrow played 178 NRL matches. His first-grade career started in 2016 with 24 games across two seasons for the Brisbane Broncos, followed by 56 games for the Gold Coast Titans, then finally 98 games for South Sydney from 2021 - 2025.

World.title: LA Clippers fined $40m over 'flagrant' rules breaches
World.content:
The NBA has imposed a sweeping punishment against the Los Angeles Clippers for violating salary cap circumvention rules, suspending owner Steve Ballmer for one year, fining the team $US30 million ($41.5 million) and forcing it to forfeit five draft picks.

Two-time NBA Finals MVP Kawhi Leonard was also hit with a $US700,000 ($977,000) penalty, president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank was banned for six months and team president of business operations Gillian Zucker was suspended for one year.

The league came down hard on the organisation on Wednesday after a nearly year-long investigation led by an outside law firm.

The Clippers had said multiple times that they had done nothing wrong and expected to be exonerated.

"I think that we're going to be in the clear," Leonard said in April, "so I'm not stressing it."

At the same time, Frank said: "If you know Steve and know Steve's integrity, you know there's nothing to it. We believe and we've very confident we're on the right side of this."

The team maintained that stance on Wednesday.

Steve Ballmer (left) will sit out the next 12 months as part of his punishment for the breaches. (Getty Images: Katelyn Mulcahy)

"We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence," the team said in a statement.

"What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner [Adam] Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure its fairness and accuracy."

The Clippers said they will "now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence. We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process."

The league said it and the players' union agreed to confirm the penalties as final and binding on all parties. It said the outside law firm continued to receive information involving the investigation, and the league "will consider further action as appropriate".

"I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct," Silver said in a statement.

"The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations."

Adam Silver says he is "deeply disappointed" in the Clippers' breaches. (Getty Images: Elsa)

The NBA began investigating in September 2025 whether a $28 million endorsement contract between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC — a company that filed for bankruptcy last year — broke league rules, following a report by journalist Pablo Torre.

Earlier this year, Aspiration co-founder Joseph Sanberg was sentenced to 14 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to defrauding investors and lenders of at least $248 million.

The Clippers released a letter from Ballmer's attorney David Kelley to Silver, in which he described the investigation as "a witch hunt" and the subsequent penalties as a "gross injustice".

Kelley accused Silver of not keeping his promises that the investigation would be governed by due process and fundamental fairness, as well as the burden being on the league to prove any violations through evidence.

"League counsel has acknowledged in our discussions that the league does not believe there was an agreement between the Clippers and Aspiration to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard. League counsel also agreed with the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and a federal judge that Mr. Ballmer was a victim of Joe Sanberg's fraud — not a participant," wrote Kelley, a partner in the firm O'Melveny and Myers.

"Mr Ballmer's reputation has been irreparably damaged as he now finds himself embroiled not only in this heavily biased investigation, but in civil litigation, the Aspiration bankruptcy proceeding, and more," Kelley wrote.

Kelley wrote that no league rule prohibits team personnel from making introductions to both sponsors and vendors in response to player requests.

"Retroactively punishing the Clippers for violating a rule that never existed is hardly consistent with due process," Kelley wrote.

The league said Ballmer knowingly sought to help Leonard obtain off-court income deals, approved a business deal that he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to enter into an endorsement contract with Leonard, and for failing to create conditions under which his team followed league rules.

"I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgement by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family," Leonard said in a statement issued through his new agent, Harrison Gaines.

The NBA said Leonard, through his former business manager and uncle Dennis Robertson, "violated the circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities, successfully obtaining those opportunities, and failing to reimburse payments by the Clippers for personal expenses."

"I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap," Leonard said in his statement.

The league said Ballmer was suspended for "knowingly seeking to help Mr Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities," among other issues.

Kawhi Leonard is set to return to Toronto for the upcoming season. (Getty Images: Patrick McDermott)

Leonard's trade to the Toronto Raptors has been on hold pending the outcome of the investigation. The Raptors had said they still want Leonard, and he apparently is just as eager to return to the team where he won an NBA title and was Finals MVP in 2019.

"As I return to Toronto, I am focused on what I can control, closing this chapter, and moving forward with a clean slate," Leonard said in his statement.

The Clippers and their personnel will be under a compliance and monitoring program by the league for five years and Robertson was banned from doing business with NBA teams for five years.

The league penalised Frank for his involvement with the impermissible endorsement arrangements and for approving impermissible expenses incurred by Leonard and his family.

Zucker was banned for being primarily and directly culpable for the illegal endorsement arrangements and for lying to investigators. Both will lose their salaries during their bans.

It is not the first time the Clippers have run afoul of NBA rules under Ballmer, who bought the team for $2 billion in August 2014.

They were fined $250,000 a year later for violating rules against offering unauthorised business or investment opportunities to players during their courting of free agent DeAndre Jordan. A presentation to him improperly included a $200,000-per-year deal with luxury car maker Lexus.

Ballmer, 70, was CEO of Microsoft from 2000 to 2014.

World.title: Prime-time era Magbegor leads Opals' World Cup charge
World.content:
The Opals have produced a consistent pipeline of global superstars throughout their silverware-packed history, an impressive feat in one of the world's most competitive sports.

In the 2026 incarnation of the Opals, Ezi Magbegor, 27, carries that tag.

After bursting onto the international stage as a highly promising 18-year-old, she is now a defensive linchpin, a leader, and the type of player whose influence will likely dictate how far the Opals go at the Women's Basketball World Cup.

And she is in her prime-time era.

Magbegor was part of the team that won bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

Throwing a fit

Magbegor entered this WNBA season as a hot commodity — becoming the equal highest paid Australian player in the league, and one of the richest female Australian athletes overall.

But an Achilles injury, then broken nose, wiped her out for most of the season, delivering a harsh reality check for the Seattle Storm forward-centre.

Magbegor has been wearing a mask for the Seattle Storm, since returning from a broken nose. (Getty Images: Olivia Vanni)

"I've been so blessed to not have many injuries at all in my first seven years of my W season," she told ABC Sport.

"You just realise injuries are a part of sport and it's about how you reset your mind and bounce back and prepare for the next thing.

"And so, yes, I was injured, but I just used it as a great opportunity to work on my body and put myself in the best position to be ready."

It also gave her a chance to spend some time on her 'tunnel fits', aka the casual outfits that players wear when arriving at arenas, which have become a core part of the WNBA.

"This year I really wanted to lean into my Nigerian culture and heritage, and my mum's been begging me to wear traditional clothing," she said.

"My favourite was definitely my traditional attire. My parents had bought the material from Nigeria and then one of our friends had sewn it together in Melbourne.

Loading Instagram content

"I worry about being too dressed up sometimes, but my mum's like, yeah, it's not enough, nothing's too dressed up. So, it was really fun to be able to share that with her."

She traded high fashion for a protective face mask when she returned to the court for the Storm in late July, adding to her already intimidating aura as one of the league's best shot blockers.

And while her domestic season has been stunted, she is coming back to full fitness and form just in time for the World Cup, tipping-off in Berlin this weekend.

Opals going big

Magbegor was part of the team that won World Cup silver in 2018, bronze at home in Sydney in 2022, and bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

Magbegor is known as an elite rim defender and shot blocker. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

There has been substantial turnover since Paris with the emotional core of the team including Tess Madgen, Lauren Jackson, Cayla George, and Marianna Tolo, all missing.

And with captain and point guard Sami Whitcomb belatedly ruled out of this World Cup, the side's star power now largely shines around Magbegor and Alanna Smith.

"It's expected for me to pass on the cultural values and expectations onto the next group coming up," Magbegor said.

"But for me it's just about leading by example, touching base with my teammates, making sure that I'm being the best professional, best teammate, best person I can be come tournament play, and in the lead up as well.

"I've been in the Opals team and squad for a while now and I want to have an impact for the team in any way I can, whether that's on the floor, off the floor.

"But definitely looking to play my best basketball for the group and hopefully come away with the medal."

Smith, who was last year named WNBA defensive player of the year, had her own injury interrupted start to the season.

Alongside Magbegor, Dallas Wings player Alanna Smith is regarded as one of the Opals' best players. (Getty Images: Stacy Revere)

Coach Sandy Brondello is confident Magbegor and Smith are recovered and ready to lead Australia's charge in Berlin.

"They can hold themselves with any of the best post players in the world here. And that's what we're going to need from them without putting pressure," Brondello told ABC Sport.

"I've coached [Ezi] since she was 18. And this is her time, back healthy.

"The best is to come to her, but I'm just excited for her to get out, her athleticism, her rim protection. But now she's a three-level scorer, so that's a great asset.

"And Alanna was our best player in Paris, most consistent player over the whole tournament.

"And it's good to see her getting some rhythm now and getting that confidence back because we need them. We have to lean into them. They're our two best bigs."

Chasing the elusive gold

The Opals enter the World Cup ranked third. The Olympic bronze was followed by a breakthrough Asia Cup win last year, without any WNBA players, and they had a limited preparation for this tournament.

Coach Sandy Brondello says the team's culture is key to its continued success over many years. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

"The results that we've had, it shows that the continuity that we've developed over many years, not just one year, is showing because our chemistry is strong, our culture is strong," Brondello said.

"Everyone's accepting their roles and coming in and playing at a high level. And that's the beauty of Australian teams that we have."

Culture is always the constant with the Opals and what they attribute their sustained performance over decades to.

"It really just comes down our sisterhood and how gritty and tough we are and how we play together and we'll play whatever role to help us to have great success," Brondello said.

"These players, they've become family.

"Playing at the highest level just means everyone has to buy into the values for the success of the program. And there's no one player bigger than the program."

While the Opals are perennial podium finishers at major tournaments, gold has eluded them since their one and only world title in 2006.

Players from the 2006 World Champion Opals met with the current squad during a series in Melbourne in July. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"It's just something that comes with being an Opal, that legacy piece and recognising and acknowledging who put us in this position and who started that legacy," Magbegor said.

"Medals is quite synonymous with Opals, and we've won in the past and want to continue to win."

As had been the case for decades, the world number one USA is a seemingly immovable object from the top step of the podium, although was pushed all the way by France in the gold medal match at the Paris Olympics.

"[The USA are] the best of the best and they're great, but they've got the best talent," Brondello said.

"But we've got a talented group, we've built some more chemistry over the years, and that's what we have to lean into."

Growing the game

Half the Opals squad plays in the WNBA, the rest are in the local WNBL, and both leagues have experienced significant changes in the past year.

Zitina Aokuso is one of the local WNBL players in this World Cup squad. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

After drawn out, often bitter negotiations, the WNBA and players' association finally signed a new collective bargaining agreement which saw player salaries skyrocket.

Magbegor went from earning $US186,000 ($260,000) a year to $US1.25 million, a figure matched by Smith at the Dallas Wings, and significantly larger than the base salaries of other leading Australian female athletes in team sports, including the top Matildas and cricketers.

"I think that's just a testament to people that came before us and really pushing for the growth of women's basketball in particular, but just women's sports in general," Magbegor said.

"And I think now is a greater time than ever to push forward, invest in women's sports and just advocate for ourselves, but each other as well."

The WNBL has been making its own moves on a much smaller scale, including a new ownership group taking over last year.

And after starting her career there, Magbegor hopes it too can thrive.

"That's what is probably lacking right now, exposure, and knowing that it's going to pay off in the long run," she said.

"People need to see the product and see the game and realise that women's basketball, basketball is incredible.

"We have great athletes, especially coming up, and I think it's just a matter of investing, a matter of showing up and a matter of supporting."

World.title: More Aussies tumble as de Minaur finally concludes first round match
World.content:
Taylah Preston's US Open adventure has ended abruptly in the second round.

The first Australian through to round two was the first to exit following a 6-1, 6-1 loss to big-hitting American Taylor Townsend.

The 20-year-old wildcard was eliminated in just 48 minutes.

Preston was one of five Australians scheduled for day-four action at Flushing Meadows.

Australian women's number one Daria Kasatkina was also removed from the draw, but not before offering more considerable resistance against Spaniard Paula Badosa.

The pair resumed their stop-start affair that was halted on Tuesday morning (AEST) in sensational fashion.

After first being forced off court because of rain early in the second set while trailing Badosa 6-1, 1-2, Kasatkina was delighted when officials called it a night immediately after she saved a third match point.

Badosa was furious and had to return 15 hours later trying to serve out the contest at 5-4 and deuce in the second set.

Kasatkina saved her first two match points in an epic 22-point game serving at 3-5 in the second set, before fighting off another six more.

Kasatkina also conjured two break point chances to level up at 5-5 before Badosa, a one-time world number two, finally closed out the contest to book a second-round date with 2023 champion Coco Gauff.

Maya Joint is scheduled to take on ninth seed Elina Svitolina this morning, hoping to reach the third round in New York for a third straight year.

Meanwhile Kim Birrell is up against Russian Ekaterina Alexandrova believing she can also topple the Russian 18th seed after taking down world number five and 2024 US Open finalist Jessica Pegula at the French Open.

De Minaur through after delay

New York's lousy weather dealt Alex de Minaur's US Open title hopes another setback with the top-ranked Australian's first-round clash delayed further by rain.

Former champion Daniil Medvedev and American home hope Alex Michelsen were already safely through to round three before de Minaur even made it on court for his tournament opener.

When he finally opened his campaign on day four, de Minaur looked intent on making up for lost time, racing to a 6-2, 4-2 lead over Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri in just 49 minutes.

Then the heavens opened again, forcing de Minaur scampering back to the locker room.

He eventually went on to win 6-2, 6-2, 6-4.
